# TO THE MOST DISTINGUISHED

->Philip Imsser, Mathematician, and<-
->most learned in various matters, Gualtherus<-
->H. Ryff of Strasbourg<-
->sends many greetings.<- <note>original: "S. D. P.", abbreviation for *Salutem Dicit Plurimam*</note>

UNLESS I WERE CERTAIN of your most generous character and your most refined nature, I would not have undertaken this task of writing to you recently, and would instead have persisted in my long-standing silence. However, because I have convinced myself—not so much by the talk of others as by my own judgment—that you are the kind of man who never rejects those devoted to you, I wanted these short lines, though late, to be witnesses of my affection for you. Although I do not entirely excuse myself from the laziness or the rudeness of my past silence, I hope nonetheless that you will look favorably upon my continued devotion to you. You desire then, most learned Philip, to be written to more frequently, and to be made aware of those things which the storehouse of my mind produces daily. I will therefore now reveal to you a brief contemplation <note>original: "contemplatiunculam"</note> into which I once fell. I have long known that the ancient philosophers, those most eager students of nature, scrutinized these things with frequent investigation and no small amount of wonder. They believed that all things seen beneath the Moon <note>The "sublunary" sphere, which in ancient science referred to the Earth and its atmosphere where things are subject to change and decay.</note> are composed of <term>matter</term><note>Latin: *materia*. In the philosophy of the time, this refers to the raw "stuff" of the universe.</note> and <term>form</term><note>Latin: *forma*. This refers to the organizing principle or essence that makes a thing what it is.</note>...

<summary>In this dedicatory preface, the author Walther Ryff apologizes to the mathematician Philip Imsser for his long silence and begins a philosophical discussion on the Aristotelian principles of matter and form.</summary>
<keywords>Walther Ryff, Philip Imsser, Strasbourg, dedication, natural philosophy, Aristotelianism, matter and form, sublunary sphere</keywords>

<meta>The previous page ended with the description of "matter and form" as the organizing principles of the universe. This page continues the sentence, defining how these two components interact to create physical reality.</meta>

mass, and established two things: **matter** and **form**, as the total and complete substance of any thing. Yet matter and form together fulfill the <term>quinary</term><note>Latin: *quinarius*, the number five. Ryff is explaining how the four physical elements plus one spiritual form equal five.</note>. For matter is a certain quaternity, a combination of the four Elements (the simplest bodies of the world). **Form**, however, is a unity which imposes peace upon the four Elements and governs the quaternity of things. Therefore, the quinary is the measure and number of the composition of all sensible substances. For whatever is in any mixture, besides its form, belongs to the nature of one of the Elements; but no one will deny that form is not elementary in nature, but rather imitates a celestial nature.

Thus it happens that every sensible creature is forged from the quinary—that is, composed of five essences. For the creature is similar to the greater and visible world <note>The "macrocosm," or the universe at large.</note>, which consists of five greatest and visible bodies: **Earth, Water, Air, Fire,** and **Heaven**. These act as matter and form, for the form of the world is indeed changeable and fluid. 

But the unity of Heaven is fixed and stable, being the very form of the world; this is surely our celestial <term>fifth essence</term><note>Latin: *quinta essentia*, the origin of the word "quintessence." In alchemy, this was a purified spirit or medicine that contained the life-force of a substance.</note>. This quintessence is what remains from every sensible substance as a more secret, principal, and incorruptible essence of the four primary elementary substances. It is suited for various human uses—a true sanctuary of medical science. Indeed, its virtue extends so widely and its powers are so effective that some have held the opinion that every single disease (at least those that can be cured) might be rightly cured by this alone,

# **RAYMOND LULL OF MAJORCA**,
## most acute philosopher and most celebrated physician,
### *Preface to the first book on the secrets of nature, or the Fifth Essence.*

The Book of the SECRETS OF NATURE, or of the fifth essence <note>Latin: *quinta essentia*. In medieval science, this was a "fifth element"—distinct from earth, water, air, and fire—thought to be the pure substance of the stars and the key to universal medicine.</note>, which teaches its extraction and application to human bodies, for the performing of wonderful and almost divine works. Through this, the philosophical path of the entire medical art is to be completed; while this path is hidden, the true medicine is also hidden, and even the transformation <term>transmutation: the alchemical process of changing one substance, usually a base metal, into another, like gold</term> of metals is blocked. But when these secrets are unlocked, whatever belongs to them is revealed. This book is indeed the image <note>original: *imago*, here used in the sense of a summary or a representative model.</note> of all books treating these matters, which glorious God has shown to us, so that He might preserve our body from corruption as much as is naturally possible, until the end ordained for us by God; and also so that even imperfect metals themselves may be perfected and transformed into one another. For truly it is my desire that the practitioners <note>original: *artistae*, meaning those who practice the "Great Art" of alchemy or medicine.</note> of this art, contemplating God, might rather understand, remember, and love God through good works—by helping the poor, widows, and orphans in distress without demanding a high price, and by doing divine works of this kind. Let them not be like the one who hid the lord’s talent and did not put it to the use committed to him, as Matthew writes in chapter 25 <note>A reference to the Biblical Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30), where a servant is punished for burying his master's money rather than using it fruitfully.</note>. Trusting, moreover, in Him who said through Moses: "I will be in your mouth, and I will teach you what you shall speak," <note>Exodus 4:12</note> we have decided that this most secret of secrets, this mystery of mysteries <note>original: *archanorum archanum*. An "arcanum" refers to a deep, hidden secret of nature known only to initiates.</note>, must be declared to you, with divine power inspiring us and His infinite goodness helping us, while making a brief mention of the principles and rules, and of the course of nature itself.

<summary>In this preface, Raymond Lull introduces the "Fifth Essence" as a divine tool for both healing the human body and perfecting metals. He frames the pursuit of alchemical knowledge as a religious duty, urging practitioners to use their secrets for charitable works rather than greed.</summary>
<keywords>Raymond Lull, Fifth Essence, alchemy, medical ethics, transmutation of metals, Parable of the Talents, divine inspiration, secrets of nature</keywords>

<meta>This page transitions from the general introductory praise of the previous page into the technical opening of the treatise. Here, Raymond Lull (or the author attributed as Lull) begins Book One by defining the foundational "principles" required for the alchemical and medical arts.</meta>

# ON THE FIFTH ESSENCE,
# OR THE SECRETS OF NATURE,
# by Raymond Lull, the most
# acute philosopher.

## BOOK ONE

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'I' within a rectangular woodcut border. The letter is flanked by two winged or naked infant figures (putti) standing on stylized clouds or rocky pedestals, supporting the vertical stem of the letter.</image-desc>

NOW INDEED, SO THAT WE MAY begin the matter itself suitably, we say that there are principally three principles, through the knowledge of which the practitioner <note>original: *artista*; in this context, it refers to the "artist" or practitioner of the Great Art of alchemy and medicine.</note> of this art operates. According to his own judgment, whether in medicine or in the alchemy of metals and the making of stones <note>original: *lapidifica*; this refers to the creation of the "Philosopher’s Stone," the goal of alchemy.</note>, he achieves that which he intends, or that which nature has hidden.

For the first principle is matter, which the practitioner of this work must understand, and through which the medicine or the stone receives its substantial being. For if the matter is such as nature requires, it will be of a receptive form, which can by no means be stripped away through a defect of impression <note>The "impression" refers to the way a "form" or soul-like quality is fixed onto raw matter.</note>, since a power <note>original: *uirtus*; the inherent active quality or "virtue" of a substance.</note> operates there. This power is the principal medium <term>medium: an intermediary substance or agent that connects two different things</term> between the said matter and the other essences, as we shall explain to you throughout the course of this book.

The second principle is truly very simple in comparison to the first, since it is the intermediary for the first, and it is through this second principle that the first must be immediately perfected.

<sig>A iiij</sig>

<summary>Raymond Lull begins his treatise by identifying the foundational principles of alchemy and medicine, focusing on the necessity of understanding "matter" and the "virtue" that allows it to be perfected into a higher state.</summary>
<keywords>Raymond Lull, Fifth Essence, alchemy, first principle, matter, Philosopher's Stone, virtue, medical art</keywords>

-># ON THE FIFTH ESSENCE<-

<meta>catchword: pij, ma= (Note: These characters at the bottom of the page indicate the first syllables of the next page: "principij, materia".)</meta>

The third principle belongs to the **fifth essence** <note>The "fifth essence" or *quintessence* was believed to be a pure, incorruptible substance distinct from the four earthly elements of earth, air, fire, and water.</note>, upon which seven virtues depend—both in their operation and their ability to give "form" <term>informatiue: the power to give a specific "form" or identity to matter</term>. These work through five essences in the lower material world, acting as intermediaries. For the first principle—or the matter of the first principle—consists of **common mercury** <note>original: *Mercurius uulgaris*; in alchemy, this refers to the metallic element mercury, but also the philosophical principle of fluidity and volatility.</note> along with all its alterable metals, during that process of **whitening** <note>original: *dealbatione*; a crucial stage in the alchemical "Great Work" where impurities are cleansed, turning the material white.</note> which we shall reveal in the third section.

Furthermore, the second principle (or the source of that matter) consists of **subtle waters** <note>original: *limphæ subtiles*; refers to refined, clear liquid extracts or distillates.</note> in which the impurities <note>original: *limositates*; literally "muddiness" or dregs</note> of the first principle are dissolved. This results in a moderate substance and a subtle matter in which the **mineral virtues** <note>The inherent active powers or "spirit" within minerals.</note> truly reside. Indeed, the matter of the third principle is highly essential to the existing virtues of the fixed and wandering stars <note>The "non-fixed" stars are the planets.</note> and their astrological alignments. This essence is infused through daily celestial influences into matter that has been prepared by the art of the second principle; this power rests directly within the mineral virtue found in plants and animals as much as in metals.

The second principle, therefore, acts as the cause and the suitable receptacle for the third, and for all its virtues descending from heaven. These celestial virtues provide the perfection and the "form" <term>form: the guiding blueprint or vital spark that gives a substance its specific properties and life</term> of every generated thing, as is clearly seen through these inherent principles. That which is generated materially from the first principle is the source of the **mineral virtue**, which is the **elemental fifth essence**. This is a simple matter, and it is truly perfected when it receives its "form" through the **celestial fifth essence**, which flows into it and leaves its mark. Thus, this "middle virtue"—full of potential and sharp in its power—is perfected artificially through a material reflux, along with the virtues of the first principle...

<summary>This page defines the three principles of alchemy, explaining how common mercury and "subtle waters" act as vessels for celestial influences from the stars to create the Fifth Essence. It establishes a hierarchy where heavenly "forms" descend into earthly matter to give it its specific medicinal and transformative powers.</summary>

<keywords>Fifth Essence, common mercury, whitening, mineral virtue, celestial influence, elemental quintessence, alchemical principles, distillation, astrology in alchemy</keywords>

### BOOK ONE

A v

...principle, <note>The text begins with "pij," completing the word "principij" (principle) from the catchword on the previous page.</note> it places the matter into a perfected state of being through an intermediary **mineral virtue** <term>uirtus mineralis: the inherent active power or "spirit" within the earth that drives the growth and transformation of minerals</term>. This power is common to stones, medicines, and metals alike, as we have discussed at length in our *Testament* <note>original: *testamento*; likely referring to the *Testamentum*, a major work of alchemy attributed to Ramon Llull</note>, in a general way in the first part.

We report to you, <gloss>that</gloss> since this mineral virtue is common to stones, metals, and plants, every difference that one receives from another is driven by the **giving of form** <term>informatione: in medieval philosophy, "informing" matter meant giving it its specific identity or essence</term>. This "informing" is administered in various ways, for the said virtue requires one type of formation in the creation of metals, or in their generation and their transmutation into **elixir**. This transmutation and forming is achieved through the governance of **external heat**, which moves the formative mineral virtue toward its goal, following the known intention of the **natural practitioner** <note>original: *operarij naturalis*; the alchemist who works in harmony with nature's laws</note>, as we declared in the *Testament*, and as will be explained below in the third section.

Furthermore, it is our intention to briefly discuss the *Testimony* and the *Codicil* <note>Referring to the *Testificatio* and the *Codicillus*, two other influential alchemical treatises</note>, as we were requested to do so by the illustrious **King Robert** <note>Robert of Anjou, King of Naples (reigned 1309–1343), a patron often associated with alchemical scholarship</note>. Moreover, the other method of formation—which the said mineral virtue requires for the purpose of transmuting the matter of metals into **precious stones**—is performed with a slower external heat and a more gradual movement. This is formed as much by the surrounding heat as by the common heat of things joined or distinct, just as was explained in our *Lapidary* <note>A "Lapidary" is a book describing the medical and magical properties of stones</note>.

Likewise, the other kind of formation, which the said virtue requires for the composition of **medicine**, is performed with a greater heat and a sudden, rapid motion.

<summary>This page defines "mineral virtue" as the universal force behind the creation of metals, gems, and medicines, explaining that the alchemist differentiates these products by varying the intensity and speed of external heat. It also mentions the author's patronage by King Robert of Naples and references several of his other famous alchemical treatises.</summary>

<keywords>mineral virtue, transmutation, elixir, external heat, King Robert, Testamentum, precious stones, alchemical medicine, information of matter</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "three principles" and the "mineral virtue" from the previous page. # ON THE FIFTH ESSENCE

Furthermore, you must not be ignorant of the **power** <term>uirtus: the inherent active strength or spiritual essence of a substance</term> that is produced by the joining of the three stated principles and their derivation. The knowledge of this power is gained through its primary effect, which arises from distinct quantities and qualities, and even from the movement of the heavens and stars, and from things that can be generated and destroyed—those things which are moved and **given form** <gloss>informed</gloss> by it.

Truly, we do not say that it is the task of the practitioner to work with astrological figures or images of the sky through a technical knowledge of their movements, as many philosophers claim. Instead, it is enough to have knowledge of the influence of **celestial heat**, which is shaped by the configuration of the sky and stars. By reason of these configurations, powers are poured into suitably prepared matter.

The matter receives these powers through the natural industry of the practitioner, along with the **dissolution** <term>resolutione: the process of breaking a substance down into its primary components or "resolving" them into a liquid state</term> which is likewise performed by the art of nature. This process changes hard matter back to its natural beginning so that, in the end, it is fit for generation—ready to receive the powers infused into the waters of strong mineral virtues, just as the matter of an embryo takes and receives its formative power.

And at this stage, the philosophers were misled—to their own discredit—even though they understood how celestial power is common to all nature made of the elements. Because of its great nobility, this power is always receiving its definition; in mixed things, it is influenced as much by art as by nature. Furthermore, every practitioner should note that nature cannot work except through a succession of minute moments, nor can it receive any **virtues** <term>uirtutes: the inherent active powers or spiritual essences of a substance</term> except through the succession of its own operation. These things cannot happen all at once, nor can the **constellations** <term>constellationes: specific alignments of planets and stars believed to transmit celestial influence</term> endure a stay in any specific temporal point of a certain virtue, for it is immediately changed, even if it were possible to remain still. Indeed, the time of a constellation is so brief, by reason of the revolution of the heavenly spheres, that it passes from one virtue into another almost before it begins. 

Why then—not without knowledge of their movements in quality and quantity, but rather through art—do we come to the aid of the work to capture and "hunt" these aforementioned celestial virtues? Since these virtues are common to all lower things on Earth, we also enclose them in "pregnant" waters derived from mineral virtues for this purpose: so that in a short time we might manifest many virtues and impress them into the work, whether it be an **elixir** <term>elyxir: a potent alchemical preparation intended to transform or heal</term>, a **human medicine**, or a **precious stone** <note>referring to the Philosopher's Stone</note> as it reaches its completion.

By these powers, the empty vessel is filled, and they enter through a subtle, penetrating influence into other powers within the **spiritual matter** <note>matter that has been refined and "exalted" to a quasi-spiritual state</note> which has been refined into simplicity by the ingenuity of nature and the **restorative art** <term>artis restaurativæ: the practice of returning matter to its pristine, uncorrupted state</term>.

# CONCERNING THE QUINTESSENCE

Through this subtlety, they receive a general virtue and a commonality within the lower nature; they flow everywhere and into specific matter. At that point, they receive a fixed determination through the method of consideration, which is taken from material things; these materials retain those virtues just as the spirit retains the soul. And then, they follow the virtue of their own kind, according to the "merit" <note>original: "meritum," referring to the specific quality or suitability of the receiving material</note> of the matter into which they are infused.

# ON THE FIFTH ESSENCE

...[con]trariety and corruption; but no such medicine has been revealed to many in which there is such a great perfection of the "longing for being" <note>original: "appetitus ad esse." In scholastic philosophy, this refers to the inherent tendency of a thing to maintain its existence and resist decay.</note> that, however much it produces a miraculous and wonderful effect in human bodies, it is regarded almost as a miracle. But no medicine in this world can achieve this except our celestial, animal, and vegetable menstruum <term>menstruum: not referring to the modern biological term, but to a "universal solvent" used in alchemy to extract the essential properties of a substance</term>, which is called the **Fifth Essence**. For it preserves flesh from corruption, strengthens the elemental nature, and through it, former youth is restored. It vivifies the spirit, digests what is raw, hardens the porous, softens the hardened, fattens the thin, thins the fat, cools the inflamed, warms the chilled, dries the moist, and moistens the dry. 

In every way, one and the same thing is capable of contrary operations; only the action of the single thing is diversified according to the nature of the recipient. This is just like the **heat of the sun** <note>original: "calor solis." A common medieval analogy used to explain how a single divine or natural cause can produce different results depending on the material it acts upon.</note>, which has contrary operations because it dries clay and melts wax. Yet the action of the sun is one in itself, nor is it internally conflicted.

Likewise, it was stated above that this spirit, elevated in subtle matter, has a longing for this or that temperament <term>complexio: the specific balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that determines a person's health</term>, because the "First Matter" <term>prima materia: the fundamental, formless substance that alchemists believed could take on any shape or property</term> is asserted by the philosophers to be the very existence of things. For just as universal form has a longing for every specific form, so the **Fifth Essence** has a longing for any temperament. From this it is clearly evident that the Fifth Essence of things is said to be of that temperament to which it is joined; for example, if hot things are added to hot things, it becomes hot in the same degree—and even more strongly—because of the subtle matter in which its form and actions are elevated, through which it operates in this way...

### BOOK THE FIRST

...just like the **basilisk** and the lightning, of which we spoke above.

Indeed, some had said that this nature is neither hot, nor moist, nor cold, nor dry, because by its own nature it possesses harmony with all things. Those who have erred in this, however, we oppose with the following reasoning:

Everything that exists is either intellectual or sensual <note>original: "intellectuale, aut sensuale." In medieval philosophy, "intellectual" things belong to the realm of pure mind or spirit, while "sensual" things are those that can be perceived by the physical senses.</note>. Since in vegetable things there is no intellect, nor in minerals, it is therefore sensual. Now, everything sensual is composed of the four elements. And because it is composed of the four elements, it is necessary that in any given thing the elements exist in actuality <note>original: "sint actu." A Scholastic term meaning the elements are truly present and active, rather than just being there as a potential possibility.</note>. Otherwise, material things would not be composed of anything except the **accidents** <term>accidents: in Aristotelian philosophy, these are qualities (like color, smell, or temperature) that can change without changing the essential nature of the substance itself</term> of the elements. Thus, individual things would be mere accidents and not substances, or they would be composed of some substance other than the elements—which is impossible.

Furthermore, it would otherwise be possible for the action of some inseparable accident to exist without its proper subject in an individual—such as the heat of fire, which cannot exist in individuals without its own subject—and this is impossible. Therefore, the **Fifth Essence** is composed of the four elements, and within it are all the elements in actuality, with all their active powers.

But all things are gathered within it in such a subtle matter, and in such a subtle form, and so close to "simplicity" <note>In alchemy, "simplicity" refers to a state where a substance is so pure and unified that it acts as a single force rather than a clashing mixture of parts.</note> in a relative sense, just as in the eye of a **basilisk** <note>The basilisk was a mythical serpent whose gaze was said to be lethal; here, the author uses it as an example of a material object possessing intense, subtle powers.</note>. This is clear through experience in the curing of diseases, in the **transmutation** <term>transmutation: the alchemical process of changing one substance into another, most famously base metals into gold</term> of metals, and in the making of precious stones.

However, you should not understand us to mean this only regarding one specific...

# ON THE FIFTH ESSENCE

...to have said, but spoke in general terms regarding any of the **fifth essences** <note>original: "quinque essentijs." The author is distinguishing between the specific substance and the general category of refined essences.</note>, according to their manner and operation. This nature, indeed, the philosophers called **heaven** <note>original: "coelum." In alchemy, "Heaven" refers to the Fifth Essence because it is considered the most refined state of matter, mirroring the incorruptible and influential nature of the celestial spheres.</note>, because just as heaven influences us sometimes with heat, sometimes with moisture, and so forth, so the **Fifth Essence** acts within human bodies at the will of the artist <term>artist: in this context, the alchemist or physician preparing the medicine</term>. And some have called this nature, when condensed into one substance, a **menstruum** <term>menstruum: a technical term for a solvent or medium that can dissolve other substances; it was believed to "nourish" the reaction like a womb</term>, because it retains the properties of a solvent, as we shall discuss in the third book. For we know that this nature is hidden from the moderns, and they grasp absolutely nothing of its truth.

To this "heaven," we apply its "stars," which are **plants**, **stones**, and **metals**, so that they may grant life and health to everyone. **Hippocrates**, the prince of physicians, skillfully introduced this nature to medical men when he said in his *Prognostics*: "There is also something celestial <note>original: "quoddam coeleste." This refers to the famous *divinum* in Hippocratic writings—a factor in disease that comes from the environment or the divine, which a doctor must recognize.</note> which it behooves the physician himself to foresee. If his wisdom be so great, he is to be admired and regarded with wonder; for is it not his duty to entirely prevent the danger of things occurring, or to make the restoration of health more bearable with suitable assistance?"—as if to say, that it is so.

Certainly, Hippocrates spoke the truth, because future danger can be avoided by physical bodies, for the reason that this essence expels all **corruption** <note>original: "incorruptibilitatem." Likely a scribal error or specific usage for "factors of decay," as the text says these factors are what cause illness.</note> from which infirmity can arise, and it balances the unequal **humors** <term>humors: the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) which medieval medicine believed must be perfectly balanced for health</term>. ON THE QUINTESSENCE

## THE FOURTH CANON WHICH WILL TEACH
->*you to extract the Quintessence from all plants,*<-
->*fruits, and roots, and meats,*<-
->*eggs, and blood.*<-

There is another of the secrets of nature, that you may know how to draw the <term>Quintessence</term> <note>original: "Quintam essentiam"; the "fifth essence," or the purest, most potent medicinal core of a substance, separate from the four physical elements</note> from all plants, fruits, roots, the flesh of animals, eggs, birds, blood, and so forth. Take, therefore, whichever of these things you wish, and grind it very strongly in a mortar, and set it to undergo <term>putrefaction</term> <note>original: "putrefaciendum"; the process of breaking down organic matter through gentle heat and moisture, often lasting for forty days—a period known in alchemy as a "philosophical month"</note> in a vessel for forty days. Afterward, extract it and distill the liquid through an <term>alembic</term> <note>original: "alembicum"; a distillation apparatus consisting of a boiling vessel and a cap to collect and condense vapors</note> three or four times. In this way, you have created <term>burning water</term> <note>original: "aquam ardentem"; a high-proof alcohol or spirit produced from the organic matter</note>. Place this in any of the aforementioned vessels to <term>circulate</term> <note>original: "circulandum"; the alchemical process where a substance is heated so its vapors rise, condense, and fall back down repeatedly to refine its spirit</note> until you achieve the sign of the odor already mentioned <note>the sweet, heavenly fragrance that indicates the Quintessence is ready</note>. Alternatively, you may draw the <term>four elements</term> <note>original: "quattuor elementa"; earth, water, air, and fire</note> from any of these things, and place the "air" and "fire" <note>the most volatile and refined parts of the distillation</note> in the vessels already mentioned, and cause them to circulate until you achieve the predicted sign. Indeed, this is the greatest work performed in the <term>mastery of medicine</term> <note>original: "magisterio medicinæ"</note>.

All these Quintessences are extracted by any of these methods; they are a thousand times more effective than the medicines made from those materials before their extraction, so much so that the results are regarded as a miracle throughout the whole world. Indeed, we add nothing to these five essences <note>likely referring here to the "Quintessence" itself</note> during their extraction, except that through a new <term>artifice</term> <note>original: "artificium"; a technical skill or specialized alchemical method</note> we must remove the superfluous materials.

BOOK ONE

## FIFTH RULE, WHICH WILL TEACH how to extract the four elements <note>The four elements of the pre-modern world: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note> from all things, namely plants, animals, and metals.

We shall now reveal to you for a brief moment the secret—namely, how you can extract the elements from all things, including metals, plants, and animals. The general rule is that those plant materials which require grinding should be ground; and after they are crushed, let them be placed in a glass vessel in **horse manure** <term>fimo equino</term> <note>Horse manure was a standard alchemical heat source, providing a gentle, steady temperature for "putrefaction" or the breaking down of matter.</note> to rot for a month and a half. When that time has passed, place its head <note>The *alembic* or still-head.</note> upon the vessel, and distill the water through a **water bath** <term>balneum mariæ</term> <note>Literally "Mary's Bath," a double-boiler system used for gentle heating.</note>, which we described to you above with an illustration, until nothing more can be distilled by that method. At that time, remove the **cucurbit** <term>cucurbita</term> <note>A gourd-shaped glass distilling flask.</note> from the bath, and pour the water which you distilled back over the **dregs** <term>fæces</term> <note>The solid residue remaining at the bottom of the flask.</note>, and seal it well with a **seal** <term>sigillum</term> <note>An airtight closure, often made of wax or clay.</note>, and close it, and set it to rot for ten days. Afterward, take it out, and place the head of the **alembic** <term>alembicus</term> upon it, and distill by means of an **ash fire** <term>ignis cinerum</term> <note>Heating a vessel buried in hot ashes, which provides a higher temperature than a water bath.</note>, until no more can be distilled. Then you should know that you have extracted two elements separately. Now, therefore, to separate those which are **air** and **water**, you shall do this: take that water which you distilled through the second distillation and place it in the distillation cucurbit; replace the head of the alembic and distill in the water bath. That which you have distilled is nothing but water, since at that degree of heat nothing else is released. For the fire of the water bath is called **fire of the first degree**, the ash fire is called **fire of the second degree**, and a burning <insert>direct</insert> fire is called **fire of the third degree**. It is very useful...

# ON THE FIFTH ESSENCE

this knowledge of the **degrees of fire** <term>graduum ignis</term> <note>Alchemists used a scale of four "degrees" of heat: first degree (lukewarm/manure), second degree (ash bath), third degree (sand bath), and fourth degree (naked flame).</note> is most powerful for knowing these things in metal because of the confusion of heat. At that stage, the **Air** remains at the bottom of the vessel because it was not strong enough to exit by the heat of the second degree. Then, set it aside and pour the water which you extracted from the air back over the **dregs** <term>fæces</term>, and do as before: set it to rot in **manure** <term>fimo</term> for the same amount of time as you did for the air. Then, set it to distill in a **fire of the third degree** <note>original: "ignis tertij gradus"</note> and give it fire until it is all distilled. After this, repeat the distillation in a **water bath** <term>balneo</term>, and the **Water** will come out, while the **Fire** will remain at the bottom of the vessel because it is not able to escape through that degree of heat; keep this aside.

Understand these things we have told you concerning all **vegetable matter** <term>uegetabilibus</term> which abound in juice. You shall also do the same with metals: first, you shall cause them to be dissolved with our **solvent** <term>menstruo</term> <note>In alchemy, a "menstruum" is a powerful solvent used to dissolve solids, named after the belief in its cyclic or creative power, not referring to biological menses.</note> under manure for one week. Ensure that the solvent is sharpened with certain vegetables—those which we shall describe below in the **questionnaire** <note>original: "quæstionario"; likely referring to a specific diagnostic or instructional section of the book.</note>.

After the metals have indeed been dissolved, set them to distill in a **fire of the first degree**; the solvent will come out, and the **metallic calx** <term>calx metalli</term> <note>A "calx" is the crumbly powder or oxide left after a metal has been roasted or chemically dissolved.</note> will remain at the bottom. After this, indeed, pour new solvent over the metallic dregs in the same weight as the metal, and set it to rot for a month and a half. After this, distill just as you did with the vegetables, but each time add new solvent over the dregs. There have been many opinions of the philosophers regarding the extraction of elements from **minerals**, but we do not care to record them here, because we shall treat them in a different manner in the third book.

# THE SIXTH RULE

->**THE SIXTH CANON**<-

Many philosophers used to dissolve their **metallic bodies** in common **strong water** <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>Nitric acid, typically made by distilling saltpeter and vitriol; it was the primary solvent used by medieval alchemists to dissolve silver.</note> made from **vitriol** <note>A sulfate mineral, often iron or copper sulfate.</note> and **saltpeter**. They would draw off that water through evaporation, and the **calx** <term>calx</term> <note>The powdery residue or oxide left after a metal has been roasted or dissolved.</note> of the bodies remained at the bottom of the vessel. Afterward, they washed that residue with common fresh water and drew that water off again through evaporation. After this, they would attempt to dissolve that calx with a **solvent** <term>menstruo</term> <note>A powerful liquid used to dissolve solids; in alchemy, it often refers to a "mercurial" or "philosophical" solvent.</note> for their operations—which did not reach the desired end in the way that was fitting.

The reason for this is that the dissolution which occurs with strong water is not such as nature demands. Furthermore, those who performed such things were ignorant of the **vegetable substances** <note>Organic materials, such as tartar or spirits of wine, used to "sharpen" or increase the chemical potency of a solvent.</note> that sharpen our solvent; they were also ignorant of the **water of common mercury** <term>mercurij uulgi</term> which we revealed in a summary sent to **King Robert** <note>Robert of Anjou (1277–1343), King of Naples, to whom many alchemical works in the "Lullian" tradition were dedicated.</note>. This composition is based upon the *Testament* and the *Codicil* <note>Two of the most famous alchemical texts attributed to Ramon Llull.</note> in that part which treats the composition of **pearls** prepared in this manner, and so forth.

But in this chapter, we shall reveal to you a method of **calcination** in which none of the metals lose their essential form, and the solvent will dissolve them within a very short time. The mastery of this secret is as follows: you must take **gold** or **silver** reduced into thin plates. Take a small portion of it with an equal amount of common **quicksilver** <term>argento uiuo</term> <note>Mercury.</note> and place it over a slow fire. When it begins to smoke, add the plates and stir them with a wooden stick. After this, place it in a **cooling vessel** <term>gazola</term> in water that is cold. If the resulting paste is such that it breaks like **bell metal** <note>A hard, brittle bronze alloy; the author uses it here as a comparison for the desired texture of the amalgam.</note>, unless the mass is returned to the **alembic** <term>alembici</term> <note>The top part of a still, used here to capture or regulate the mercury vapors.</note>, let more of the quicksilver evaporate and put it into the water again. After it has become hard, as was said, place the paste in a **vessel** <term>galaiade</term> so that...

### DE QVINTA ESSENTIA
### ON THE FIFTH ESSENCE

This knowledge of the **degrees of fire** <note>Medieval alchemists categorized heat into four "degrees," ranging from the gentle warmth of a water bath or dung to the intense heat of a furnace.</note> is most important for understanding these matters, especially regarding **metals** because of the potential **confusion of heat** <note>An alchemical term for when the internal elements of a substance become "tangled" or fail to separate properly due to incorrect temperature.</note>. In such a case, the **air** <note>The "aerial" or volatile fraction of the substance being distilled.</note> remains at the bottom of the vessel because it was not able to exit through the heat of the **second degree**. 

Then, set it aside, and repeat the process by pouring the **water** which you extracted from the **air** over the dregs. Do as you did before and place it to **putrefy in dung** <note>original: "fimo." A horse-manure bath, which provided a steady, gentle heat for slow chemical "digestion."</note> for the same amount of time as you did for the **air**. Then, set it to be **distilled** in a fire of the **third degree**, and give it fire until everything is distilled. After this, repeat the distillation in a **water bath** <term>balneo</term>; the **water** will come out, and the **fire** <note>Here, "fire" refers to the elemental quality or the oily, sulfurous portion of the substance that remains after the more volatile parts have evaporated.</note> will remain at the bottom of the vessel, because it is not able to evaporate through that level of heat. Keep this aside. 

Understand that these things we have told you apply to all **vegetable substances** that are abundant in juice. You shall also do the same with **metals**: first, you shall cause them to be **dissolved** with our **solvent** <term>menstruo</term> <note>A powerful liquid used to dissolve solids; in this context, it refers to a "philosophical" or "mercurial" solvent.</note> under dung for one week. Ensure that the solvent is **sharpened** <note>Made more chemically reactive or acidic.</note> with certain vegetable substances, which we shall discuss below in the **Questionnaire** <note>Likely a reference to the *Interrogatio*, a companion text in the Lullian alchemical corpus.</note>. 

After the metals have indeed been dissolved, set them to distill in a fire of the **first degree**; the solvent will come out, and the **metallic calx** <term>calx</term> <note>The powdery residue or oxide left after a metal has been roasted or dissolved.</note> will remain at the bottom. After this, repeat the process over the **dregs of the metal** with new solvent equal to the weight of the metal. Place it to putrefy for a month and a half. After this, distill it just as you did with the vegetable substances, but at each turn, you must add **new solvent** over the dregs. 

There have been many opinions among the philosophers regarding the **extraction of elements from minerals**, but we do not care to set them down here, because we shall treat them in a different manner in the **Third Book**.

### THE SIXTH CANON.

Many philosophers used to dissolve their **metallic bodies** in common **strong water** <term>aqua forti</term> <note>Nitric acid, typically made by distilling saltpeter with vitriol.</note> made from **vitriol** <note>A term for various sulfate minerals.</note> and **saltpeter** <note>Potassium nitrate.</note>. They would draw off that water through evaporation, leaving the **lime** <term>calx</term> <note>The powdery residue or oxide left after a metal is heated or dissolved.</note> of the bodies at the bottom of the vessel. Afterward, they would wash it with common **sweet water** and draw that water off again through evaporation. Then they would attempt to dissolve that lime with a **solvent** <term>menstruum</term> for their works; however, the desired end did not follow as it should have.

The reason for this is that a dissolution performed with **strong water** is not of the kind that nature requires. Furthermore, those who did such things were ignorant of the **vegetable substances** <note>Organic additives used to "sharpen" or modify the chemical action of the solvent.</note> that sharpen our solvent, and they were also ignorant of the **water of common mercury** <note>original: "aquam mercurij uulgi." Likely a reference to a specific prepared form of quicksilver rather than raw mercury.</note>. We revealed this in a **compendium** <note>A summary or handbook.</note> sent to **King Robert** <note>Likely King Robert of Anjou (r. 1309–1343), to whom many alchemical works, especially those attributed to Raymond Lull, were dedicated.</note>, which was composed based on the *Testament* and the *Codicil* <note>The *Testamentum* and *Codicillus* are two of the most famous works in the pseudo-Lullian alchemical corpus.</note> in that section which treats the composition of **pearls** prepared in such a way, and so forth.

But in this chapter, we shall reveal to you **calcinations** in which none of the metals lose their **species** <note>The essential nature or "form" of the metal, which medieval alchemists feared was destroyed by harsh acids.</note>, and the solvent will resolve it within a short time. 

The mastery of this secret is as follows: take **gold** or **silver** reduced into thin sheets. Take a portion of this with an equal amount of **common quicksilver** <term>argentum uiuum</term>, and place it over a slow fire. When it begins to smoke, add the sheets and stir with a wooden rod. After this, place it into a **cooling basin** <term>gazola</term> containing cold water. If the resulting paste is so brittle that it breaks like **bell metal** <note>original: "metallum campanarum." An alloy of copper and tin known for being hard and brittle.</note>, [it is ready]; otherwise, return the mass to the **distilling vessel** <term>alembicus</term> and allow more of the quicksilver to evaporate. Put it in the water again, and once it is hard as described, place the paste in a **vessel** <term>galaiade</term> <note>A specific type of alchemical pot or crucible.</note> so that...

<summary>This page critiques the use of harsh nitric acid for dissolving metals, arguing it destroys their "species," and proposes a gentler method using mercury to create a brittle amalgam (paste) for further refinement.</summary>

...as we said, with a fourth part of its common salt, and grind it strongly until the paste and the salt together appear to be a black salt. Take therefore that salt and place it in a **sublimator** <term>sublimatorio</term> <note>A vessel used for sublimation, where a substance is heated into vapor and then condensed back into solid form.</note> if you wish to preserve the **quicksilver** <term>argentum uiuum</term> <note>Mercury; in this context, it was likely used to form an amalgam with the precious metal before being driven off by heat.</note>; but if not, place it in a certain **crucible** <term>gazola</term> <note>A heat-resistant earthen pot.</note> that can withstand fire, and apply fire until you see that all the **mercury** <term>mercurius</term> has evaporated or sublimated. After you have truly completed this, put that salt into another crucible and pour very hot water over it, as much as seems right to you, and mix it with a piece of wood; the salt will dissolve and turn into a black water. Let this rest, and afterward draw it off and pour it out bit by bit, until it is all drained, and the **lime** <term>calx</term> <note>The powdery metallic residue or oxide remaining after the mercury and salt are removed.</note> will remain at the bottom. Again pour very hot water over it and do as before, and again add the aforementioned water to it until it comes away from the lime completely clear, just as it was when poured in. Then place the lime in the sun to dry, and you will have it most perfectly reduced into a very fine powder for the use of the artist, for whatever purpose you wish. Likewise, other metals have a different method of **calcination** <term>calcinatio</term>. For **copper** <term>uenere</term> <note>Literally "Venus," the alchemical name for copper.</note>, calcination is done just as **burnt copper** <term>aes ustum</term> <note>A prepared form of copper oxide or sulfide, often made by heating copper plates with sulfur or salt.</note> is made. **Lead** <term>Saturnus</term> <note>The alchemical name for lead.</note> and **tin** <term>Iuppiter</term> <note>The alchemical name for tin.</note> are calcined with prepared common salt by stirring them in a **shallow pan** <term>alboth</term> <note>A wide, flat-bottomed vessel used for heating materials.</note> with a piece of wood and adding a small amount of salt; after this, let it be washed with very hot water as was said, and afterward set it to dry, and it is done.

# BOOK ONE.

God has generally granted such a heavenly virtue to the **Fifth Essence** <term>Quintæ essentiæ</term> <note>The "Fifth Essence" or Quintessence was believed by alchemists to be the purest, most potent medicinal core of a substance, distinct from the four physical elements.</note> that you may extract it from every wood, fruit, flower, root, leaf, stone and metal, flesh, seed, and spice which God, the creator of nature, has made. Indeed, the instruction of this secret is such: once you have obtained the Fifth Essence of wine <note>original: "uini Quintam essentiam"</note> separated from its dregs, you will know how to extract the proper Fifth Essence of other things within three hours, so that such great labor and boredom may be avoided.

Therefore, take in the name of God whatever thing from which you wish to separate the Fifth Essence, and put it into our Fifth Essence of wine. Place it in the strong sun in springtime, or place it in a vessel over a gentle fire; within three hours you will have the Fifth Essence of that thing mixed with the Fifth Essence of wine. This mixture will be converted into the same nature as the thing which was put into it. Thus, whether the thing is hot, cold, moist, dry, or laxative, or whatever other condition and scent it possessed, the resulting essence will be of that same nature. This is because—as we revealed to you above—it has an affinity for this temperament <term>complexionem</term> <note>In medieval science, "complexion" refers to the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that determines a substance's properties.</note> or for that specific one.

Therefore, you will have a Fifth Essence that is just like the thing you introduced—possessing the same scent, taste, temperament, virtue, and operation. This is the greatest skill in the work of medicine: that with one and the same medicine you know how to perform various operations, which perhaps a stubborn <note>original: "duræ ceruicis", literally "stiff-necked." This is a biblical idiom for someone who is proud or refuses to learn.</note> practitioner might not achieve, and so forth. And thus, with our heaven—

->by its stars which we named above,<-
->it shall be done through nature what will be considered<-
->a miracle.<-

## THE EIGHTEENTH RULE WHICH
## teaches what things are cold in the fourth degree, and that you should use them when it shall be necessary.

Let it be certain to you that it was the opinion of many that no thing was established by nature in the fourth degree of coldness; we make this argument against them.

Every element, or whatever other thing, desires to be in a greater perfection than its nature can contain; by reason of which any element within compound bodies <note>original: "elementatis," things composed of the elements.</note> desires the fourth simple point <note>A "point" or "degree" refers to the intensity of a quality in Galenic medicine.</note>, so that it may repress its contrary, or at least be equalized to it through resistance, so that its being is not stripped away from individual things. If, therefore, water were not found by nature in individuals in the fourth degree, just as it is in the first, second, and third, then water would not desire a greater perfection of simplicity than it can have in individual things; and thus the likeness of its simplicity, multiplied in a greater degree, would be naturally hateful to it, and its contrary would be lovable to it—which is impossible.

Furthermore: no hot disease in the fourth degree would be curable, which is inconsistent and against the purpose of medicine.

Likewise, water itself would be destroyed by its contrary <note>Heat/Fire</note>; and therefore it is a rule that elements do not transform their own likeness outside of themselves except by the mode of their perfection and their parts, and they operate in individual things through the likenesses of said parts. The reason for this is because such a defect in the nature of goodness and vir— <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "virtutis" (virtue or power).</note>

<meta>This page continues the theoretical transition from the previous page's list of medicinal substances. ### ON THE FIFTH ESSENCE

The four elements have their own proper spheres, where the nature of each is greater than it is in the spheres of the others, although any element may be present within the sphere of another—that is, one element exists throughout the spheres of all, and all exist throughout the sphere of one. Nature crafts the world in this way so that from their mixture, the individual things of the spheres might arise, in which the elements actually exist (as we have proved above). These things would not be able to exist if they were not mixed in turn; for if the universal mixture of the world were lacking to the elements, then special and individual mixture would also be lacking, because when the general <note>The "universal" or "general" refers to the cosmic balance of elements.</note> fails, the particular thing falls into its own corruption. Finally, every element—because according to its nature its <term>temperament</term> <note>original: "complexio"; the specific balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—within a substance.</note> is greater in its own sphere (just as heat is greater in its sphere of fire than dryness or any of the other qualities)—follows this same pattern for the others.

Likewise, each of the said elements has its own proper subject among individual species, in which its heat is greater than the qualities of other elements. For example, in pepper, the property of fire thrives more than it does in saffron; and in aloe, there is more of the temperament of air than in <term>myrobalans</term> <note>Dried plum-like fruits used in medieval medicine to purge humors.</note>; and so it is with other things similar to these. From this, I form this reasoning: every effect must follow the nature of its cause. If, therefore, fire—which is the cause of all things capable of being heated—has a greater amount of its own property in its own sphere, and its property is found there more than the property of others, then in heatable things of the temperament of fire, it is necessary that the heat be greater than the hu-

<meta>catchword: miditas (humidity)</meta>

<summary>This page explains the cosmological and physical theory of the four elements, arguing that while elements mix to form individual things, each substance retains a dominant elemental quality based on its "sphere" and "cause."</summary>
<keywords>four elements, spheres, temperament, complexion, fire, air, pepper, aloe, myrobalans, natural philosophy</keywords>

*From which it is very well concluded that the quality of fire in a fiery subject is greater than any of its other qualities. In the individual substance, the [King] is the **form**, while the **Queen**, the **Soldier**, and the **Slave** are the **matter**. Therefore, the action of a single quality existing in different individual substances is not equal, for the reason mentioned above <note>The author argues that the "governing" quality (the King/Form) determines the substance's primary effect, even if other substances share the same degree of heat or cold.</note>. Consider Sea Onion <note>original: *squilla*; often used as a diuretic or expectorant</note> or Tutty <note>original: *thucia*; an ash-like byproduct of zinc ore used in medicinal ointments</note> which is hot in the 3rd degree, and Chasteberry <note>original: *agnus castus*</note> which is also hot in the third degree. If either of them is applied to our body, the Chasteberry pours a greater heat into us than the Tutty does. The reason for this is that the heat in Chasteberry is the **King**, but in Tutty it is the **Queen**. And because a king possesses greater power than a queen, the result follows accordingly.

Likewise, it is because the heat in Tutty is "terrified" <note>original: *terrificata*; a technical term suggesting the quality is constrained or repressed by its opposite</note> and exists in a state of passivity <note>original: *passionem*</note>, whereas in Chasteberry it exists in a state of action; and because an acting thing is of a greater nature than a passive thing, it follows [that it is more powerful]. Likewise, in Tutty, the heat has two points of coldness opposing it. In Chasteberry, however, they only have two points of a single degree as an opposing force.

Furthermore, the heat existing in Tutty dries in the highest degree, because it is inseparable from its nature and formed by dryness. In Chasteberry, however, it heats more than it dries, because there heat is the **King** and is not formed by anything else; rather, the dryness within it is "ignited" <note>original: *ignificata*; literally 'turned to fire' or made intense</note>. First, through the nature of heat, it warms, and only afterward does it dry. This is because in any natural thing, the proper and co-essential <term>co-essential<gloss>A quality that is fundamental to the substance's very existence, rather than a secondary characteristic.</gloss></term> act of that thing must occur within itself before its secondary <note>original: *appropriatus*</note> act. Even the lower heats in an individual substance, being shaped by some specific nature, act first in our body according to the nature of the [governing] form before they exist as formed by their own...

*Question.* Why are some medicines of the fourth degree deadly, and some not?

*The Solution.* Because some are hot, moist, dry, or cold at the final point of the fourth degree, while some are only at the third, second, or first point within that degree. Therefore, you shall follow this general rule:

Every medicine that is at the fourth point of the fourth degree—whether it be hot, moist, cold, or dry—is deadly. For example:
Among hot substances: monkshood <note>original: "napellus"</note>, thistle <note>original: "cardus"</note>, mistletoe <note>original: "uisci"</note>, sea squill <note>original: "squilla"</note> when used alone, and oleander, which is used to kill deer. 
Among moist substances: quicksilver <note>Mercury; original: "argentum uiuum"</note>. 
Likewise, among cold substances: hemlock <note>original: "cicuta"</note> and the brain of a head <note>In medieval medicine, animal brains were classified as being extremely cold and moist in nature.</note>. 
Among dry substances: white or red arsenic, orpiment <note>A yellow arsenic mineral; original: "azarnech"</note>, burnt copper <note>original: "æs ustum"</note>, verdigris <note>original: "uiride æs"</note>, gypsum, and so on. 

Therefore, the more they decline from that fourth point, the less deadly they are. For instance, sea squill is not fatal when it is mixed with a multitude of other things as it is when used alone; and nightshade <note>original: "solatrum"</note> is not as harmful as arsenic; and henbane <note>original: "iusquiamus"</note> is not as harmful as hemlock; and mercury-herb <note>original: "mercurialis"</note> is not as harmful as quicksilver...

<summary>This page explains the mathematical hierarchy of humoral qualities and provides a list of lethal substances—including arsenic, hemlock, and monkshood—classified by their "degree" of intensity.</summary>

**Question.** *Why do substances existing at the final point of the fourth degree of heat, moisture, etc., kill more than substances existing at the final point of other degrees?*

**Solution.** *Because more of the simplicity of the component essence is retained in them; this simplicity exists in the subtle <term>naturalized matter</term> <note>Matter that has been refined by natural processes or alchemical preparation to its most potent state.</note> more so than in other degrees. Regarding this, the example we mentioned above concerning the basilisk <note>A mythical reptile said to kill with a glance; often used in alchemy to represent the most concentrated and "quick" form of poison or spirit.</note> and lightning is sufficient for you. To help you understand the degrees of medicines more easily, we will provide eight figures <note>Diagrams or charts used in medieval manuscripts to visualize complex relationships between the humors.</note> here, through which you can guide your intellect as a direct means to understand what we have previously established about degrees. In the first four figures, the knowledge of the four simple medicines existing in the final point of the fourth degree is contained; and in the next four, those things in the fourth degree but in the [other] three points; and in another four, those in the third degree; and another four in the second; and finally another four for those in the first degree.*

*Having spoken of the degrees of medicines, it is appropriate that we speak of their virtues and properties, so that when we apply them to our <term>heaven</term> <note>The author uses "heaven" (cœlum) as a metaphor for the Quinta Essentia (likely highly distilled alcohol), which acts as a celestial, incorruptible medium that magnifies the power of herbs and minerals.</note> they are rendered a thousand times more powerful than if they acted on their own.*

*Canon 25 follows, which will first teach you which things are attractive.*

# THE TWENTY-SIXTH CANON, WHICH
## teaches which things are substances that purge the offending humors
### in our body in general; and first,
### ->concerning those that purge the blood.<-

Some things loosen the belly and sometimes provoke vomiting because they are made repulsive to nature. Some, however, truly attract humors similar to themselves—such as rhubarb, scammony, and fleawort <note>original: "psilium"</note>—aided by the <term>expulsive power</term> <note>The natural biological force believed to drive waste and excess humors out of the organs.</note> of the limbs toward the intestines, and from the intestines to the outside. Some of these purge by means of their viscosity, such as mercury-herb <note>original: "mercurialis"</note> and fleawort; some through astringency <note>original: "stipticatate"</note>, such as myrobalans <note>A plum-like fruit highly valued in medieval medicine for balancing humors.</note>; some through acridity, such as the seed of orache <note>original: "triplicis"</note>; some through sweetness, like scammony and purging cassia <note>original: "cassia fistula"</note>; and some indeed through bitterness, such as aloes. Others purge this humor or that; these, however, are the ones that purge the **blood** in whatever part of the body it may be.

## RULE XXXIX. IN WHICH IS
contained the knowledge of things that cause sleep, so that you may use them by applying them to our heaven <note>original: "cœlo nostro"; the author's term for the Fifth Essence</note>. When it is necessary, they cause sleep; these are of excessive coldness, because by their coldness they constrict the nerves, and by their moisture they soothe the spirits and the brain. These are the following, namely:

| | |
|---|---|
| Henbane seed <note>original: "Semen iusquiami"</note> | Opium |
| Black poppy seed <note>original: "Semen papa. nigri"</note> | The fish called the torpedo <note>original: "Piscis qui dicitur torpedo"; the electric ray, known for its numbing sting</note> |
| White poppy seed <note>original: "Semen papa. albi"</note> | Salamander <note>original: "Salamandra"; in medieval lore, the salamander was considered intensely cold</note> |
| Mandrake <note>original: "Mandragora"</note> | Twice-cooked bread [biscuit] with cold water <note>original: "Biscocta cum aqua frigida"</note> |
| Water lentil [duckweed] <note>original: "Lenticula aquatica"</note> | |
| Purslane <note>original: "Portulaca"</note> | Fleawort <note>original: "Psilium"</note> |

Truly, fix these things in our heaven, and they will cause any animal eating or drinking it to sleep wonderfully.

## RULE XL. IN WHICH IS CONTAINED
the knowledge of corrosive agents <note>original: "mordificatiũ"; substances that bite or eat away at tissue</note>. In effect, corrosive agents are those that have a sharp quality [acuity], and they are these, namely:

| | |
|---|---|
| Olive leaves <note>original: "Folia oliuæ"</note> | Orpiment <note>original: "azarnech"; a yellow arsenic mineral</note> |
| Red arsenic <note>original: "Arsenicum rubeum"</note> | Juice of black hellebore <note>original: "suc. ellebo. nigri"</note> |
| Juice of white hellebore <note>original: "Succus ellebo. albi"</note> | Alum <note>original: "alumen"</note> |
| Copperas <note>original: "Cupperosa"; green vitriol or iron sulfate</note> | Ink [vitriol] <note>original: "atramentum"; used to describe black metallic salts</note> |
| Flower of copper <note>original: "Flos æris"; verdigris or copper acetate</note> | White arsenic <note>original: "arsenicum album"</note> |
| Leek <note>original: "Porrum"</note> | Spanish flies <note>original: "Cantarides"; blistering beetles</note> |
| Root of wild cucumber <note>original: "Radix cucumeris Agrestis"</note> | Burnt copper <note>original: "asustime"; a corruption of *as ustum*, used as a caustic</note> |

<summary>This page details two categories of medicinal substances: soporifics (sleep-inducers) characterized by their "extreme coldness," and corrosive agents characterized by their "sharpness." These lists reflect the medieval medical theory of balancing bodily humors and qualities like heat and moisture.</summary>

Therefore, fix these medicines in our heaven <note>The "heaven" (*coelum*) is the author's term for the Fifth Essence or highly distilled alcohol.</note> and it will become for you a corrosive agent <note>original: "modificatiuũ"; likely a scribal variant for *mordificativum*, referring to the corrosive agents discussed in the previous Rule.</note> so that you may apply it to our body when it shall be necessary.

### RULE FORTY-ONE
which teaches which things are strengthening to our body.

# HERE BEGINS THE SEC-

### ond book of this volume, which is called concerning the
### ultimate general remedies established for the 
### benefit of our body.

IN THIS present book, we intend to treat the application of the Fifth Essence <term>Fifth Essence: also known as the Quintessence; a celestial, incorruptible substance believed to be the "spirit" of matter, capable of restoring health.</term> to human bodies to the end that, through it, all diseases considered incurable according to the judgment of the new-theoretical physicians <term>new-theoretical physicians: likely referring to the contemporary academic doctors of the era who relied on theory rather than the practical alchemy the author proposes.</term> may be cured. But let him who wishes to search deeply into the principles of nature—which we have uncovered here—know that although one cannot fully grasp every detail through the mind alone, these things exist among beings. Let them also know their natures, temperaments, and virtues <note>original: "naturas & complexiones & uirtutes"</note> against the misfortunes of nature. Indeed, through the remedies we designate in this present book, know that you may provide for the human body suddenly and almost miraculously.

Because in this present book the doctrine of the cure of all diseases from head to toe <note>A traditional medieval medical structure called "a capite ad calcem," organizing treatments starting from the brain down to the feet.</note> is specified, we have composed this book even contrary to our original intention, for we previously said it would be made as a concise summary. Therefore, we shall provide one general rule by which all ailments from head to toe may be cured with our Fifth Essence. Afterward, we shall descend to specific cases for comparison, so that according to the instruction we give regarding them, any seeker of truth <note>original: "inuestigator ueritatis"</note> will know how to proceed with others.

### RULE II: WHICH TEACHES THE MASTERY
### in the resuscitation of the dead, which is one
### of the greatest secrets in this book

In this rule, we call "dead" not those who are simply deceased, but those for whom hope is ultimately lost—those who have been abandoned by doctors and the activities of life to such an extent that they no longer even use their senses. To such a "dead" person in this state of desperation we bring help, so that he may rise again quite quickly, speak, and live, unless it be that final end appointed by God. The mastery of this secret is this: you must give him the Fifth Essence <term>Fifth Essence: *Quinta essentia*, the most refined and spiritualized part of a substance, believed to hold the power of life itself.</term> by itself, and immediately in a short time he will rise alive, provided that by swallowing it into the stomach, it pours the ray of natural life into the heart. You will see him repair that defunct nature itself. 

If you wish this to happen in a fraction of an hour, or as if in 20 points of a clock <note>original: *punctis horologij*. Medieval clocks often divided the hour into "points" or "moments" rather than minutes.</note>, so that it is believed by bystanders to be an illusion or an evident miracle, you must have celandine <note>original: *celidonia*. Greater Celandine was highly valued in alchemy for its yellow sap, which was linked to the sun and gold.</note>, whose flower and fruit is the color of gold. Let it stand for three hours, and give it to the patient in the quantity of one full nut-shell. Continue this for three days, and anyone having this fever will be perfectly cured. Because in "untrue" tertian fever phlegm <note>original: "flegma"</note> is mixed in, add to this medicine turbith <term>turbith: the root of *Operculina turpethum*, used to purge phlegm</term>, senna, and polypody <term>polypody: a type of fern used as a mild laxative</term>. Give this to the patient, and they will be cured perfectly and without fail, provided the disease was sent by nature—that is, that it was not sent by the hand [of God]...

### CANON XII. WHICH TEACHES YOU 
->the treatment for quotidian fevers.<-

Quotidian fever <term>Quotidian fever: a fever that recurs daily, traditionally attributed in humoral theory to an excess or corruption of phlegm</term> is generated from the corruption of phlegm <term>phlegm: one of the four bodily humors, characterized as cold and moist; its imbalance was thought to cause lethargy and specific types of fever</term> and from its abundance. Therefore, there is a "true" kind and another "not true" kind, for the true kind is caused by natural phlegm. The "not true" kind, however, is caused by unnatural phlegm, with which some other humor is simultaneously corrupted. Whichever [type] it is, this fever is perfectly cured with our Quintessence <term>Quintessence: the "fifth essence" or highly rectified alcohol/spirit of wine, believed by alchemists to be a universal solvent and medicine</term> by itself alone, if you give it in a drink for a period of three days. If, however, you add those things that purge phlegm, which you will find above in the tables <note>original: "areolis," referring to specific sections or charts in the manuscript</note>, the effect will be marvelous.

Likewise, if you add the herb called mercury <note>original: "mercurialis"; likely *Mercurialis annua*, used as a purgative</note> to this Quintessence by itself, it will be a more powerfully acting medicine. For it is an experimental fact that if you take its juice and instill three drops into the right nostril or the ear of the patient, it removes the pattern <note>original: "typum"</note> of the quotidian fever. It will do the same if you add it to our Quintessence along with medicines that purge phlegm.

### CANON XIII. WHICH CONTAINS
->the knowledge for curing all<-
->continuous fevers.<-

Continuous fever <term>Continuous fever: a fever that persists without significant remission, unlike the intermittent "intermitting" fevers like tertian or quartan</term> is multifaceted. Some arise from the blood, and this is divided into two parts: for one arises from an excess <note>original: "multitudine"</note> of blood, and the other from its corruption <note>original: "incorruptione," though likely meaning a lack of purity or a specific type of putrefaction in this context</note>.

Likewise, some arise from choler <term>choler: also known as "yellow bile," the humor associated with heat and dryness; an excess was thought to cause irritability and burning fevers</term>, and this is divided into another two parts: because one is that which arises around the region of the heart, and the other arises in the brain.

### CANON 14. WHICH CONTAINS
->*the knowledge against pestilential fevers.*<-

So that you may know the cure for those fevers—since no other physicians know how to apply a remedy to them, and none of the moderns <note>original: "modernorum"; referring to the university-trained doctors of the 14th or 15th century whom the author considers less enlightened</note> except for one has known how to apply a useful remedy for pestilential fevers because they are ignorant of nature. If, however, you wish to make a stronger medicine, place into our Quintessence the quintessences of gentian <term>gentian: a bitter herb used to treat digestive issues and fevers</term>, red dittany <term>red dittany: an aromatic plant highly valued in the Middle Ages for its supposed ability to draw out poisons and heal wounds</term>, wood avens <note>original: "gariofilatae"; likely *Geum urbanum*, known for its clove-like scent and antiseptic properties</note>, Armenian bole <term>Armenian bole: a medicinal red clay from Armenia, used as an astringent and to treat the plague</term>, castoreum <term>castoreum: a secretion from the beaver, used in historical medicine to treat hysteria and skin conditions</term>, butcher’s broom <note>original: "scopa regia"; literally "royal broom," typically identified as *Ruscus aculeatus*</note>, and wild rue. We tell you in truth that after they have tasted it, the patient will be safe and will not be in danger from that fever, provided you come to the aid of the sick person within one day.

I have already told you many times that before you administer the medicine proportioned to this or that pain, you should let those medicines that have an affinity for that pain <note>original: "quæ aspectum habent"; literally "those which have an aspect/regard," meaning medicines that are astrologically or medicinally targeted toward a specific ailment</note> stand first for three hours in the Quintessence <term>Quintessence: the "Fifth Essence," a highly distilled medicinal alcohol thought to contain the life force of substances</term>, and afterward administer it to the patient.

*Solution.* We command you to administer laxative medicines with our Quintessence for the purpose that the offending matter <term>materia peccans: "sinning matter," the harmful or diseased humors believed to cause illness</term> may be extracted better and more strongly from the body, and so that such great expenses are not incurred <note>because less of the expensive raw drug is needed</note>.

Also, regarding the hundredfold virtue—because they cannot be applied in full doses without danger to the body—we say that it is not necessary to administer them in as great a quantity as they are administered before the application of our Quintessence. 

*Example.* If one dram <term>drachma: a small unit of weight, approximately 3.9 grams</term> of some laxative medicine is usually administered, only the weight of one grain <note>original: "areæ"; likely a specific small measure or a corruption of "aureus" or "ordei" (barleycorn weight)</note> should be given with the Quintessence. Or if the weight of one ounce <term>uncia: a unit of weight equal to eight drams</term> is usually given, let only the weight of one dram of the Quintessence-mixed medicine be given, and so on for other weights of other laxative medicines according to their manner. Thus, our Quintessence can be administered without harm or danger.

In the cure of the gout <note>original: "unius guttæ"; literally "a drop," the medieval term for gout, which was thought to be caused by drops of waste humors falling into the joints</note>, God in His supreme goodness created our Quintessence and the Quintessence of blood...

<header>PREFACE ON METALLIC THINGS</header>

...[substances] can exist as <term>composed: structured mixtures of the four elements (Latin: complexionata)</term> things before they are <term>animated: living things, such as plants or animals (Latin: animata)</term>. Therefore, the discussion of these things follows immediately after the science of <term>Meteorology: the study of phenomena in the "upper atmosphere," which for ancients included the formation of minerals in the earth (Latin: Metheororum)</term>; for they seem to possess little more than a simple mixing of the elements. However, we have not seen the books of *Aristotle* on these subjects, except for certain excerpts. Furthermore, the things which *Avicenna* handed down concerning these matters in the third chapter of the first book of his treatise are not sufficient. Therefore, we shall first conduct an inquiry into stones, then into metallic things, and finally into those things that are intermediate between them; for the generation of stones is indeed easier and more clearly manifest than that of metals. We shall condense our discourse because the causes of many things to be said here have already been determined in the book of *Meteorology*. In treating stones in general, we shall investigate the general matter of stones, their specific and immediate <term>efficient cause: the force or agent that brings a thing into being (Latin: efficiens)</term>, and their place of generation. Then, we will look at the manner in which stones are mixed, and the cause of the diversity of their colors and other <term>accidents: non-essential properties like color or weight (Latin: accidentium)</term> found within them—such as greater or lesser hardness, <term>workability: whether a stone can be shaped or hewn (Latin: dolabilitas)</term> and unworkability, porosity and density, weight and lightness, and other such traits. In these qualities, stones seem to possess no small diversity, not only in species and number but also in their very genus. There are, however, certain men of the greatest authority in philosophy who, making a treatise not on all but on only certain kinds of stones, claim to have made sufficient mention of them. Such men are *Hermes, Evax the King of the Arabs <note>original: "Euates," referring to the legendary King Evax, supposed author of a famous book on gems</note>, Dioscorides, Aaron, and Joseph*, who, by treating only precious stones, did not treat the general nature of stones.
