Pliny, however, provided insufficient knowledge in his <term>Natural History: a vast encyclopedia of the natural world written by Pliny the Elder in the 1st century AD (Latin: historia naturali)</term>, as he did not wisely assign the general causes of stones; nor is it necessary for us to introduce the opinions of all these authors, because the science of the matter is not so hidden that we must gather it from the errors of many. Rather, the natures and <term>complexions: the specific proportions or balance of the four elements within a substance (Latin: complexiones)</term> of stones will be sufficiently known once their proper matter, their proximate <term>efficient cause: the immediate force or agent that brings a thing into being (Latin: efficiens proximum)</term>, their form, and their proper <term>accidents: non-essential properties such as color or hardness (Latin: accidentia)</term> are understood, according to the inquiry already established in the fourth book of the <term>Meteorology: Aristotle’s treatise on the physical world (Latin: Methororum)</term>.

For we do not intend here to show how any of these substances is transmuted into another, nor how, through the antidote of that medicine which the <term>alchemists: early practitioners of chemistry and metallurgy (Latin: alchimici)</term> call the <term>elixir: a substance believed to transform base metals or prolong life (Latin: elixir)</term>, their "sick men" <note>original: "curantur ægri homines eorum." This is an alchemical metaphor where base or "imperfect" metals are described as "sick" and the elixir "cures" them into gold.</note> are cured, nor how their hidden qualities are made manifest, or conversely, how their manifest qualities are concealed. Instead, we intend to show their mixing from the elements, and how each one is established in its own proper species. 

For this reason, we do not care to investigate the difference between "stone" and "spirit," or "soul" and "body," or "substance" and "accident," of which the alchemists speak. They call "stone" everything that does not evaporate in fire, and they likewise call this "body" and "substance." However, that which evaporates in fire—such as <term>sulfur: a volatile yellow mineral (Latin: sulphur)</term> and <term>quicksilver: mercury (Latin: argentum uiuum)</term>—and those things from which various colors are made (which are commonly called stones), they call "spirit," "soul," and "accident." It belongs to another science <note>This likely refers to the practical or "operative" alchemy, whereas this text focuses on "speculative" or natural philosophy.</note> to inquire into these things which are supported by very hidden reasoning and instruments. 

The method, however, which we have held in each of our works, we shall also maintain here, dividing the work into several books, many treatises, and many [chapters...]

# ON THE MATTER OF STONES.
### CHAPTER I.

Beginning our treatment of the nature of stones in general, we say that the matter of every stone is either a type of certain earth or a type of certain water. For one of these two elements prevails in stones; and even in those in which a certain type of water seems to dominate, there is also something of earth dominating at the same time. A sign of this is that almost all kinds of stones sink under water—which we stated abounds in the matter of earth in the books <term>On the Heavens and the World: Aristotle's treatise concerning the nature of the elements and their natural places (Latin: de coelo & mundo)</term>. For if the <term>superior elements: fire and air, which naturally move upward (Latin: superiora elementa)</term> were dominant in them, they would undoubtedly float upon the water. As it stands, however, no kind of stone floats unless it is spongy or burnt—and made spongy and porous through burning, such as <term>pumice: a light, volcanic rock (Latin: pumex)</term> and the stone which hot springs vomit forth, or volcanic fire; even if these are reduced to powder, the powder itself sinks under water. 

Furthermore, if in transparent stones there were not an earthy <term>limiting agent of moisture: a dry substance that binds or gives a definite shape to a fluid (Latin: terminatiuum humidi)</term> mixed with the water, they would not sink under water. This applies to <term>crystal: clear rock crystal (Latin: cristallus)</term> and <term>beryl: a transparent gemstone (Latin: berillus)</term>, just as ice and other things in which water is pure or superabundant do not sink <note>Ice floats because it lacks the "earthy" weight, while clear stones sink because they are water "limited" or solidified by earth.</note>. Moreover, all stones that are generated in the kidneys and bladders of animals are generated from a viscous, thick, and earthy moisture. 

It is necessary, therefore, that such is the matter of stones. Speaking specifically about those stones in which the matter is earth, it can easily be seen that in these, not only earth <note>The sentence ends abruptly here, following the catchword "est terra" for the next page.</note>

is the matter, for otherwise it would not be joined together into the solidity of stone. For we say that the cause of cohesion and mixing is **moisture**; for by its subtlety, it causes one part of the earth to flow toward another, and this is the cause of the good blending of the parts of the matter. If, however, this moisture were not well-infused everywhere among the earthy parts, nor were it retentive, and if it evaporated during the <term>coagulation: the process of hardening or solidifying from a fluid state (Latin: coagulatio)</term> of the stone, then there would remain a non-continuous dust of earth. 

For this reason, it is necessary that the moisture be <term>viscous: thick, sticky, or glue-like (Latin: uiscosum)</term> and glutinous, so that its parts lie together with the earthy parts like the **hooks of chains**. Then the dry earthy part retains the moisture, and the watery moisture existing within the dry part brings about cohesion. 

And this is testified to by <term>Avicenna: Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian polymath whose works on geology and medicine were foundational to medieval science (Latin: Auicenna)</term> when he says that pure earth does not become stone because earth does not create cohesion through its dryness, but rather fragmentation; for the prevailing dryness in it does not allow bonding to occur. The same philosopher gives the reason that sometimes mud is dried out and becomes a middle stage between stone and mud, and then in the course of time it becomes stone. 

He says again that the mud most suitable for being transformed into stone is <term>unctuous: oily or fatty in texture, providing a "greasy" stickiness (Latin: unctuosum)</term>. That which is not like this is prone to being broken down or <insert>reduced</insert> to powder, because of the ease with which moisture is separated from it. A sign of this is that in stones themselves, <margin>veins of earth</margin> frequently remain; this is hard, dry earth which, when squeezed or struck, becomes dust. The cause of this is none other than that its moisture, not being sufficiently oily and viscous, evaporated during the hardening of the stone, and therefore it remained as hard, breakable earth.

The author cites Avicenna to support the theory that "viscous" moisture acts like interlocking chain links to create solid mineral structures.</summary>

breakable because of the power of the <term>coagulation: the process of hardening or solidifying from a fluid state (Latin: coagulatio)</term> of the surrounding stone. There is also another sign of this: when stones are generated not as a continuous mass, but in the manner of layers <note>original: "per modum asserum," literally "in the manner of planks," referring to sedimentary stratification</note> such that one is generated upon another, they will not be joined together continuously. That it is a <term>viscous: thick and sticky (Latin: humiditas uiscosa)</term> and oily moisture which holds the matter of the stone together is indicated by the fact that animals called <term>shellfish: literally "tortoises," but here referring to any shelled creature like snails or mollusks (Latin: testudines)</term> are very frequently generated with their shells within stones. This is most common in small stones that are found containing many cavities shaped like the shells of these creatures, which some people call "lunar stones." 

The cause of this is the moisture that evaporated to that spot; being held back by the surrounding material, it was coiled within itself. As it first became solid on the outside, it was stirred within and received a <term>vital spirit: a life-giving force believed to animate matter (Latin: spiritum uitalem)</term>, just as we said in the fourth book of the <term>Meteorology: Aristotle’s treatise on natural phenomena and minerals (Latin: metheororum)</term>. This, then, is the common matter of those stones which are neither transparent nor sparkling; however, they are differentiated in various ways, as will appear in the following sections.

### On the Transparency of Stones. Chapter 2.

Regarding stones that are transparent to a greater or lesser degree, such as those called gems, it can be stated as a general rule that their common material is an impure water. For these stones are a kind of glass produced by the work of nature; because of this, they are even finer in their mixture and possess a clearer transparency than the <term>glass of art: man-made glass (Latin: uitra artis)</term>, because although art imitates nature, it cannot fully attain the perfection of nature’s work. 

A sign of what we have said—namely, that water which has been acted upon by dry heat or cold serves as the common material of these stones—is that glass is made from the kind of moisture that is melted out from various ashes, whether of lead, fern <note>original: "filicis"; fern ash was a primary source of potash for medieval glassmaking</note>, iron, or something else, by means of a very intense fire. That this moisture is indeed water is shown by the fact that it is solidified by cold and is liquefied when dissolved by intense dry heat. 

Furthermore, that it has been acted upon by a burnt, earthy dryness is proven by the fact that it does not liquefy except from ash through a very intense roasting, as we have said. This is visibly demonstrated in the art of glassmaking, which is <term>subordinate: a field of study that derives its principles from a higher science (Latin: subalternatur)</term> to alchemy. For a very subtle vapor within the earth or within a stone is sometimes contained by the surrounding material; being coiled within itself, it becomes moist, just as happens in a hot, covered pot.

<meta>catchword: in which</meta>

<summary>Albertus Magnus explains that gems and transparent stones are essentially a form of "natural glass" created from impure water and mineral vapors. He argues that while humans can make glass using intense heat and ashes, nature's "alchemy" produces a more perfect, transparent result.</summary>

in which there is some water. And when moisture has thus been <term>acted upon: a philosophical term (Latin: passus) meaning to be changed by an external force</term> intensely by dryness, and the power of dryness is constant within it, it solidifies into stone. But here we should not speak of the specific method of the generation of stones, but rather of the material of stones in general; whether their solidification occurs by cold or heat will be shown later. 

That water is the material of this kind of stone is also demonstrated by the fact that in certain places where there is a strong stone-generating power, water descending as rain—whether in drops or poured out in another way—hardens into stone. For as it falls, it is first acted upon by an earthy dryness through the natural operation of that location, and thus it becomes the proper material for stone. 

This is also shown by the abundance of transparency found in such stones. Since the transparency of air and fire are not stable <note>original: "incorruptibilia"; meaning the transparency in gases or flames is fleeting and cannot be "fixed" into a solid</note>, it necessarily follows that this transparency arises from the transparency of water; therefore, their proper material must be of the nature of water. 

As for what some of the ancients say when explaining the material of stones—that a certain substance settles at the bottom of running water and this becomes stone—I do not approve of this view. My reason is that whatever settles out from water is an earthy substance; therefore, the stones generated in this way do not take as their material water that has been acted upon by an earthy power, but rather earth that has been acted upon by the powers of water. 

The sign of this is that such stones are often not transparent, but <term>opaque: literally "bounded" (Latin: terminati), meaning light cannot pass through them</term>, and they are said to be not easily carved but rather easily shattered; these are commonly called <term>flints: hard, non-transparent stones (Latin: silices)</term>.

**Crystal** and *Beryl* testify most strongly to these things we have said, for they have taken on a form almost entirely like that of frozen water <note>original: "aquæ glaciei"; the author is comparing the appearance of clear gems to ice</note>. Concerning these, *Aristotle* said that they are formed from water once the heat has been universally removed. Just as we stated in the previous chapter regarding those stones whose material we said was not simple earth but earth <term>acted upon: (Latin: passa) a philosophical term meaning a substance has been changed or "suffered" the influence of an external quality or force</term> by oily and viscous moisture, so too must it be understood here. Simple aqueous moisture cannot be the material for transparent stones, because, as we have shown elsewhere, such moisture does not become firm through <term>decoction: (Latin: elixatio) the process of "cooking" or boiling a substance to change its state</term>, nor is it solidified by dry heat, nor frozen by any kind of cold <note>The author argues that if gems were just frozen water, they would melt like ice; therefore, a more complex process is at work</note>. Because of this, it is necessary that the water be slightly mixed with the finest earthy substance and, moreover, be very strongly acted upon by earthy dryness. In this way, the power of that dryness now holds sway over all parts of the moisture, yet it has not yet transformed the substance of that moisture into earth.

For in every <term>transformation of the elements: the Aristotelian theory that the four elements (earth, air, fire, water) can change into one another</term>, this state of being "acted upon" precedes the change of the substance itself. This means that the power of the transforming element takes hold of the whole, and the parts of the element being transformed are shaped within it before the substance actually changes. And if they are mixed in this way into some <term>compound: (Latin: elementatum) a physical body made of a mixture of elements</term>, that body will have the material of one element and the powers of another. This is the supreme insight of the alchemists, which *Hermes* <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> teaches in his *Secret of Secrets* through metaphorical words, saying: *“The Stone ascends gently with great skill from the earth to heaven, and again descends from heaven to earth; its nurse is the earth.”* <note>This is a famous quote from the "Emerald Tablet," a foundational text of Western alchemy</note>

"...is, and the wind carried it in its belly." <note>original: "portauit eum in uentre uentus suo"; this is a famous quote from the *Tabula Smaragdina* (Emerald Tablet), a foundational text of alchemy attributed to Hermes Trismegistus</note>. For when he intends to teach the works of alchemy, he says that the substance "ascends into heaven" when, through roasting and <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air to reduce it to a powder</term>, it takes on the properties of fire. Alchemists call calcination the burning and roasting of the substance which reduces the matter into powder. This matter then "descends again from heaven to earth" when it takes on the virtues of the earth through <term>inhumation: (literally "burial") in alchemy, this refers to placing a substance in the ground or in warm horse dung to provide a steady, gentle heat for maturation</term>. For then, through inhumation, that which had previously been "killed" (mortified) through calcination is brought back to life and nourished.

Furthermore, when he says that "the wind carries it in its belly," he is demonstrating the <term>levigation: the process of refining a substance into a very fine, light state, often through vaporization</term> of the matter by the power of the air. Because of this, he says the wind carries the matter in its belly when the matter is placed in an <term>alembic: a traditional distillation apparatus consisting of a boiling flask and a cooling cap with a "beak" or tube</term>, which is a vessel made in the same way as those used to make rose water. For then, by evaporating, the substance is made subtle and light, aligning with the powers of the air; for this reason, he says the wind carries the matter in its belly. Further, the liquid of water or oil <term>distills: drips down or flows from</term> the mouth of the alembic, containing within it all the virtues of the elements.

And indeed, art <note>In this context, "art" refers to human technology and alchemy</note> performs this with great labor and many errors, while nature does so without difficulty or labor. The reason for this is that the virtues existing in the matter of stones and metals are moved by certain and effective celestial powers when the matter is processed. Those virtues are the operations of <term>intelligences: in medieval cosmology, these were non-material beings or "Angels" that guided the movement of the stars and the development of life on Earth</term>, which do not err except by accident—specifically, due to the unevenness or impurity of the physical matter. In human art, however, none of these celestial powers are present; instead, art relies on the "begged assistance" <note>original: "mendicata fuffragia"; a metaphor suggesting that human craft is a poor, artificial imitation of divine nature</note> of human ingenuity and fire.

### Concerning the generative cause according to the diverse opinions of philosophers. Chapter 3.

The **efficient cause** <note>original: *causa efficiens*; the active agent or force that brings something into being</note> of stones is said by almost everyone who has written about stones to be the **mineral power** <term>mineral power (*uirtus mineralis*): a specialized force in nature believed to direct the formation of minerals and metals within the earth</term>. Since this power is common to both stones and all metals alike, it seems that the efficient cause of stones has been insufficiently defined, as these authors have not confirmed with any distinction or specific detail exactly what this "mineral power" they speak of actually is. Nor is anything more found in the works of <note>Avicenna (c. 980–1037): a Persian polymath whose writings on geology and medicine were foundational to Western science</note> **Avicenna** except that stones are generated from earth and water through this mineral power. 

**Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus: a legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational alchemical and philosophical texts were attributed</note>, however, in the book he wrote concerning universal power, seems to say that the generative cause of stones is a certain power which he claims is one and the same in all things, but which takes on different names because of the diversity of the things generated. He gives the example of the light of the sun, which alone...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical critique of the "efficient cause" of stones. The previous page introduced Hermes Trismegistus; here, the author examines Hermes's theory that planetary influence (specifically Mars) is the primary driver of mineral formation, before contrasting this with the views of Empedocles.</meta>

<page-num>119</page-num>
<header>BOOK I.</header>

[Hermes claims that this power] alone is the generative force of all things, and when it is shared, it works diverse operations within them, and not through only a single power of the passive elements. It pleased him to grant this power first indeed to **Mars** as the fountain of that virtue, but only to vary it according to the proportion of the application of the light of other stars and of the matter receiving it, as we have said. He argues that from this, diverse kinds of stones and metals are generated in diverse places. However, this statement is entirely unscientific <note>original: *innaturale*; in this context, it means contrary to the principles of natural philosophy or physics</note>, because here we are not seeking the first moving and acting causes—which are perhaps the stars and the powers and dispositions of the stars—for this belongs to the study of another science <note>likely referring to astrology or metaphysics</note>. Rather, we are seeking the **proximate efficient causes** which, existing within the matter, actually transform the matter. 

For if the statement of Hermes were sufficient, then by knowing the cause of the generation of all things capable of being generated, we would know the specific efficient cause of stones. We know that the motion and power of the heavens is a cause of a different nature than the physical world, involving the rising and setting of the stars and their rays. Furthermore, these celestial causes are **equivocal agents** <term>equivocal agents (*agentes aequivocae*): causes that produce effects different in kind from themselves, such as the sun (hot) producing coldness in certain objects or hardening clay while melting wax</term> and have no direct commonality with the matter of the things being generated. But we, according to the proper methods of natural science, seek causes that are specific to their effects and, most importantly, those that transform the matter **univocally** <term>univocal cause (*causa univoca*): a cause that produces an effect of the same nature or species as itself, like a fire producing fire</term>. 

Because of this, **Empedocles** <note>Empedocles (c. 490–430 BCE): a Greek philosopher who famously proposed that all matter is composed of four elements: earth, air, fire, and water</note>, who lived long after Hermes, confirmed the assertion that stones are generated by a parching heat. He drew this claim from the ancient fable told of **Pyrrha and Deucalion** <note>In Greek mythology, the only survivors of a great flood who repopulated the earth by throwing stones—the "bones" of their mother, the Earth—over their shoulders</note>, in which stones are called the "bones of the Great Mother."

<page-num>120</page-num>
-># ON MINERAL AFFAIRS<-
->## BOOK I##<-

<meta>catchword: These</meta>

Bones, according to **Empedocles**, are composed for the most part of the parts of **Fire** <note>original: *Vulcani*; the author uses the name of the Roman god of the forge to represent the element of fire</note>, but this is entirely false, since we know—and it will be shown below—that certain stones are generated from cold. For we have already stated in the book on *Meteorology* <note>referring to Aristotle’s *Meteorologica*</note> that those things whose material is water are solidified principally by cold. Furthermore, the saying of **Empedocles** is not sound because we have already shown in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle’s *De Anima*</note> that the hot element has the power to burn things into ashes, but it does not refine them into a specific form <term>specific form (*determinatam speciem*): the essential nature or "blueprint" that makes a thing what it is</term> unless it is moved by some other power and directed by it toward that form. This is similar to how digestive heat, moved by the soul, converts that which it transforms into the form of flesh, nerve, bone, and similar parts of a living body.

**Democritus**, however, and certain others say that every **elemental entity** <term>elemental entity (*elementatum*): a physical object composed of the four elements</term> possesses a soul, and that these souls are the causes of the generation of stones. For this reason, he claims that a soul exists in a stone just as it does in any other seed of a thing to be generated, and that this soul moves the heat intrinsic to the matter during the stone’s generation, in the same way that a hammer is moved by a blacksmith for the production of an axe or an iron tool. 

We have shown elsewhere that these views cannot stand. For a soul is not found in inanimate things, but first appears in **plants** <note>original: *uegetabilib.* (vegetabilibus); in medieval philosophy, plants possessed the lowest level of soul, responsible for growth and nutrition</note>. Indeed, stones possess no operation suitable to a soul, since they use neither nutrition nor sensation, nor life at all according to any vital act. To say that a soul exists in stones solely for the purpose of their generation is not sound, because their generation does not follow the same process as the generation of living plants and sentient animals.

-># BOOK I.<-

For we see all these things <note>referring to plants and animals mentioned on the previous page</note> produced from their own seeds, generated according to their specific kind; a stone, however, does none of these things at all. Nor do we see stones generated from other stones. Instead, we see each stone generated from some cause present in the place of its creation. Because of this, it appears that a stone possesses no **generative power** <term>generative power (*virtutem generativam*): the internal ability of an organism to reproduce its own kind, like a plant producing seeds</term> whatsoever.

However, some of those who have studied **alchemy** in our own time seem to claim that every stone is generated **by accident** <term>by accident (*per accidens*): occurring as a side-effect or by chance, rather than through a purposeful, essential process</term>, and that there is no other specific cause for its generation. For they say that fiery heat, wherever it is found, turns suitable material into stone by "roasting" it, just as happens with stone that is baked through the parching of fire <note>original: *lapide cocto*; likely referring to the production of bricks or quicklime</note>. 

And these stones are said to possess no specific **generative principle**, but only a **material principle** <note>meaning they are defined only by what they are made of, not by a guiding "force" that makes them what they are</note>. Furthermore, they claim that stones do not have any **substantial form** <term>substantial form (*formam substantialem*): the essential nature or "blueprint" that makes a thing what it is</term> according to their species, but rather they possess certain "passions" or accidental qualities of matter. They argue, for example, that a stone's "form" is simply its hardness, as was determined in the book *Meteorology* <note>referring to Book IV of Aristotle’s *Meteorologica*, which discusses the solidification of minerals</note>. According to this view, coagulation and the effects of coagulation are merely types and qualities of matter, and not substantial forms. 

These thinkers are persuaded toward this opinion by the operations of alchemists. In alchemy, stones and metals all seem to be produced and generated by one such effective force—**strong roasting**—because there is no need for a specific natural cause in a process where nothing is actually brought to a "substantial species" <note>a unique, essential category of being</note> due to the lack and defect of that very species. From this, however, follows an intolerable error: namely, that every stone would be of the exact same species as every other stone, and they would only differ by being "more or less" of that same material substance.

*It is also clear why the operations of the alchemists are difficult and imperfect—especially in the making of stones, even more so than in the making of metals. This is because they do not provide a formative power to the matter; instead, their uncertain art serves as their "formative power," and burning heat serves as their "instrument." This works in a most uncertain way. However, the power given by **heaven** <note>medieval science believed the stars and planets exerted a physical influence on the generation of minerals on Earth</note> to the location and the matter—which is called the formative power—is certain. It has the matter proportioned to the instrument, and the instrument proportioned to the matter, in a fitting way; and therefore nature is most certain in its operations. ### On the Substantial Form of Stones.
### Chapter 5

To doubt that stones have **substantial forms** <term>substantial forms (*formae substantiales*): the internal essence or "blueprint" that gives a physical object its specific identity and unique properties</term> would seem to be the act of a madman. Our own sight confirms that stones are all solidified, and the matter within them is fixed into a certain **species** <term>species: a distinct, stable category of being</term>. 

If stones were merely temporary arrangements of elements—caught in the middle of changing into one another or into other things, such as clouds, rain, and snow—they would undoubtedly not last very long. Like the weather, they would soon be broken back down into their original elements. Yet we observe the exact opposite to be true in the nature of stones; they are enduring and stable.

Furthermore, we find **virtues** <term>virtues (*uirtutes*): the inherent, often miraculous powers or "specialties" of a substance</term> in stones that do not belong to any simple element. These include powers such as driving away poison, repelling **carbuncles** <note>original: *antraces* — likely referring to deep red gemstones like garnets, which were historically believed to ward off infection or glow in the dark</note>, or the ability to attract or repel iron. Regarding these powers, as will be proven later, it is the common opinion of all wise men that such a virtue is a consequence of the specific form and species of this or that stone. 

It is clear, therefore, from these facts that stones possess determined forms and species. However, these forms are not **souls** <note>original: *animae*</note>, as it seemed to some of the ancient philosophers. For as we have shown in the book *On the Soul* and as was made clear in the beginning of the *Physics* <note>Referring to the works of Aristotle, which were the standard textbooks for natural science in the Middle Ages</note>, the soul is not

...[a soul] performs many actions of its own accord rather than by chance, but the nature of a stone performs only one action, and it does so by necessity—something a soul does not do. Furthermore, the primary function of a soul is life, yet not even a trace of this is found in a stone. For if a stone consumed nourishment, it would need to have pores and channels through which that food could pass into it. The very hardness and density of most stones prove this is not the case, as they cannot be divided or opened up to receive nourishment.

Moreover, if it used food, it would need a specific part to take it in—like the roots of plants or the mouths of sentient animals—but we see nothing of the sort in stones. Nor is it correct to say, as many <term>physiologists</term><note>original: "phisiologorum"; here meaning early natural philosophers who studied the laws of nature.</note> have, that a stone's soul is simply "weighed down" by its earthy material and thus unable to manifest life or sensation. If that were true, Nature would fail in providing the necessary tools for a stone to fulfill its needs; stones, therefore, do not have souls. 

Instead, they possess other <term>substantial forms</term><note>In medieval philosophy, the "substantial form" is the internal essence that makes a thing what it is.</note> granted by heavenly influences and the specific way their elements are mixed together. For the most part, these internal "forms" do not have specific names. Instead, we rely on the various names of the stones themselves—such as <term>tufa</term><note>original: "thofus"; a type of porous limestone.</note>, pumice, flint, marble, sapphire, emerald, and the like. Because the true inner nature of these stones is hidden from us, we cannot define them directly; instead, we must describe them indirectly by observing their outward characteristics and signs. ### BOOK I.

...there are differences between bodies that are simply mobile and changeable, and those that are a mixture—and a stone belongs to the category of mixtures. Since a mixture is divided into that which is merely mixed and that which is <term>complexioned</term><note>original: "complexionatum"; in medieval science, this refers to a balance of the four humors or qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) found in living organisms.</note>, we know that a stone is in the category of non-complexioned mixtures. Gathering all that has been said, we define a stone as a non-complexioned mixture, coagulated into its form by the power of minerals. 

From this, it is further clear that a stone is of a more <term>homogeneous</term><note>meaning uniform in its physical structure throughout.</note> nature than a living thing, even though the different natures of the elements are essentially present within it. For this reason, the science of stones must be studied before the science of complexioned [living] things. There are, moreover, many forms of stones, such as those in the genus of marble: <term>porphyry</term><note>a hard reddish-purple stone</note>, alabaster, and the like. 

It is the same in other kinds of stones, which it is not profitable to pursue here, because their forms will be revealed later through the <term>accidents</term><note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "accidents" are physical properties like color, texture, or hardness that do not change what a thing essentially is.</note> of their body and their hardness. These properties are specific to them, and once they are known, their nature is clear enough. As for the <term>final cause</term><note>original: "fine"; the purpose or goal for which a thing exists.</note>, there is no need to search for it, because in the study of physics, the "form" of a thing is its end. Therefore, since we consider ourselves to know a thing when we recognize its essential and proper causes, the nature of stones has now been universally understood in a general sense.

->ON METALLIC MATTERS<-

### On the discussion of the places in which stones are generated. Chapter 6.

Let us therefore make mention of the places in which stones are frequently generated, and let us inquire into the power of these places and their differences. We observe, moreover, that many stones are found on the banks of perennial waters, and through this we recognize that the banks of certain waters are places that generate stones. These types of banks differ, however, in that some produce stones more quickly and others more slowly. For in certain places on the banks of the river called the <term>Gion</term><note>original: "Gion"; likely referring to the Gihon, one of the four rivers of Paradise mentioned in Genesis, often identified by medieval scholars with the Nile or other major rivers.</note>, stones are generated within a span of 33 years, as <term>Avicenna</term><note>original: "Auicenna"; the Latinized name of Ibn Sina, a Persian polymath whose "Book of the Cure" included influential theories on the formation of minerals and stones.</note> and certain other philosophers testify. Yet not every body of water is generative of stones on its banks, because the marshy water of "corrupt earth" <note>meaning stagnant, boggy, or sulfurous soil that lacks the necessary mineral "virtue" to solidify matter.</note> destroys stones rather than generating them. This we see in certain regions where, although the locations are watery, they do not produce many stones.

Furthermore, we frequently find mountains to be stony, from which we know that in mountainous regions there is a place for the generation of stones. However, we sometimes find mountains without stones, but these are usually neither large nor joined to other mountains, but are found in isolation—so that there is perhaps only one alone, or at most two or three. Whenever many mountains are joined together, then stony mountains are found; and many stony mountains are also sometimes found in flat land with a solid surface, though this cannot happen everywhere, and those places are generative of stones. For this power is productive and generative of every element and of everything composed of elements.

And such a power is gathered in these places from three specific powers: The first is the power of the **motor** <note>In medieval cosmology, "motors" or "intelligences" were spiritual beings that moved the celestial spheres.</note> of the moved sphere. The second is the power of the moved sphere itself, with all its parts and the arrangements of those parts, which result from the motion of the parts as they relate to one another in different ways because of the varied speeds and slowness of the motors. The third is the **elementary power**, which is the qualities of hot, cold, moist, and dry, or a mixture of these.

The first of these powers is like a directing and forming "form" of everything that is generated, just as the skill of an artist relates to the material of the craft-work. The second is like the operation of the hand. And the third is like the operation of the tool, which is moved and directed by the hand toward the goal intended by the craftsman. For this reason, <term>Aristotle</term> says that "every work of nature is a work of intelligence"; for the location receives these powers just as the womb <note>original: "matrix"</note> receives the formative power of the embryo.

Therefore, this power—specifically directed toward the generation of stones in earthy or watery matter—is the common factor in all places where stones are created. For just as a life-giving power is infused from the stars into animals that are generated through <term>putrefaction</term> <note>original: "putrefactione"; the historical theory of "spontaneous generation," where life was thought to arise from decaying matter through celestial heat.</note>, so it also happens in the matter of stones: a stone-forming power is infused in the manner described above. # ON METALLIC MATTERS
<meta>catchword: converts</meta>

There is certainly a specific place for the **generation of stones**. For this reason, many stones are produced on a solid earth surface from which such **vapor** cannot escape. However, in soft, muddy earth—which stains the water rather than absorbing it—stones cannot be generated within its own properties. 

This explains why many stones are formed on the banks of permanent rivers; such banks are very solid and trap the rising vapors within themselves. These banks are full of vapor because heat—aroused by the reflection of light upon the water—is driven toward the shore by the coldness of the water. Once trapped in parts of the earth, this heat "cooks" <note>original: "decoquit"; a term from alchemy and Aristotelian physics referring to a process of maturation or hardening through heat, similar to how fruit ripens or clay is fired.</note> and hardens the earth that has been mixed with water. 

For this same reason, the beds of such rivers become stony. The heat on the banks penetrates the soil beneath the water, and since the water fills all the pores through which the heat might otherwise evaporate, it simultaneously mixes and "cooks" the mixture into stones. This is why such locations are generative of stones. 

Furthermore, there is a flow of certain waters through very powerful <term>mineral virtues</term> <note>original: "uirtutes minerales"; the inherent, quasi-magical or biological "powers" that medieval thinkers believed resided in nature to shape matter.</note>. When they flow through such materials, they become saturated with those minerals. Consequently, both the water and the objects submerged in it are converted into stone, sometimes quickly and sometimes slowly, depending on whether the **formative and creative power** of the stones is strengthened or weakened. 

The reason why a small amount of water separated near a riverbank or poured from a spring turns to stone faster than the main body of a flowing spring, river, or sea is that this power overcomes a small, isolated quantity more quickly than a large, unified mass. This is true for every power that transforms something; for every such power **converts** <note>This follows the catchword "conuertit" at the bottom of the original page.</note>...

That water can receive and be imbued with such a power is proven by other qualities water can take on, such as the taste of sulfur or **orpiment** <term>orpiment</term> <note>original: "auripigmentum"; a deep yellow arsenic sulfide mineral. Its name comes from the Latin "auripigmentum" (gold pigment) because of its color and its use in alchemy to attempt to create gold.</note>, or even bitterness. Water does not acquire these flavors unless it passes through the places where those substances exist.

The whole body of water becomes "infected" <note>original: "inficitur"; in this context, it means thoroughly permeated, saturated, or stained rather than a biological infection.</note> with this spirit and vapor; when this force is strong enough to overcome the nature of the water, it converts that water into stone. 

Yet, this power more easily converts earthy objects—such as wood, plants, and the bodies of animals or similar things. Because these objects are immersed in the water, they are seized by this power and drawn toward an earthy nature that matches the material of the stone. This mineral force, diffused like a vapor through the water, dries them out, coagulates them, and brings them into the form of a stone. 

In the highest mountains, there is a perpetual and extreme cold (the cause of which was explained in the *Meteorology* <note>original: "metheororum"; referring to Aristotle’s *Meteorologica*, the standard university textbook on natural phenomena and weather during the Middle Ages.</note>). By squeezing out moisture, this cold seizes water that has been frozen from snow and induces in it the property of "dryness"—which is the natural result of extreme cold. From that dryness, it coagulates the ice into **crystal** or some other transparent stone. By this reasoning, it is simple enough to understand the places where stones are generated, as well as their similarities and differences.

->ON MINERAL AFFAIRS<-

### On the power of a place and how it works upon the nature of stones, Chapter 8.

There remains one point that clarifies the understanding of everything that has been said. It is this: we must determine how the power of one thing seizes the substance of another and converts it into itself. This is explained by what we have said regarding the mutual **transmutation** <term>transmutation</term> <note>original: "transmutatio"; the process by which one substance changes into another by losing its original qualities and taking on new ones.</note> of the elements. 

For when earth converts water into itself, first the powers of the earth enter the substance [of the water] and alter it. Having achieved a kind of dominance over the water, these powers hold it fast; then the water begins to "stand" and take on a definite boundary, yet for a time it still retains its transparency. Finally, the water is **corrupted** <term>corrupted</term> <note>original: "corrumpitur"; in medieval science, "corruption" is the necessary breakdown of one form so that a new form (generation) can arise.</note> and passes into earth, receiving the qualities of earth, which are opacity and dryness. 

The same is true for other elements being transmuted into one another. Indeed, the process is entirely similar regarding the powers of **mixed bodies** <term>mixed bodies</term> <note>original: "mixtorum"; substances made of a combination of the four elements, such as plants, animals, or minerals.</note>, as is evident in the sap of plants and the food of animals. In these, the powers of living things <note>original: "animatorum"; literally "those with a soul," referring here to the biological processes of plants and animals.</note> first alter the matter, then hold it as if it were seized, and afterward convert it into a part of the body being nourished.

In exactly the same way, the **stone-making power** <term>stone-making power</term> <note>original: "uirtus lapidificatiua"; the specific formative force in nature that directs raw matter to crystallize or harden into a stone.</note> operates when it is diffused in a certain place. Whether it encounters water or earth, it first alters the matter it touches, then dominates and holds it, and once it has held and overcome the matter, it converts it into stone. This operation generally occurs in three ways, although in number...

->BOOK I.<-

<sig>I iv</sig>

Indeed, the ways of this power are infinite. One of these is when the power, seizing the **matter** <term>matter</term> <note>original: "materia"; the raw substance being acted upon, such as water or earth.</note>, alters it only according to the active and passive qualities by which it works within it; this is a weak **power** <term>power</term> <note>original: "uirtus"; the inherent force or "virtue" that drives natural change.</note>. 

In the second way, it happens that the power alters the matter both according to its qualities and according to the immediate effects of those qualities—which are hardness and softness—yet in such a way that **transparency** <note>original: "diaphanitas"; the quality of being clear or light-permeable.</note> and opacity are not removed from the matter. This is a stronger power, and it is in this manner that **transparent stones** <note>original: "lapides diaphani"; clear minerals like quartz or crystals.</note> are generated. 

In the third way, the power seizes the whole of the matter, both in its immediate and its subsequent effects; it then introduces new qualities, hardness, and softness, and changes the specific color of that matter entirely. In this way, non-transparent stones—or those not fully transparent—are sometimes generated from water, such as **chalcedony** <note>original: "calcedonius"; a translucent, often milky-blue variety of quartz.</note> and that which is called **toadstone** <note>original: "lapis buffonis"; a stone popularly believed to be found in the heads of old toads, but often actually fossilized teeth of ancient fish.</note>, as well as other stones. There are, however, many degrees in all these ways, which will be mentioned further below when **precious stones** are discussed. 

An example of this process is when an earthly force—which operates by cold compressing the moisture and by dryness—acts upon water in such a way that it remains water only by virtue of such dryness. Then, items washed in such water are dried and chilled intensely. **Alchemists** <term>alchemists</term> <note>original: "alchimici"; practitioners of the "Art" who sought to transform base metals and understand the secrets of matter.</note> study intensely how to produce such waters—which possess the qualities of various elements in potential <note>original: "uirtute & non actu"; literally "in power and not in act," meaning the qualities are latent within the substance rather than active.</note> rather than in actuality—so that through them they may dry and coagulate whatever they wish to **transmute** <term>transmute</term> <note>original: "transmutare"; the core alchemical goal of changing one substance into another.</note>. For this reason, they have books written concerning the **seven waters** <note>original: "septem aquis"; likely a reference to the various distilled liquids or "spirits" used in alchemical recipes.</note>.

### ON THE MATTER OF METALS ###

Sometimes, however, an **earthy power** <term>earthy power</term> <note>original: "uis terrea"; a natural force or "virtue" inherent in the element of earth that influences the formation of minerals.</note> seizes water such that the cold squeezes out the moisture, and the dryness fixes the matter within itself, while the transparency of the water remains. For the **clarity** <note>original: "peruietas"; the quality of being "pervious" to light, or transparent.</note> of water does not belong to it insofar as it is cold or moist or possesses both qualities, but insofar as it corresponds with the **celestial body** <note>In medieval science, transparency was considered a property shared with the "quintessence" or the unchanging material of the heavens/stars.</note>; therefore, this clarity belongs to the substance of water prior to its active and passive qualities according to nature, because it is more fundamental to the elements than any of those qualities. 

And when the coldness and dryness of the earth work in this way, their immediate effects—which are hardness and **coagulation** <note>original: "coagulatio"; the process of a liquid thickening or solidifying into a solid mass.</note>—are necessarily brought into the water, and thus a **transparent stone** <note>original: "lapis peruius"; a stone that light can pass through, such as crystal or quartz.</note> is formed. 

Sometimes, however, this power prevails further, bringing the substance of water toward opacity and the nature of earth. And then, an **opaque stone** <note>original: "lapis opacus"</note> and perhaps a very black one is made from water, just like certain pebbles found in abundance on riverbanks; these, however, are sometimes generated from earthy matter, as we shall show below. 

Just as we have spoken regarding earth, so it should be understood regarding the qualities of all elements. It must be added that the power of the element is the material cause, while the **celestial power** <term>celestial power</term> <note>original: "uirtus cœlestis"; the astrological or spiritual influence from the stars that provides the "form" or "blueprint" for the stone.</note> is the instrumental and formal cause—the power of the "mover." What results from all these is a power infused into the matter and the location of the stones, as has been sufficiently stated in the preceding sections. 

Therefore, let the causes from which the **generation of stones** <note>original: "generatio lapidum"</note> is generally known be sufficiently determined in this manner.

BOOK I.

# PREFACE TO THE SECOND TREATISE OF THE FIRST BOOK ON
### minerals and metallic things, which is concerning
### the properties of stones
### Preface.

Now, however, we must speak of those things which happen to stones essentially. The **accidents** <term>accidents</term> <note>original: "accidentia"; in medieval philosophy, these are non-essential properties or characteristics (like color, texture, or hardness) that "happen" to a substance, rather than being its core essence.</note> that primarily occur in stones in general are many; however, the first among them is the **mixture of matter** <note>original: "commixtio materiae"; the way the constituent elements of earth and water are blended.</note>. 

Let us say that if the matter is extremely dry, then it will not be easily mixable, and then the site of formation will be either porous and not solid, or solid. If it is not porous but solid, a single, very **sandy stone** <term>sandy stone</term> <note>original: "lapis sabulosus"; likely referring to sandstone or a friable mineral aggregate.</note> is generated. When such a stone is handled, it sheds sandy fragments; its character varies according to the degree of dryness and the heat **coagulating** <note>original: "coagulantis"; the process of thickening or solidifying into a solid mass.</note> it, because sometimes it is easily rubbed into sand when excessive heat has dried it out. 

And if the place of formation is very porous, through which the heat "cooking" the **oily earth** <note>original: "terram unctuosam"; medieval mineralogists believed minerals were formed from a combination of "watery" and "unctuous" or oily substances, the latter being associated with sulfurous properties.</note> escapes in every direction, then that heat divides the matter into small pieces and cooks it into fine sand. And if the matter was very **viscous** <note>original: "uiscosa"; sticky or glue-like.</note>, then once divided, it is reduced into small pebbles of various sizes which are very hard and of various colors due to the diversity of the matter. 

Stones, however, which are perfectly smoothed when they are cut, and whose scraped-off dust is extremely fine, are made from matter that is perfectly mixed. In these, moisture first operated to make every part of the dry matter flow toward every [other part]...

# ON METALLIC THINGS
### Page 136

Sometimes, however, an **earthy power** <term>earthy power</term> <note>original: "uis terrea"; the formative force associated with the element of earth, which provides solidity and dryness.</note> seizes the water in such a way that the cold then squeezes out the moisture, and the dryness defines the matter, while the **transparency** <note>original: "transparentia"</note> of the water remains within it. For the **perviousness** <term>perviousness</term> <note>original: "peruietas"; the quality of being "pervious" to light, what we today call transparency.</note> of water does not belong to it insofar as it is cold or moist, or possesses both qualities, but rather insofar as it corresponds with the **celestial body** <note>original: "cœlesti corpore"; medieval thinkers believed that transparency was a "heavenly" property shared by the stars and clear substances like water or crystal.</note>. Therefore, this transparency belongs to the substance of water prior to its active and passive qualities according to nature, because it is more fundamental to the elements than any of the active and passive qualities <note>The "active" qualities are hot and cold; the "passive" qualities are moist and dry. The author argues that transparency is a more basic property than these four.</note>. 

And when the coldness and dryness of the earth operate in this way, their immediate effects are necessarily brought into the water—namely, **hardness and coagulation** <note>original: "durities et coagulatio"; the process of a liquid thickening and hardening into a solid.</note>—and then a **transparent stone** <term>transparent stone</term> <note>original: "lapis peruius"; likely referring to rock crystal or clear quartz.</note> is formed. At other times, however, the earthy power prevails further, bringing the substance of water toward **opacity** and the nature of earth. Then, from the water, an **opaque stone** is formed, perhaps even a very black one, like certain small stones found in abundance on riverbanks. These, however, are sometimes generated from earthy matter, as we shall show below. 

Just as we have spoken about the element of earth, so it should be understood to happen regarding the qualities of all elements. It must be added that the power of the element becomes the **material cause**, while the celestial power—acting as both the instrument and the **formal cause**—becomes the moving power. What results from all of these is a power infused into the matter and the specific location where the stones are found, as has been sufficiently stated in the preceding sections. Therefore, let this be the conclusion of our determination regarding the general causes from which the generation of stones is understood.

->DE REB. METAL.<-

...and afterward the moisture that was taken up was dried out; therefore, such a stone is well-mixed. For that which is **fine** <note>original: "subtile"; refers to matter that is thin, refined, or composed of very small particles.</note> and **moist** is easily mixable, since it can penetrate the parts and the "parts of the parts," just as was stated in the second book of *On Generation and Corruption* <note>original: "perigeneos"; referring to Aristotle's *De Generatione et Corruptione*, a foundational text for medieval science.</note>. Above all others, however, those stones are well-mixed which are composed **by means of vapors** <note>original: "uaporabiliter"; the theory that minerals form from underground gases or "exhalations" rather than just liquid or solid sediment.</note>, and these above all others can be polished well and made brilliant. This is because the substance of vapor already approaches the fineness of air and moisture, and these two are finer and more mutually-penetrating when in the form of air than when in the form of water and earth. 

From these same causes come **compaction** <term>compaction</term> <note>original: "compactio"; the density or "tightness" of the stone's internal structure.</note> and good **continuity**—or their opposites. For whatever materials are excellently mixed, provided that the cooking heat does not dry out the moisture [too quickly], these possess the best continuity and a strong compaction. 

We see a sign of this in the works of art <note>The author uses "art" to mean human craft or technology, which mimics the processes of "nature."</note> which change the nature of things. For those who make **bricks** first mix the earth with certain things that cause the parts to hold together, such as horse dung or something of that sort; once the material has been made sticky, they strive to mix these things perfectly. The better these are mixed, the smoother and more compact the stones [bricks] become. 

**Potters** do the same thing: they do not take just any earth, but a tenacious kind called **clay** <note>original: "glis"; a term used by ancient writers like Pliny for a particularly sticky, fatty type of clay.</note> when they wish to mold something from mud. They mix it thoroughly before they mold it, then they allow the moisture to settle in it for a time, draw out the excess moisture in the sun, and finally harden the vessels in the fire by the process of digestion called **firing** <note>original: "optefis," a Latinization of the Greek *optēsis*, meaning baking or firing in a kiln.</note>. It is necessary, therefore, for Nature to follow this same method in its mixing.

...mixture of stones. Therefore, the earth is first penetrated by moisture, whether in physical [liquid] or **vaporous** <note>original: "spirituali"; referring to the "spirits" or gases that medieval philosophers believed moved through the earth.</note> form. Then, either the excess moisture is separated from it, or over a long period, a binding moisture becomes entwined within it, which cannot be extracted by **transformative heat** <note>original: "calorem opteticum"; from the Greek *optētikos*, referring to the "cooking" or "baking" heat of the earth that matures minerals into their final form.</note>. Through this process of **digestion** <term>digestion</term> <note>In medieval science, "digestion" refers to the steady application of heat to mature or transform a substance, much like how the stomach processes food.</note>, the material is converted into stone.

If we find some earth near those stones that is not fully bonded together, we know that the material was subjected to the process but remained "undigested." Furthermore, the types of stones formed from water—which has been acted upon by cold, dry, earthy qualities—are excellently compacted and appear polished. This is because water is naturally smooth, and its parts flow into one another, **coagulating** and **freezing** into stone with such continuity. Let this conclude our discussion on the mixture of stones.

### On those things which are well and poorly mixed. Chapter 1.

The method for determining the **colors of stones** <note>original: "coloribus lapidum"</note> must be drawn from the book *On Sense and the Sensed* <note>original: *De Sensu et Sensato*; a foundational work by Aristotle on how we perceive physical qualities.</note>, the science of which we will present later at the appropriate time. Therefore, what we assume here will be made clear there. 

It is assumed here that whatever is **transparent** <term>transparent</term> <note>original: "perspicuum"; used to describe materials like glass, crystal, or clear water that allow light to pass through.</note> in any kind of body arises from many transparent parts that come together in the composition of that body. Furthermore, **whiteness** is caused by many transparent parts arranged or "determined" in a different manner.

# ON METALLIC MATTERS

**Blackness**, however, arises from the opaque parts of a body overwhelming the transparent parts contained within that same body. **Intermediate colors** are caused by a combination of these in three ways, as will be explained in the science concerning the generation of sensible things <note>original: "scientia de sensibilium generatione"; a reference to Aristotle’s *On Sense and the Sensible*, a standard textbook in medieval universities.</note>. 

Let us say, then, that all **transparent stones** are formed from a great deal of the matter of **air and water** which has been frozen and gathered together by a gripping **earthy substance** <note>original: "terrestri appræhendente materia"</note>. If that transparency lacks any specific color and remains the transparency of air or water, it is a sign that only intense cold has seized the matter. This is seen in the transparency of **Crystal**, **beryl**, **adamant**, and the stone called the **Iris**. 

However, these stones differ in their transparency and their "watery" nature. **Crystal** <note>original: "Cristallus"; usually referring to clear quartz.</note> seems to possess not just the matter of water, but a wateriness that leans toward **airiness**; for this reason, it is extremely transparent and tends toward perfect clarity. **Beryl**, however, leans more toward water; thus, when it is turned, it looks as if large drops of water are flowing within it.

**Adamant** <term>adamant</term> <note>From the Greek *adamas*, meaning "unconquerable." While this often refers to the diamond, medieval writers used it for any exceptionally hard, dark mineral.</note>, on the other hand, has a wateriness pulled toward **earthy dryness**. Because of this, it is darker and exceptionally hard, to the point that it can crush other metals—except for the hardest **steel** <note>original: "calibem"; referring to *chalybs*, a high-quality steel named after the Chalybes, ancient ironsmiths.</note>. This is because steel also consists of very dry wateriness and earthiness. Therefore, it happens that when an adamant has sharp angles, it cuts and carves through all **iron** and penetrates every metal by slicing into it. 

The **Iris stone** <note>original: "Yris"; likely a reference to a prismatic crystal or a rainbow-colored gemstone like opal or iridescent quartz.</note> is formed from water that is almost like falling dew, frozen partly from vapor and partly from melted dew. Because of this, when placed in the sun, it casts the colors of the **rainbow** onto the opposite wall. Other stones similar to these are produced from similar materials

...materials. For along the banks of rivers, stones of varying degrees of dim transparency are very frequently found. Their color is caused solely by a transparent substance, either on its own or mixed with an obscure earthy matter in part or in whole. Because the cause of these colors is easily known from what has already been said, I shall pass over them.

**Black color** in stones is most frequently caused by burnt earthy matter; because of this, black stones are often very hard and are more suitable for polishing than for cutting. This color arises only from the lack of transparency within the mixture, as will be shown when the science of colors is discussed <note>original: "de scientia colorum"; referring to the medieval study of optics and the nature of light and color.</note>.

**Intermediate colors** consist of the genus of red, green, and yellow, and their various shades. As will be stated in the book *On the Senses* <note>original: "libro de sensibilibus"; likely a reference to Aristotle's *De Sensu et Sensibili*, a foundational text for medieval physics.</note>, red occurs when a thin, ignited smoke is infused into a luminous, transparent substance. For this reason, Aristotle says that all of these are hot by nature.

They differ, however, in their redness. If there is great transparency and the diffused smoke is very thin and bright, the color is that of the stone called the **Palace Ruby** <note>original: "Palacius" or "Palacium"; commonly known as the Balas ruby, which modern gemology identifies as a spinel.</note>. If, however, there is great transparency and the smoke is thick, like a kindled fire, then the color is that of what is truly called a **carbuncle**. This stone, when it truly reaches the perfection of its kind, shines in the darkness like a **night-shiner** <note>original: "noctiluca"; usually a reference to a glow-worm or something bioluminescent. Medieval lore claimed the finest rubies could illuminate a dark room.</note>, and especially when clear and limpid water is poured over it. Although there is a different kind of greenness in each of them, the colors of all these are generated from one and the same cause. For they are formed from a transparent watery substance mixed with strongly burnt earthy matter; and according to whether this is clearer or less clear, that greenness also becomes brighter or dimmer. **Evidence of this is found in glass that is made from a mixture of lead; for this is very green, and it is made purer the more often and the more intensely it is burned. In repeated burning, the transparency is purified and refined, and the brightness of the fiery light is more deeply infused into the watery nature, and therefore it is made clear.**

# CONCERNING METALLIC MATTERS
## ON THE COLORS OF GEMS

...stone <note>original: "lapidem"; continuing from the previous page's discussion of the onyx.</note>. Moreover, onyx stones <note>original: "onichini"</note> are found having very red veins and very white ones; it is not difficult to find the causes of these colors from the principles stated previously. 

The snowy spark <note>Referring to the unique brilliance of the "Orphan" stone mentioned on the previous page.</note> is undoubtedly caused by the fact that the stone itself is mixed from a transparent body that is, as it were, solidified. For the dust of every transparent substance is found to be extremely white, and when this "dust" is continuous and compacted, the result is a shining white body, like a pearl <note>original: "margarita"</note>. This occurs from the reverberation of light against the surfaces of the polished internal parts, because of which the stone is said to shine somewhat in the dark like a glow-worm <note>original: "noctiluca"; literally "night-shiner," referring to bioluminescent organisms or phosphorous materials.</note>. For during the day, the light that is incorporated into the transparency within the stone is hidden because of the greater ambient light; but in the night it shines, and therefore during the day that stone appears white, but acts like a night-shiner. A perfect account of all these matters is to be handed down in the science of the generation of sensible things <note>A reference to Aristotle’s *De Sensu et Sensibili* (On Sense and the Sensible), which medieval scholars used to explain the physics of light and color.</note>. 

Moreover, a stone is found of very many colors, because of which it is also called the panther <note>original: "panthera"; likely a variety of multi-colored agate or jasper whose spots resembled the hide of a panther.</note>. All of its colors are caused by the diverse substances from which its parts are composed; for the same reasoning applies to the whole and to the part regarding the tinting of the body. 

Thus, so many and such things have been said regarding the knowledge of the colors found in precious stones. Furthermore, the amethyst <note>original: "Ametistus"</note> follows the ruby <note>original: "rubinum"</note> in having a dark transparency. And chalcedony <note>original: "calcedonius"</note> follows beryl <note>original: "berillum"</note> in being a substance that is, as it were, a yellow and dregs-filled <note>original: "feculenta"; referring to a cloudy or sediment-like appearance.</note> transparency, just as lead imitates silver.

### Chapter 3: On the colors of transparent stones that are not bounded and are not precious.

These stones, however, which are found to have a transparent and non-bounded <note>original: "non terminatæ"; referring to stones that do not grow in specific crystalline shapes or are found in large, indefinite masses rather than individual gems.</note> substance, are of very many colors. Generally speaking, they are of four types: namely, flint <term>flint; original: "silices"</term>, tufa <term>tufa; original: "thophi," a porous rock formed from volcanic ash or calcium carbonate</term>, freestone <term>freestone; original: "quadrum," a stone that can be cut in any direction, often used in masonry</term>, and marble <term>marble; original: "marmor"</term>. In all these types, many colors are found, such as black, a bluish-gray <note>original: "glaucus"</note> that is slightly greenish, and white. Outside the category of marbles, a large red stone is rarely found, but small red ones are found especially within the various types of marble.

Regarding all these types of colors, the same reasoning applies as was stated in the preceding sections. However, it happens in the various types of marble that pieces broken off from them sparkle somewhat, as if metals were mixed into them. This occurs because a transparent substance enters into their mixture; when the surface of this substance is thickened in certain parts, it shines or sparkles. This is one of the reasons why the genus of marble is considered more noble than other types of stone.

Blackness, however, in such a type of stone is frequently caused by a mixture of sooty earth <note>original: "terrestri fuliginoso"</note> that has been coagulated. Whiteness, on the other hand, comes from a very fine earthy substance mixed with much water; for this turns white when "cooked" <note>original: "decoctum"; a reference to the Aristotelian idea that heat "digests" or matures mineral substances.</note> by heat, just as the earthy substance does in cheese and milk.

<summary>This page categorizes common, non-precious stones like marble, flint, and tufa, explaining their color and luster. It attributes the sparkle of marble to transparent inclusions and explains the presence of black and white tones through the "cooking" of earthy and watery mixtures.</summary>

->ON METALLIC MATTERS<-

Bluish-gray <note>original: "glaucus"; a color ranging from pale yellow-green to light blue-gray</note>, however, is caused by an opaque earthy substance that has slightly altered a white substance, which itself began to coagulate from fine earthy and watery components. Green <note>original: "virens"</note>, in every kind of stone, is caused by a large amount of watery substance, with vapors bedewing the mixture as it coagulates. The genus of freestone <term>freestone; original: "quadrum," a stone that can be cut in any direction, often used in masonry</term>, however, possesses several or all of these mixtures in its various parts because of the many types of matter gathered in that location. 

Tufa <term>tufa; original: "thophia"</term> is frequently either earthy in color or white like pumice. For this type of stone is generated from earth in which foaming water has mixed with that same earth; therefore, when it is coagulated by heat through the process of digestion <note>In medieval science, "digestion" refers to the transformation of matter through steady heat.</note> called *optesis* <note>original: "optesis"; an Aristotelian term for "baking" or "roasting" by dry heat.</note>, it is found to be spongy and light. Pumice, however, is formed from a large amount of water whose foam has been strongly affected by the earthy matter mixed into it; it is white because of the whiteness of such foam. 

Among the varieties of marble, the white type called alabaster <term>alabaster; original: "alabastrum"</term> is undoubtedly composed of a large amount of transparent substance that has been altered and intensely affected by fine earthy matter; this results in its most noble, sparkling color. That which is called porphyry <term>porphyry; original: "porphyriticum marmor"</term> has the color of dark flesh with small white spots <insert>and we have already explained the cause of such a color</insert>. Flints <term>flints; original: "silices"</term> are truly for the most part dark in color, the cause of which has also been sufficiently explained. Let what has been said thus far regarding the colors of stones be sufficient.

## On the cause of the various degrees of hardness found in stones.
### Chapter 4.

We shall speak next about the overall nature of hardness, which is found in many varieties among stones. For all types of precious stones are so hard that a file cannot remove anything from them; indeed, when struck together forcefully, as if against hardened steel, they give off sparks of fire.

On the contrary, however, almost every kind of tufa <term>tufa; original: "thophus," a porous rock formed from volcanic ash or calcium carbonate</term> is found to have so little hardness that it can be cut with a small tool. Moreover, certain white stones, which are commonly called chalk <term>chalk; original: "creta"</term>, and even some that are found to be softer and whiter, possess the least amount of hardness in the genus of stones. Every kind of flint <term>flint; original: "silex"</term> is extremely hard, and after these, marbles follow in their own category. Freestone <term>freestone; original: "quadrum," a stone suitable for masonry that can be cut in any direction</term>, however, is of medium hardness among stones, and yet within that type, one finds both greater and lesser degrees of hardness. 

But this commonly happens to the harder stones: when they have lain in the open air for a long time during cold weather, they later split into many pieces when exposed to the sun. On the other hand, those stones that are less hard—unless they are poorly mixed, almost like burnt lime <term>lime; original: "calx"</term>—become better and harder for use in buildings the longer they lie in the air, provided they are properly hardened through the process of "baking" <note>original: "optesi coagulante," referring to the Aristotelian concept of *optesis* or roasting by dry heat mentioned on the previous page</note>; such stones do not split because of the cold. It is the task of the natural philosopher <note>original: "Physici"; in this historical context, one who studies the physical laws of nature</note> to assign the cause of these properties based on the material and the efficient cause, just as has been stated regarding other matters. Let us say, therefore, that the general cause of hardness is dryness <term>dryness; original: "siccitas," one of the four primary qualities in medieval physics</term>.

[Vocabulary: hardness, stones, tufa, chalk, flint, marbles, freestone, lime, dryness]

<meta>catchword: in cementi</meta>

Since a hard thing has the natural power to resist what touches it, and a soft thing, by its nature, lacks that power, hardness cannot be caused except by dryness, which stands firm by itself and does not yield to anything else. In the nature of stones, dryness is caused by two things, as was shown above. Either it arises because heat has "drunk up" the moisture from earthy material, thus leaving the earth hardened; or it arises because extreme cold dryness <note>Medieval science often attributed the formation of crystals and gems to extreme cold "freezing" moisture into a permanent state.</note> has violently seized hold of transparent moisture and, by converting it into its own property, has squeezed out the liquid, violently compressing and hardening the material and binding it together excellently. This is the case in transparent stones, which is why they are extremely hard, emit sparks of fire when struck, and cannot be worked with a file <note>original: "non sustinent limam"</note>; instead, they must be polished by a process of sliding and rubbing. 

In other stones made from earthy material, the cause of greater hardness is nothing other than a greater aridity. This is caused either by a stronger or weaker heat on the part of the efficient cause <note>In Aristotelian terms, the "efficient cause" is the agent that brings something about—here, the heat acting upon the matter.</note>, and by how easily or difficultly the moisture can be separated from the material. As far as the matter itself is concerned, moisture that is very oily <note>original: "unctuosum"</note> is held together easily, while that which is entirely watery evaporates easily. For this reason, stones like chalk <term>chalk; original: "creta"</term>, or those even softer than chalk, are very white and leave a white stain on things they touch. This is because they were mixed with a moisture that evaporates very easily, and they were burned by intense heat beyond the proper limit of coagulation <note>Coagulation refers to the process of a liquid thickening into a solid.</note>. They have even begun to calcine <term>calcine; original: "calcinari," to be reduced to a powdery residue by heat</term>; for this reason, they do not remain stable in walls, because they are always rough on the outside from the calcined dryness, and this flakes away

When they are extremely hard, their dryness is great and they possess very little moisture to hold their parts together. When this moisture is frozen by cold, it leaves the outer parts and flees to the interior. Such moisture is not well-incorporated into the parts of the stone, and thus it moves easily between the interior and exterior; because of this, after the compressing cold has made the moisture mobile, it is "drunk up" by the nearby heat of the sun, and then the stone is split apart.

On the other hand, stones that are somewhat moist—where the moisture is well-embedded into the "limbs" of the stone—are dried out thoroughly by the air, and therefore they become harder and better for buildings over a long period of time. In types of tufa <term>tophus: a porous, lightweight rock often formed from volcanic ash or calcium deposits</term>, however, the cause of their softness is that the moisture has not been strongly extracted nor excellently mixed with the earthy matter.
