...unless they were softened with **goat's blood** <note>original: "sanguine hircino"; medieval lapidaries frequently claimed that only goat's blood could soften a diamond or other hard gems for engraving</note>, and even then it would be a waste and far too expensive, because we sometimes see gems of little value that have been engraved. Therefore, what we have learned by experience we also state here: **steel** <term>chalybs</term> is distilled and purified repeatedly until it has almost the whiteness of silver, and from it are formed iron instruments and engravers' tools with appropriate and fine angles. Then, **radish juice** <note>original: "succus raphani"</note> is squeezed out and mixed with water extracted from **earthworms** <note>original: "lumbricis terræ"</note> that have been crushed and pressed through a cloth, in equal parts of each. These things, then, have been said concerning the cause of the **images** <note>here referring to natural patterns or figures that appear to be "pictures" inside stones</note> that appear in gems. If anyone should ask why images are not found in other stones except gems, we would say that we have previously introduced the fact that they sometimes appear in **marble** <note>original: "marmore"</note>, but they do not appear in other kinds of stones because their material is heavy, coarse, and earthy, and it is disobedient to the **moving powers** <term>uirtutibus mouentibus; the celestial influences believed to shape the physical world</term>. For this reason, the heavens cannot move or impress it. However, precious stones and certain marbles, as we said above, possess **vaporous materials** <note>original: "uaporales... materias"</note> that easily obey these moving powers, and therefore such images are generated in them. An example of this is found in **seminal vapors** <note>original: "uaporibus seminalibus"</note> in which images easily appear, whereas they are not impressed in the solid substance of the brain, the head, or the bone. ...and the unsuitability of the material, as we have said frequently in preceding sections. It is like this: if a **seal** <note>original: "sigillum"</note> touches a stone or hard earth, it is not impressed at all. However, if it touches water, it is impressed; and if that water is then frozen, the shape remains in the ice. These explanations are not entirely based on **physics** <note>original: "physica"; here referring to the natural science of the time</note>, yet they are included here for the sake of clear instruction.

### On the reason why gems were first ordered to be engraved, and what benefit lies in these seals.

### Chapter 3.

Now let us determine the reason why gems were first ordered to be engraved by the **wise men** <note>original: "sapientibus"; the author refers to the ancient masters of natural philosophy and astral science</note>, and what benefit is found in those seals of theirs. The cause of this must be understood through the **science of the Magi** <note>original: "scientia magorum"; in this context, it refers to the study of how celestial bodies influence the earthly realm, rather than "magic" in the modern sense</note>. This science was established by **Magot the Greek**, **Germa the Babylonian**, and **Hermes the Egyptian** <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of hermetic philosophy</note> in the earliest times. Later, the wise **Ptolemy** <note>the famous 2nd-century astronomer and astrologer</note> and **Geber of Seville** <note>Geber Hispalensis, likely Jabir ibn Aflah, a 12th-century mathematician and astronomer</note> shone marvelously in this field, while **Thabit** <note>Thabit ibn Qurra, a 9th-century scholar known for his work on talismans and the "motion of the eighth sphere"</note> transmitted the art in its entirety.

The fundamental principle in this science is that everything that is produced—whether by nature or by art—is moved primarily by **celestial powers** <term>uirtutibus cœlestibus; the spiritual or physical influences believed to emanate from the stars and planets</term>. In the case of nature, this is beyond doubt. Regarding art, it is also evident because something incites the heart of a person to act at a specific moment and not before; this cannot happen except through a celestial power, as the aforementioned wise men state. For there is in man a twofold principle of works: nature...

...namely both the will and nature. Nature, indeed, is ruled by the **stars** <note>original: "syderibus"</note>, while the will is indeed free; but unless the will resists, it is drawn along by nature and becomes hardened. And since nature is moved by the motions of the stars, the will then begins to be inclined toward the motions and **celestial configurations** <note>original: "figuras"</note> of the stars. **Plato** <note>The author likely refers to the Platonic idea that the soul's inclinations are shaped by its cosmic origin, or perhaps to the *Timaeus*.</note> proves this from the actions of children, who, in the freedom of their will, do not yet resist nature and the inclination of the stars. 

For these children, through the power of the stars, demonstrate in themselves beforehand a natural aptitude for one art or another. If they are trained in that art, they will be made perfect; but if they resist it and practice other things, they never achieve perfection because of the ineptitude of their nature for that specific art. Now, we do not doubt that everything which is in some way a cause of a cause is also, in some way, the cause of the result. Therefore, if the force and **influence** <note>original: "afflatus"; literally a "breathing upon" or inspiration</note> of the stars pours a certain artistic causality into the artisan, then certainly—unless it is hindered—it will pour something of its own power into all the works of that art. 

With these principles established, we accept from the aforementioned philosophers (which must also be proven elsewhere) that the figures of the heavens are the primary figures, existing before the figures of all things produced by nature or art. Furthermore, that which is first in the genus and order of things that generate undoubtedly pours its **causality** <note>the capacity to act as a cause</note> into all things that follow, in a manner suitable to each. 

For we do not intend to speak here of figures taken from **mathematics** <note>original: "mathematica"; referring to abstract geometric shapes without physical power</note>, but rather of figures insofar as they bring about the diversity of things that generate and are generated, in their order, species, and the nature of their form and matter. ...nature is [formed] according to how it proceeds from its celestial principle. The source of this principle is the **practical intellect** <note>original: "intellectus practicus"; in medieval philosophy, this refers to the mind’s ability to apply knowledge to action or the creation of objects.</note>, just as that same intellect is the source of art, as we have frequently stated in our works on the *Heavens and the Earth* and *Physics*. From these points, it is necessarily concluded that if a figure is imprinted into matter by nature or by art while observing a **celestial figure** <note>original: "cœlestem figuram"; the specific arrangement of stars and planets at a given moment.</note>, then some power of that celestial figure is infused into the work of nature or art.

It is for this reason that the wise **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer and astrologer whose works were foundational to medieval science.</note> prescribes that the performance of tasks, departures and arrivals, and even the cutting and wearing of clothes should be done while observing the images of the heaven. This is also why, in the science of <term>Geomancy</term> <note>A method of divination that interprets patterns of points; the author argues these points must correspond to astrological signs to be effective.</note>, it is commanded that the figures of points be reduced to such images, for otherwise they are of no use. 

Considering this diligence, the first teachers and professors of **natural philosophy** <note>original: "physici"; in this context, those who study the laws of the physical world.</note> ordered that gems and metallic images be engraved according to the images of the stars. They did this at observed times when the celestial power was proven to be strongest for that specific image—for instance, when it was mixed with many celestial virtues—and they performed wonders through such images. 

These images of the heaven are indeed assisted by many factors, but there are five principal things to be observed: 
1. First, the image of the **non-stellar circle** <note>original: "circuli non stellati"; likely referring to the tropical zodiac or the *Primum Mobile*, which provides the primary motion and mathematical framework of the heavens.</note>, because the circle of signs without stars is the first to possess the motion of figure and life. 
2. Second, it is helped by the **stellar images** <note>The actual constellations of fixed stars.</note>, which must also be duly observed. 
3. Third is the position of the **planets** in the signs, which strengthen those signs. 
4. Fourth is the quantity of elevation and distance—measured by longitude and latitude—from the **equinoctial line** <note>The celestial equator.</note> and the **ascendant** <note>The point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at a specific time.</note>. 
5. And fifth, from the relationship of all these things to the latitude of the **climate**... <note>original: "cli="; likely *clima*, referring to the geographic latitudinal zones of the Earth.</note>

But let it not escape our notice that, just as natural powers endure for a certain time and no longer, so it is with the powers of images. For no power is flowed down from heaven except during a certain time within a **period** <note>original: "periodi"; a specific cycle of time or planetary alignment.</note>, as we have said at the end of the *Perigeneos* <note>original: "perigeneos"; likely a reference to a work on the generation of things, possibly Albertus Magnus’s own commentary on "Generation and Corruption."</note>. Afterward, the cause [of the power] ceases and the image remains cold, dead, and useless. This is the reason why certain images do not work in this current time as they did in ancient times. Hence, in **Astronomy**, different "years" are distinguished for the images of the heaven, the **planets**, and certain **stars**. They are said to have "greater," "middle," and "lesser" years, during which they manifest their effects more strongly, less strongly, or moderately.

For the exact same reason, the triplicity of the watery signs is called northern, **&** the fiery triplicity is called Eastern, **&** the fourth, the airy, is called western. To say that an image is northern or southern, etc., is the same as saying that such an image is impressed with [the power of] this triplicity; it does **not** mean that it has more or less power in this or that region of the world. Nevertheless, if at the time of the fashioning of the image the wind of that triplicity is blowing strongly, the **celestial effect** is known to be strong, **&** therefore the image is presumed to be more effective.

Furthermore, it must be known most skillfully that specific celestial effects require specific **observed materials** for their images; **&** therefore the ancients—who did not work with only one stone or metal, but now with one and now with another according to the variety of the celestial figures—commanded that the materials which were to be shaped be prepared accordingly. In this way, for the sake of obtaining wisdom, it is read that **King Pyrrhus** <note>Pyrrhus of Epirus (c. 319–272 BCE), a Greek king and general.</note> wore an **agate** on his finger in which, with marvelous beauty, the nine **muses** were engraved, with **Apollo**, the god of wisdom, in the middle holding a lyre in his hand. ## 5. On the Meanings of Images on Stones.

Although the points already discussed are undoubtedly sufficient for our current purpose, we shall nevertheless, for the comfort of our readers, set down certain things concerning the **meanings of images**, and afterwards concerning their **bindings and suspensions** <note>original: "ligaturis & ſuſpenſionibus"; refers to the practice of wearing talismans bound to the body or hanging as pendants.</note>, and finally, we shall complete this treatise on stones. To speak generally and in common terms, then: **Aries**, **Leo**, or **Sagittarius** engraved [on stones]—on account of the element of **fire** and the **eastern triplicity** <term>triplicity: In astrology, a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, or Water).</term>—designate those stones as having properties against **fevers** and infirmities such as **dropsy** <note>original: "hydropiſis"; an old medical term for edema or swelling caused by excess fluid.</note>, **paralysis**, and the like. Furthermore, because heat moves well, those who wear them are said to become **ingenious** and **eloquent**, and to be exalted in the honors of this world, especially by the **Leo** (the Lion). 

**Gemini**, **Libra**, and **Aquarius**, on account of the **aerial and western triplicity**, are said (if they are properly engraved on stones) to temper hot humors. They are also said to prepare those who carry them for **friendship**, **justice**, **good citizenship**, the diligent observance of **laws**, and **concord**. 

**Cancer**, **Scorpio**, and **Pisces**, engraved on stones on account of the **watery and northern triplicity**, temper hot and dry fevers, such as **hectic fever** <note>original: "ethica"; a persistent, wasting fever often associated with consumption.</note> and **burning fever** <note>original: "cauſon"; from the Greek 'kausos', a high fever accompanied by intense thirst.</note> and similar ailments. However, according to the "art of images," they incline the wearer toward **lying**, **injustice**, **inconstancy**, and **unreliability** <note>original: "lubricitatem"; literally "slipperiness" or moral instability.</note>. A sign of this nature is why they say that the **Scorpion** is the image of **Muhammad** <note>original: "Macumeti"; this reflects a common medieval European polemic that associated Islamic figures with unfavorable astrological signs.</note>, who never taught anything but lies and injustice. # BOOK III.

[...the proper nature] of each thing, the thing itself is known, and there is very little doubt about its **accidents** <term>Accidents|In Aristotelian philosophy, these are non-essential qualities (like color or hardness) that help us identify a substance without being part of its core definition.</term>, nor is it difficult to know this, just as knowledge about stones is investigated without difficulty. For I myself have seen pure gold found in very hard stone, and I have seen gold mixed into the substance of the stone; and likewise, I myself have found silver mixed in stone and also pure in another stone, as if it were a vein running through the stone, distinct from the stone’s own substance. I have similarly experienced this regarding iron, copper, tin, and lead, though I have not seen these as distinct from the substance of the stone myself; however, I have learned for certain from experts in such matters that they are frequently found distinct from the stone’s substance, just as grains of gold are found among sands.

For this reason especially, the science of stones precedes the science of metals, and it seems fitting that we follow this same natural order.

## On the Proper Matter of Metals.
### Chapter 2.

Through the science that has already been handed down in the **Meteorology** <term>Meteorology|Referring to Aristotle’s *Meteorologica*, which provided the standard medieval explanation for how vapors and exhalations within the earth create minerals.</term> <note>original: "Metheoris"</note>, we know that the primary matter of all **liquefiable substances** <term>Liquefiable substances|In this context, substances that can be melted, such as metals or wax, as opposed to things that burn or remain solid.</term> is water. For every liquefiable thing, as long as it is in a liquid state, seeks a **foreign boundary** <term>Foreign boundary|A concept from Aristotelian physics; liquids do not have a shape of their own (a "proper boundary") but take the shape of whatever container (the "foreign boundary") holds them.</term> and does not rest within its own boundaries. We discussed this nature of the **moist** <note>original: "humidi"</note> in the second book of **On Generation** <note>original: "perigeneos," referring to Aristotle's *De Generatione et Corruptione*</note>. 

Since, therefore, every liquefiable thing is liquefiable for no other reason than that the moisture which was bound within it has been released and restored to its own proper activity and power, this definition follows the name: when we call a liquid "moist," it is demonstrated to be "liquefied." For it cannot be otherwise than that everything that flows and seeks the boundary of an external container is caused by a single cause—namely, that substance which essentially and primarily tends to be held by a foreign boundary rather than its own; and this, as determined elsewhere, is the nature of the moist. 

Therefore, all things capable of being melted are fluid because of an abundance of incorporated watery moisture that exists within them. Furthermore, in the second book of the **Meteorology**, we showed that whatever is **congealed** <note>original: "congelantur," meaning solidified or frozen</note> by cold is watery in its primary matter. There is no doubt that metallic substances are solidified by the coldness of water; therefore, moisture must be the matter of all these things. Because of this, even **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE) was the foundational authority for medieval natural science.</note>, the prince of the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics|Followers of Aristotle's philosophy, so named because Aristotle often taught while walking (peripatētikos).</term>, says in the fifth book of the **Metaphysics** that the matter of all liquefiable things is one: water. We also know from those things proven in the **Meteorology** that watery moisture is easily evapo... <note>The text cuts off mid-word: "evaporabile" (evaporable).</note>

HEADER: DE LAPIDIBVS PRECIOSIS <note>The header says "On Precious Stones," but the text continues the discussion of metals from the previous chapter.</note>

...evaporates. **Alchemical experiments** <note>original: "experimenta alchimica"</note> also indicate this, for if water—or those things which have a purely watery moisture, whether natural and inherent or foreign and infused—is placed in an **alembic** <term>Alembic|A chemical apparatus used for distillation, consisting of two vessels connected by a tube.</term> and subjected to a gentle fire, they evaporate through a small amount of heat and effort; the water distills out of them, and the dry parts remain behind. We see, however, that all metallic things retain their moisture even in great fires. Therefore, the material moisture of metals must not be simple water, but must have undergone some change from the other elements.

If we consider those types of moisture that are difficult to separate from the things in which they are naturally found, we find none except those that are **oily** <note>original: "unctuosas"</note> and viscous. As was determined in the **Meteorology** <term>Meteorology|Aristotle’s treatise on natural phenomena, which explained the formation of minerals through subterranean vapors.</term> <note>original: "metheoris"</note>, the parts of such substances are linked together like chains, and one part cannot be easily pulled away from another. Since, therefore, the moisture of metals is not driven out even by great burning, it must be that they are oily in nature.

A sign of this is that all **radical moisture** <term>Radical moisture|In medieval science, the essential fluid within a living being that sustains life and acts as fuel for its internal "natural heat."</term> <note>original: "radicalem humiditatem"</note>—in which the natural heat of animals is warmed—is oily. Without a doubt, wise Nature would not have provided this unless it were difficult to separate and difficult to dry out. For Nature desires to remain in existence for a long time, both in the individual and perpetually in the species; and therefore, she ordained this kind of moisture as nourishment for the vital heat. 

Since, therefore, the moisture in metals seems similarly inseparable in the heat that melts them, there is no doubt that the moisture which is the matter of metals is oily. However, we see that the oily substance in oil and in all fats is easily flammable and prone to burning...

<summary>Albertus Magnus argues that the moisture within metals is not simple water but an "oily" or "unctuous" substance, explaining why metals melt rather than evaporate when heated. He draws an analogy between the "radical moisture" of living beings and the durable moisture of metals.</summary>

And we see that fire does not depart from them until they are consumed, just as we see in the oil of a lamp or in the **radical moisture** <term>Radical moisture|The fundamental, life-sustaining fluid within an organism or substance that acts as the fuel for its internal heat.</term> <note>original: "humido radicali"</note> of those suffering from wasting fevers <note>original: "ethicorum," referring to "hectics" or those with consumption whose vital fluids are being dried up.</note>. However, we see nothing of this kind in the moisture of metals. Therefore, it might seem to some that the matter of metals is perhaps not an oily moisture.

But we are excused from all such objections by what we said in the fourth book of our **Meteorology** <note>original: "metheororum nostrorum"; referring to Albertus Magnus's own commentary on Aristotle's work of the same name.</note>. We explained there that in many things there is a twofold oiliness. One is, so to speak, extrinsic and very subtle, with no dross or combustible material mixed in; this type is not flammable, but is held within the "roots" of the thing so that it cannot be pulled out or "drunk up" by fire. We gave an example of this in the liquor extracted from wine <note>Likely referring to the distillation of alcohol or "aqua vitae."</note>, in which there is one oiliness floating on the surface that is flammable, easily stripped away, and is, in a sense, accidental.

The other [oiliness] is mixed into the entire substance of the liquid itself and cannot be separated from that substance except by the destruction of the substance itself, and this type is not combustible. The same is true for all things that nature produces. A sign of this is found in the art of **alchemy** <note>original: "alchimiæ"</note>, which mimics nature more than any other art. For when the alchemist saw that a **yellow elixir** <note>original: "citrinum elixir"</note> could be made in no better way than through **sulfur** <note>original: "sulphur"</note>, yet saw that sulfur contained a violently burning oiliness—one that scorched all metals and blackened them when cast upon them in a molten state—he commanded that the sulfur be washed with "sharp" <note>i.e., acidic or caustic</note> washes and boiled. This must be done for so long that the water from the boiling no longer comes out yellow, and these washes are sublimated until all the combustible oiliness is removed from it...

# BOOK III.
### ON PRECIOUS STONES

...because then only the subtle oily part remains, which withstands the fire and is not consumed by it. It is necessary, therefore, that a similar oily moisture abound in the materials of metals produced by nature, and that this is the cause of their **ductility** <term>Ductility|The physical property of a metal that allows it to be hammered thin or drawn out into wire without breaking.</term> and **fusibility** <note>original: "liquabilitatis"; the capacity of a substance to be melted into a liquid state.</note>. This is expressly stated by the authorities **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose works on medicine and alchemy were foundational to medieval European science.</note> and **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure to whom many foundational alchemical and "hermetic" texts were attributed.</note>, as well as many others most skilled in the natures of metals.

Furthermore, we see in all types of metals that, even when liquefied, they do not "wet" surfaces <note>original: "non reddunt humida," literally "do not make things moist." The author is observing that molten metal does not soak into a surface the way water does.</note> when poured over those things upon which they are cast. Nor do they settle flat upon a surface, nor are they spread out over it at all, in the way we see almost every aqueous or oily fluid behave—such as water, wine, beer, or oil. For all of these, when poured over stone, earth, or wood, if they find a level surface, they make the surface wet by soaking into it and are spread out upon it.

Metals, however, when liquefied, do none of these things; they do not cling to what they touch, nor are they entirely dispersed. Instead, they both hold together in one respect and flow in another. It is necessary, therefore, that the subtle oily moisture be not only their material, but be perfectly mixed with a subtle **earthy substance** <note>original: "terrestri subtili"; in medieval alchemy, metals were thought to be composed of varying proportions of "Sulfur" (oily moisture) and "Mercury" or "Earth."</note> that prevents it from clinging to what it touches or from flowing away entirely, but [causes it] to hold together as if in globules. This is because the subtle earthy part everywhere within it grasps and, as if by swallowing, holds the moisture and bounds it, so that it does not allow the moisture to cling to anything but itself. And the moisture, being everywhere on the outside of [the earthy part], draws out the dry earthy part so that it flows and runs on a level surface; for if it were not protected everywhere by the moisture, the dry earthy part would surely be consumed <note>original: "combureretur," matching the catchword "reretur" for the following page.</note> in the melting fire...

This mixture allows metals to be melted and hammered (ductility) without the moisture being destroyed by heat or soaking into surfaces.</summary>

### Chapter 3.

From this, the question commonly asked—why stone does not melt, while bronze and metal do—is easily resolved. Furthermore, stone can be crushed and **calcined** <term>Calcination|The process of heating a mineral or ore to high temperatures in the presence of air, typically to remove volatile substances or to reduce it to a fine powder or "lime."</term>, which does not happen to metal at all except through fire alone. The solution to this is easily seen: for stone is composed more of earth; it does not have moisture protecting the earthy parts everywhere, nor does it have moisture as oily as metals. Therefore, when it is placed in an intense fire <note>original: "igne optico"; likely referring to a hot, visible flame or the focal point of a furnace.</note>, the watery moisture evaporates, and the stone is reduced to lime. And when the dryness in the stone overcomes the moisture, the stone is entirely capable of being crushed; whereas, conversely, in metals, the moisture overcomes the dryness, and the metal will be liquefied. This is also the reason why stone cannot be shaped by hammers <note>original: "producibilis malleis"; the ability to be extended or drawn out by hammering.</note>, but metals are shaped by hammers, because...

# ON PRECIOUS STONES.

<meta>catchword: because</meta>

Indeed, metals possess an abundant oily moisture that holds the earthy parts together most strongly, as if with sword-like bonds. Thus, when the watery part is displaced from its position by the blow of a hammer—and it is the nature of water to yield to whatever touches it, as we have stated in *On Generation* <note>original: "perigeneos"; likely referring to Aristotle's *De Generatione et Corruptione*.</note> and in the *Meteorology*—it draws the earthy parts along with it violently and inseparably. In this way, the metal is continuously extended and not divided, because of the viscosity and the excellent, strong mixing of the earthy elements with the oily, watery ones. 

In stone, however, dryness prevails, which resists whatever touches it and does not yield into itself. Since the effect of dryness is to be split apart by the blow of a hammer, and being unable to yield into itself, it shatters and is crushed into small pieces. 

Furthermore, the earthy matter floating and absorbed within the moisture in the substance of metals is very subtle; it is neither corrupted nor entirely squeezed out from the moisture (as occurs in extreme cold), but rather it is, as it were, digested by **ripening** <term>Pepansis|A Greek term used in Aristotelian physics to describe "ripening" or digestion brought about by internal, moist heat.</term> and not cooked by **roasting** <term>Optesis|A Greek term for "roasting" or parching, which refers to cooking by external, dry heat.</term>, nor is it parched, as Averroës <note>A 12th-century philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> taught. For its own cold moisture is native to it and not foreign; therefore, it is boiled and digested within itself and made "connatural" to it, so that the dry part runs and flows with the moist part, and the moist part is retained with the dry earthy part. For in this way, according to Empedocles <note>A Greek pre-Socratic philosopher who theorized that the elements combined to form body parts before they joined into whole organisms.</note>, "heads were gathered on such a neck" <note>original: "capita colliguntur Germanorum"; This likely refers to a passage in Aristotle's *Physics* regarding Empedocles' theories of biological combination, though "Germanorum" appears to be a scribe's or printer's error for a term related to budding or joining.</note>.

If, however, it were digested by roasting (*optesis*), as some unskilled alchemists claim, the moisture would undoubtedly be found both inside and outside, and the whole would not be drawn together by the moisture. The opposite would be true if it were digested by roasting, as some others have said against all reason; for then the exterior would not be held by the moisture but abandoned by it, and the interior would possess very little moisture. ### On the opinions of the ancients and on the matter of metals. Chapter 4.

This which Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose works on medicine and alchemy were foundational to medieval European science.</note> handed down, both in his physics and in his alchemy—specifically in the letter he wrote to the philosopher Hasen—is not contrary to what is said here. For he says in both of those books that **mercury** <note>original: "argentum uiuum", literally "living silver".</note> and **sulfur** are the matter of all metals. Indeed, the moisture of which we have spoken, mixed with the earthy as we described, is the immediate matter of mercury; and the substance of the oiliness which we described is the proper and essential matter of sulfur. 

Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure to whom many foundational alchemical and hermetic texts were attributed.</note> and certain others seem to say that metals are composed of all the elements. This, without a doubt, is not to be denied; however, the matter of things is not determined by those elements that are present in them in just any way, but rather by those which are abundant within them. 

But above all, there is a marvelous and "desirable" opinion that some in alchemical writings attribute to Democritus <note>Greek philosopher known for atomism, though in this context, the author refers to the "Pseudo-Democritus" of early alchemical literature.</note>: namely, that **lime** <term>Calx|A powdery substance produced by heating limestone or metals; in this context, it refers to the "burnt" earthy component.</term> and **lye** <term>Lixivium|An alkaline solution obtained by leaching wood ashes; here used to represent a sharp, transformative liquid.</term> are the matter of metals. Yet, if lime were the matter—since it is a "burnt" substance—once mixed with water it would dry out, just as happens in cement. The metal would then return to the hardness of stone, becoming brittle and incapable of being melted. Furthermore, if fire were applied, the metal would undoubtedly harden and not liquefy, just as we see with cement.

Or if one calls lye "sharp water" as the alchemists explain—removing the saltiness and bitterness from lime that results from burning, as alchemists teach in their washings—and claims this water becomes the source material of metals, this remains an unsuitable explanation. This is because lime is a terrestrial substance, and through the principles handed down in the *Meteorology* <note>Refers to Aristotle’s *Meteorologica*, the foundational medieval text for understanding the formation of minerals and weather.</note>, we know that every burnt earthy substance has contracted and constricted pores. Such lime, being in its current state, prevents water from entering into its interior; therefore, it is never well or strongly bonded. For this reason, cement easily turns to powder and falls from a wall when its moisture is evaporated by fire.

Thus, the statement of Democritus <note>A Greek philosopher (c. 460 – c. 370 BCE) often cited in alchemical texts for his theories on the nature of matter.</note> concerning the material of metals is not fitting. He was deceived by insufficient evidence: he observed that the "elixir" for the **moon**—that is, for silver—had a base which accepts lime and ceruse <term>ceruse: white lead or lead carbonate, used in alchemy to "whiten" or harden substances</term>. Because of this, he believed that something similar occurred in the physical matter and natural bodies of metals. 

However, this is not necessary; for art <note>The author distinguishes between "Art" (human alchemy) and "Nature" (geological processes).</note> requires many things that nature does not. Art requires lime and ceruse only for hardening and coloring, whereas nature achieves this in its own material through **digestion** <note>The natural process of internal heat and pressure within the earth that "ripens" or matures minerals into metals.</note> alone. Indeed, we demonstrated in the *Meteorology* that all digestion through "decoction" <note>A process of heating or boiling to refine a substance.</note> causes the digested and boiled materials to fuse and thicken, even without the addition of any external substance to the things being boiled. 

Furthermore, a certain Gilgil <note>Likely Ibn Juljul, a 10th-century physician and translator in Al-Andalus (Spain) who wrote on minerals.</note> from Hispalian Arabia <note>referring to Seville (Hispalis), which was part of Islamic Spain.</note>—which has now been restored to the Spaniards—seems to attempt to prove in his *Secrets* that infused ash is the material of metals. ### On the efficient cause and the generation of metals in general.
### Chapter 5.

In this manner, we shall speak of the <term>efficient cause</term> <note>original: "de efficiente"; in the Aristotelian tradition used by the author, this refers to the active agent or force that triggers a process or brings a thing into existence.</note>. The sign of this is that during liquefaction, in many or all of them, something is separated from their substance. It is certain that since the primary cause of these things we call metals is a water-earth mixture containing something else mixed in, [heat] causes it to stand firm and thicken into the metallic mixture. This, as is evident from what has been said, is the work of heat. 

It is necessary, therefore, for heat to be the cause of the generation of metals. But upon further consideration, it will be seen that heat alone is not the cause of their generation, because—as was stated in the book *On the Generation of Stones*—without doubt, if heat alone were the cause, it would act continuously without the drying of the natural moisture and the incineration of the earthy parts. However, we see that it settles into the **species** <note>The specific category or type of substance, such as gold, silver, or lead.</note> and **form** of the metal. Therefore, it is necessary that heat itself be like an **instrument** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "instrumental cause" is something used by a higher power to achieve a goal, like a saw used by a carpenter.</note> directed toward an end—which is the form of the metal—so that it does not deviate from its proper path in its operation.

Furthermore, we find that many **arts** <note>Human crafts or technologies.</note> have been invented so that each of them may lead its operation to a conclusion through a created instrument; thus, cooks strive in **boiling** and **roasting**, and all others who endeavor to convert materials through some other **digestion** <note>original: "digestionem"; the refining or "cooking" of matter through heat.</note>. Similarly, therefore, it must be so in **Nature**, which in its works is more certain and more direct than any art. Just as it is in all other things, so without doubt a **formative power** <note>original: "uirtus formatiua"; the internal force that guides the development of a thing into its final shape.</note> exists in the matter, influenced by the **stars** and the **heavens** <note>original: "stellis et cœlo influxa"; the medieval belief that celestial bodies exerted a physical influence on the formation of earthly minerals.</note>, which directs the heat "digesting" the matter of the metal toward its specific form.

For as has been said in other places, this heat possesses its correctness and its formal power from a "moving intelligence," and its efficacy from the power of light and the heat caused by the light of the stars and the celestial sphere. It has the power of separating **homogeneous** <note>Things of the same kind.</note> parts from **heterogeneous** <note>Things of different kinds.</note> parts through the power of fire. For it is necessary that there the unsuitable parts be consumed by the heat of the "digesting fire," since digestion is a combination resulting from natural and proper heat acting upon opposing qualities. Once these are removed from the matter, it is still necessary for the matter to be bounded and completed into its species; and this is done by a "terminating heat" which can in no way have the power...

...to be limited except through the power of that which is the limit: now, the **form** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the essential nature or "blueprint" of a thing that makes it what it is.</note> is the limit. It is necessary, therefore, that a formal power directs and gives shape to the heat that performs the limiting. This form, however, is not a form merely imposed upon the matter from the outside. It must, therefore, be the form of the **first efficient cause** <note>The primary source of change or movement; in this context, it refers to the ultimate source of natural laws.</note> which grants forms to every natural species. This cause is the **mover of the sphere** <note>original: "motor orbis"; in medieval cosmology, this is the celestial force or intelligence that moves the heavens, which in turn influences the development of minerals and life on Earth.</note>, unfolding natural forms through the motion of the heavens and the qualities of the elements, just as a craftsman unfolds the forms of his art with an ax and a hammer. For this reason, **Aristotle** says that the work of nature is like the work of art, where a house comes from the [idea of a] house and health comes from the [idea of] health—just as the qualities found in heat and cold [during a cure] arise from the idea existing in the mind of the physician. This, then, is the proper generative cause of metals.

Indeed, in certain **alchemical books** attributed to **Plato**, this "number" or "proportion" is called the metallic form. He placed this proportion in the powers of the constituent elements, because he believed that Nature generates all these things by the proportion of the power of the earth combined with the celestial power. # BOOK III.
<page-num>247</page-num>

...according to the account of the **seven planets**, as he said. If, therefore, there is a greater degree of earthly power—in terms of its three qualities—than there is of the planets' power in the transmission of light and nobility, it will produce a substance that is dark, heavy, and cold, such as **lead**. If, however, there is more of the celestial power and less of the earthly forces, it will be very bright, approaching incorruptibility <note>In medieval science, "incorruptibility" refers to the ability of a substance, like gold, to resist rust, decay, or damage from fire.</note>, solid, and because it is solid, it is necessarily heavy; and in this regard, and conversely, the proportion is said to constitute the species of **gold**. 

In this same manner, he says that other things are formed, which is why they have called the **seven types of metals** by the names of the **seven planets**, saying: **Saturn** is lead; **Jupiter** is tin; **Mars** is iron; the **Sun** is gold; **Venus** is copper <note>original: "aes"; usually referring to copper or its alloys like bronze in planetary associations.</note>; **Mercury** is quicksilver <note>original: "argentum uiuum"; literally "living silver," known today as the element mercury.</note>; and the **Moon** is silver. They assert that these metals acquire the complexion <note>original: "cōplexionem"; the specific balance of primary qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that determines a substance's nature.</note> of the seven planets due to the different proportions of their composition. 

**Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure regarded by medieval scholars as the foundational author of alchemy and philosophy.</note> seems to be the author of this opinion, although **Plato** later followed him in this view. The alchemists <term>alchemists: early practitioners of chemistry who sought to transform base metals into gold and understand the spiritual properties of matter</term> seem to have received this from them, asserting that precious stones possess the power of the stars and their celestial images, while the seven types of metals possess forms according to the seven planets of the lower spheres. Thus, the powers of the heavens are first reflected in the earth, creating, as it were, "secondary stars." 

In support of this assertion, they bring forward the truth—which is indeed a fact—that the celestial sphere moves the earth, and that this motion is the cause of the diversity of forms in things generated in the earth, as well as the reason for the great abundance of things generated in the earth rather than in any other element.

The father **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure, regarded as the author of the *Hermetic Corpus*, a series of texts foundational to alchemy and Western esotericism.</note> seems to approve of this opinion, as he says that the earth is the mother of metals and the heaven is their father; he claims the earth is impregnated by the heaven in the mountains, fields, plains, waters, and all other places. We, however, understand this opinion in this way: that the proportion of the principles of virtues—namely the active and the passive—serves as the disposition toward a **substantial form** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "substantial form" is the essential nature that makes a thing what it is.</note>, just as it is in all other things. This form is granted by the primary formal and active principles, which act as a <term>formative power</term> <note>original: "uirtus formatiua"; the innate force that shapes raw matter into a specific substance.</note> within the matter, as we have previously stated in the science of stones.

As for why the various kinds of metals are attributed more to the **planets** than to other stars, it is said that because stones possess a stable existence and a fixed form of <term>coagulation</term> <note>The process by which a liquid or fluid substance becomes solid.</note>, they are attributed to the **fixed stars** and the constellations <note>original: "imaginibus"; literally "images," referring to the figures formed by the stars in the sky.</note> of the fixed stars, which perpetually retain their positions and figures. 

By "position," I do not mean the specific location of a star on the celestial sphere—since every star moves across that—but rather the position it holds within a constellation relative to another star. For example, two bright stars are found on a single line at an equal distance from one another at all times—those in the **Horn of Aries** <note>The stars Hamal and Sheratan in the constellation Aries, the Ram.</note>, along with the star called the **Knee of Perseus** <note>likely the star Mirfak or Algol in the constellation Perseus.</note>—and so it is with other stars. If this were not so, the constellations of the heaven would be destroyed. Thus, stones are found in one disposition and figure for as long as they exist. 

Metals, however, have a movement that is, as it were, wandering <note>original: "erraticum"; the word "planet" comes from the Greek *planētēs*, meaning "wanderer."</note>; they are at one time liquid and at another time solidified. Since liquid is their primary matter, and liquid is characterized by a wandering motion, it seems appropriate for their nature to correspond to the planets. ...[in]deed, and in one way it is appropriate for a mixture to be composed of several things that differ according to their **species**. Now, the mixture of all **metals** consists of a subtle, earthy, sulfurous substance and a fundamental watery substance, whose oil has been separated from it, along with superfluous watery moisture, as is established from what was stated previously. It seems, therefore, that there is only one species corresponding to this by way of suitability.

Furthermore, it has been proven by experience that through the **elixir** <term>elixir: a chemical preparation used by alchemists to transform or "perfect" metals</term>, **bronze** <note>original: "æs"; this term often refers to copper or its various alloys in alchemical texts</note> returns to **silver**, and **lead** to **gold**, and likewise **iron** to **silver**. It seems, therefore, that they are the same in their **matter**, and consequently possess a single **form** <term>substantial form: the essential nature that makes a substance what it is (e.g., the "silverness" of silver)</term> which acts as the completion of the preceding material states.

Moreover, there appears to be no difference between them except in **accidents** <term>accidents: in philosophy, these are non-essential qualities—like color or weight—that can change without changing the fundamental nature of the thing</term>—namely heat, taste, weight, rarity, and density—all of which only affect the matter. From these and similar arguments, some have adopted the opinion that the species of metals is one and the same, and that there are simply many material "infirmities" <note>original: "infirmitates"; this reflects the alchemical theory that base metals like lead are simply "sick" or "underdeveloped" gold</note> or flaws.

However, the opposite appears to be true, because matter cannot, by any reasoning, persist in any natural thing within nature unless it is completed by a **substantial form**. We see that **silver** and **tin** persist [as stable, distinct substances], as do other metals; they would therefore seem to be completed by their own substantial forms. Furthermore, for those things whose properties and **passions** <note>original: "passiones"; here referring to the observable traits or reactions a substance exhibits</note> are diverse, it is necessary that their substance also be diverse. The "passions" of metals regarding color, smell, and sonority <note>sonority: the specific ringing sound a metal makes when struck</note> are entirely different. For it cannot be said that these accidents are merely common or coincidental, since they belong to all metals of a specific nature always and everywhere; it is therefore necessary that their substances be diverse and

...species. Furthermore, if a mixture of the same components were to produce the same species, then all things that are generated would be of one and the same species, since all things are generated from the **elements**. It is clear, therefore, that the argument they brought forward concerning the components of the elements does not hold up; for different **forms** of generated things are attributed to different proportions of mixed things, and we shall show later, when we speak of them specifically, that there are different proportions of mixture and mixing in **metals**. 

Regarding the experiment they cite, the proof offered is insufficient, because it is not certain whether it merely indicates the color of silver or the weight and scent of gold because of what is added and penetrates into the **bronze** <note>original: "æs"</note> or **lead** or hardens the substance. **Callisthenes** <note>original: "Calistenes"; likely referring to a source in the pseudo-Aristotelian alchemical tradition</note> ought to have proven that it introduced the *substance* of gold; even if it were granted that the substance of gold is introduced, this is still not sufficient proof that there is only one species of metal. 

This is because by **calcining** <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to remove impurities or change its chemical state</term>, **subliming** <term>sublimation: heating a solid until it becomes a gas and then cools back into a pure solid</term>, **distilling** <term>distillation: purifying a liquid by heating it to vapor and then cooling it</term>, and other operations through which they make the **elixir** <term>elixir: a potent substance intended to transform or "perfect" base metals</term> penetrate the matter of metals, the species of metals that were originally in the metallic matter can be destroyed. Then, once the **common matter** <term>materia communis: the underlying "stuff" of the universe that has been stripped of its specific identity</term> is left behind—rather than the matter specific to those metals—it can be led to another species with the help of art, just as seeds are assisted by plowing and sowing, and as nature is assisted by the skill of medicine. It is clear, therefore, from this that we are in no way compelled to think there is only one species for all metals, as we find their generative locations, principles, and properties to be very different.

...[one should] not call "inside" and "outside" and other such names based on the position of parts within the whole, but rather according to the properties and natures of what is dominant or not dominant. For that which is dominant, being enclosed within itself, hides that over which it dominates. According to this view, these thinkers are directly stating the opinion of **Anaxagoras** <note>a Pre-Socratic philosopher who argued that every substance contains portions of every other substance—a theory known as "universal mixture"</note>, namely that all **metals** are in all things and that the naming of a substance occurs based on which metal is most dominant. 

However, if what they say were true—since we know that **gold** is not consumed by fire but **lead** is, especially if it is sprinkled with **sulfur**—then the lead ought to be burned away when fire is applied, and the gold which is hidden within it should remain. Yet, we do not see this happen. Similarly, **silver** is protected by lead from being burned; therefore, when the lead is consumed, the silver that was within the lead (as they say) ought to remain—unless perhaps they claim that any given metal exists in another in infinite amounts, as **Anaxagoras** said. If that were the case, none of them could be entirely consumed by fire; but we have already disproved this in the beginning of our *Physics* <note>The author refers to his *Physica*, a commentary on Aristotle's works on natural philosophy</note>. 

Furthermore, if their claim were granted as true, never could enough of the manifest layer be burned away by fire so that the hidden core could be liberated and revealed; and thus the entire study of **alchemy** would be in vain. Therefore, this saying does not agree with the physical principles which we have determined in all our books. 

But perhaps they say this because of the affinity <note>original: "uicinitatem," literally "nearness" or "neighborliness"</note> of these metals which they possess in their matter. ...refinements, the superfluous watery moisture is removed and all the fatty, oily parts are burned away within it. That which is earthy and sulfurous <note>original: "sulphuratum"</note> within it is purified through sublimation <note>the process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used here to describe purification</note>. It is then mixed as a vapor in a sealed container that traps the earthy vapor together with the "radical" moisture in an excellent and perfectly formed mixture. By the power of heat, the moisture is converted to a citrine <note>a yellow-orange color typical of gold</note> heat, and it then possesses the brightness and color of gold. This "way of art" <note>the alchemical method</note> is very similar to the "way of nature," as we shall discuss further below. 

But even if this were true, it would not mean that gold exists in the "depths" of the metal. For even granting that this substance which shines forth from lead is gold, we already know that these transmutations <term>transmutation: the alchemical act of changing one substance into another, such as lead into gold</term> completely destroy the lead. Since the species <note>the essential nature or "type"</note> of lead was never present at the same time as the species of gold in the same matter, our argument seems even more true: it has not been proven that what is produced from lead is actually gold. Perhaps it is something that resembles gold but is not gold, because art alone cannot provide a **substantial form** <term>substantial form: the essential identity or "soul" of a material that makes it what it is (e.g., "lead-ness" vs "gold-ness")</term>.

Furthermore, we find that the **alchemist** <note>original: "alchimicum"</note> hardly ever, if ever, operates on the whole substance as has been described. Rather, they use a **citrine elixir** to color a metal into the appearance of gold, and a **white elixir** to color it into the likeness of silver. They strive to ensure the color remains even when placed in fire and that it penetrates through the entire metal, like a spiritual substance infused into medicinal matter. In this way of working, a yellow color can be induced while the original substance of the metal remains unchanged. Therefore, it is once again shown that it is not the case that multiple species of metals exist within one another. These and similar arguments are used to refute the claims of those who say that every species of metal is present in every other.

### Whether the species of metals can be transmuted into one another as the alchemists say. Chapter 9.

From all these things introduced, we can consider whether it is true what some say **Aristotle** <note>original: "Aristot."</note> claimed, although in truth it was said by **Avicenna** <note>a famous Persian polymath known in Latin as Auicenna; the text refers to a famous passage in his *De Conglutinatione Lapidum*</note>: namely, that the practitioners of alchemy should know that **species** <term>species: the essential, defining nature of a thing that makes it what it is (e.g., the "lead-ness" of lead)</term> cannot be changed. However, they can make things similar to them, such as dyeing a red metal with yellow <note>original: "citrino"</note> so that it appears to be gold, and dyeing a white metal until it is very similar to silver or gold, or whichever body they wish. 

Furthermore, I do not believe it is possible for the **specific difference** <note>original: "dextra specifica," likely a transcription for "differentia specifica," the logical quality that distinguishes one species from another</note> to be removed by any human ingenuity. However, the stripping away of **accidents** <term>accidents: non-essential properties like color, smell, or surface texture that do not change what a thing fundamentally is</term> is not impossible, or at least their reduction. For this is the opinion of Avicenna, which he says belongs to **Al-Hasan** <note>original: "Hasten," referring to the philosopher and mathematician Ibn al-Haytham</note>, a philosopher eminent in natural science and mathematics. 

Nevertheless, Avicenna says in his own work on alchemy that he found a contradiction among those who argued about the transmutation of metals in alchemical works. Because of this, he himself adds that species are not changed unless perhaps they are reduced into **primary matter** <term>primary matter: the formless "base" substance of the universe that has the potential to become any physical thing</term> and into the matter of metals, and thus by the aid of art they are led into the species of the metal they desire. 

But then we must say that skilled alchemists work like skilled physicians. For skilled physicians, by means of purging medicines, cleanse corrupt and easily corruptible materials that hinder health—which is the goal intended by the physician—and

Alchemy, however, proceeds in this manner: namely, by destroying one thing by removing it from its own **species** <note>original: "specie"; in medieval science, this refers to the essential nature or "form" that makes a substance what it is</note>, and with the help of those things which are already in the matter, inducing the species of another. For this reason, of all alchemical operations, the best is that which proceeds from the same materials from which nature proceeds—such as from the purification of **sulfur** through decoction <note>the process of boiling a substance to extract its essence or refine it</note> and **sublimation** <term>sublimation: the process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used to purify chemicals</term>, and the thorough cleansing of **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver: mercury; historically believed to be the "mother" of all metals</term>, and the successful mixing of these with the matter of the metal. For in these cases, through the inherent powers of these ingredients, the species of any metal may be induced. 

Those, however, who merely whiten with "Whites" and yellow with "Yellows" <note>original: "per Alba albificant, & per citrina citrinant"; referring to the use of surface dyes or tinctures (albedo and citrinitas) to change the color of a metal without changing its internal substance</note>, while the species of the original metal remains in the matter, are without a doubt deceivers. They do not make true gold or true silver, yet almost all alchemists proceed in this way, either wholly or in part. Because of this, I caused an experiment to be performed, finding that "alchemical gold" which came to me—and likewise silver—after it had sustained six or seven fires <note>referring to the process of cupellation or repeated smelting to test purity</note>, is immediately consumed and wasted away upon further heating, returning as if to dross. All these things, therefore, have been said concerning the nature of the species of metals in general.

We know also that in our land and in the land of the **Slavic peoples** gold is found generated in stones in two ways.

Since the more subtle part of that matter which has been mixed together is contained within it, it congeals in that channel <note>original: "canna"; literally a reed or pipe, referring here to the narrow, pipe-like passages or "chimneys" in the rock where ores form.</note> and is mixed as a vapor within its pores, where it is converted into metal of the same kind as the vapor itself. 

A sign of this is that in every such vein, the material found on the surface is smoky and base <note>original: "ignobile"; in alchemy and early chemistry, "noble" metals like gold do not corrode, while "base" or "ignoble" metals do.</note>; even if the metal is incorporated throughout the entire stone, that which is on the upper part is dreggy <note>original: "fæculentum"; full of impurities or sediment, like the dregs of wine.</note> and useless. Therefore, that which is found deeper inside is better and more noble. The cause of this is undoubtedly that the part of the matter which was ignited and burnt rose higher, and through that burning was reduced to a state of ash—becoming, as it were, dregs and cinders. For this reason, it is found to be dry, crumbly, and brittle. 

However, that which was "suffocated" or trapped further inside, in the bowels of the stone, was intensely mixed within itself and not burnt; therefore, it was brought to completion by a gentle and slow heat, and afterwards solidified by the coldness of the earth. 

Furthermore, if the surrounding area is compact and not porous, the vapor then forces one, two, or more paths, according to the strength of its power and its quantity, depending on whether it was able to pierce the softness of the location. Having filled those paths, the vapor is converted into metal, for it is intensely penetrating. A sign of this is that when any hot, molten metal is poured upon the ground, it penetrates the earth in various ways. This is just as in the diagram of a vessel: first, in the place where the material is received, it is like the circle **a. b. c.**, and a single vein full of metal generated from vapor becomes the line...

For if the place were open, the entire matter would escape <note>original: "expiraret"; literally "breathe out," meaning the vapor would dissipate into the air.</note> and nothing at all would be generated there.

As for the gold that is generated among sands—appearing as certain larger or smaller grains—it is produced from a vapor and a very subtle heat which is trapped and "digested" <note>original: "digeritur"; in medieval alchemy, "digestion" refers to the slow maturation or refinement of a substance through steady, gentle heat.</note> within the material of the sands, and afterwards congeals into pure gold. For the environment of the sands is very hot and dry, but the water entering in closes the pores so the vapor does not escape; therefore, it is trapped within itself and converted into gold. This is also why such gold is of better quality, for which there are two causes: 

One is that the purification of sulfur is best achieved through frequent washing; sulfur that is in watery places is frequently washed and purified. For this same reason, the earthy part of quicksilver <term>quicksilver: mercury; "argentum uiuum" in the original Latin.</term> is more often washed, purified, and refined. The other cause is the closing of the pores at the bottom of the waters or on the riverbanks; thus, the released vapor is excellently turned back upon itself, trapped, and refined nobly into the substance of gold, and congeals into gold.

# ON METALLIC MATTERS

Furthermore, the sign that a location must be of such a disposition as has been described is found in the works of skilled alchemists who best imitate nature. When they wish to create an **elixir** <note>In this context, the "elixir" is a concentrated substance capable of transforming or "tinting" base metals into gold.</note> which possesses the color and tincture of gold, they first take a wide lower vessel to hold all the material of the purified **sulfur** and **quicksilver** <note>original: "argenti uiui"; mercury.</note>, or whatever else is included in the elixir. 

Next, they arrange it so that above this there is a vessel with a long, narrow neck, and over the opening of that neck is a lid made of clay in which there is a very small and narrow hole. Then they "inhume" it—that is, they sink the bottom of the lower vessel into ashes or dung; perhaps horse dung is better, which they call a **horse-furnace** <note>original: "equiclibanum"; a method of using the steady, gentle heat produced by decomposing horse manure to maintain a constant temperature for chemical reactions.</note>. 

Then they apply a very slow fire. Those who work most skillfully use **glass vessels** <note>original: "uasa uitrea".</note>. The arrangement of the first vessel is like the shape of a **urinal** <note>A common bulbous glass flask with a wide body and a neck, used in medieval medicine and alchemy.</note>, and the second vessel stands above it and receives all the vapor that is released from the material. The contact point between the glasses or vessels is smeared thoroughly with clay so that nothing can escape through that join. 

The captured vapor is thus directed upward into its long neck, which gradually narrows; there, the vapor begins to be **suffocated** <note>original: "præfocari"; a technical term meaning the vapor is trapped and forced to condense due to lack of space or cooling.</note> and swirled around. That part of the vapor which is "burnt" flies out as a soot through the narrow hole in the lid of the neck. When it is thus filtered <note>original: "perforatur"; implying the passage through the narrow opening.</note>, it returns to a **citrine substance** <note>A yellow or gold-colored material.</note>, having been coiled within itself. This substance, once collected, tints whatever metal you wish into the color of gold—and perhaps a more beautiful color still, if it be a noble elixir in which the craftsman has made no error.

The shape of these vessels is such that the lower vessel is marked **a. b. c.**

# THE SECOND TREATISE
## OF THE THIRD BOOK OF MINERALS
### Which concerns the actions of metals.

### On the solidification and liquefaction of metals. Chapter 1.

IT IS ALSO NECESSARY to recognize those **properties** <term>accidents: in Aristotelian philosophy, these are non-essential characteristics (like color or smell) that a substance can possess without changing its fundamental nature</term> which belong to metals in themselves—such as their being **meltable** and **malleable**, as well as their colors, tastes, smells, **combustibility**, and whatever such things are seen to happen to them by their nature. 

The **meltability** of metals, however, has a certain unique quality compared to other things that melt. For other things that melt flow apart, and one part does not remain with another—such as wax, salt, and similar things, whether they are melted by dry heat or moist cold <note>The author distinguishes between substances that dissolve or liquefy into a runny state versus the "viscous" or "thick" melting characteristic of metals.</note>. In metals, however, the **moisture** <note>original: "humidum"</note> does not withdraw from the **dryness** <note>original: "siccum"</note>, but is dissolved within it; and when it is dissolved, it moves within it as if the **earthy part** had swallowed it up and it moved within its entrails. 

For this reason, **Hermes** <note>original: "Hermes"; likely referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage. This line is a variation of a phrase from the Emerald Tablet: "The Earth is its nurse."</note> also says that "the mother of metal is the earth which carries it in her womb." And this is the reason why it does not stick to what touches it, nor does it wet it, because the **earthy dryness** prevents it from wetting and sticking. The **moisture**, however, prevents the **dryness** from being at rest; and thus each acts upon the other and is acted upon by the other. However, when metal is in some state not well mixed, because

[...and because] both are not contained within each other, then in fire the **earthy part** is burned and the **moist part** evaporates. This happens because the moisture does not quench the earthy part to defend it from the fire, and the earthy part does not hold the moisture to prevent its evaporation. Such a metal, during its **liquefaction** <term>liquatio: the process of melting or turning into a liquid state</term>, possesses much "coldness" <note>likely a reference to the metal's internal quality rather than temperature</note> and is foul-smelling because of the stench of **sulfur**; it also leaves behind a great deal of **slag** <term>scoria: the stony waste matter separated from metals during the smelting or refining of ore</term> and dross because of the burning of that earthy part. 

If, however, a metal has these elements very pure and excellently mixed, the moisture does not evaporate in any perceptible amount, nor is the earthy part within it burned. Therefore, it produces little smoke, no stench, and almost no dross—as is the case with **gold**. 

The **solidification** <term>coagulatio: the process of a liquid becoming a solid</term> of these metals is not as varied as their melting. For their solidification is caused by cold compressing the moisture into the center of the **dryness** <note>In medieval science, "dryness" (siccum) and "moisture" (humidum) were seen as active qualities that combined to form all matter.</note>. Whether that moisture is pure and "radical" <note>essential to the substance's existence</note> or impure and "superfluous" <note>excessive or non-essential</note>, and whether it is well-mixed or poorly-mixed, it is compressed in one and the same way; for once it is hidden in the center, it is bound so that no "stain" of the dry, earthy part can enter it. 

The same is true of those things which do not melt from dry heat but rather soften, such as **iron** <note>The OCR reads "frigidum" (cold), but contextually and in contemporary manuscripts, this is usually "ferrum" (iron), which softens before it melts.</note>. For softening only occurs through the dissolving of the moisture, which begins to move within the dryness in which it is contained, held deep within its "innards." 

However, those things which have what **Aristotle** calls a **stuttering mixture** <note>original: "balbutientem... mixturam"; a term used to describe an uneven or imperfect combination of elements where the parts haven't fully blended into a new whole</note>—such as **tin**—become drier and more brittle the more they are melted. This is because the moist parts fly away from it, and the dry parts remain without being well "glued" together, which causes them to break more easily. 

It is called a "stuttering mixture" when the substance achieves the proper ratio of mixing in some parts but not in others; instead, it is a composition almost like...

[...mixed,] just as a stuttering man catches some words and misses others. Because these elements are not fully mixed, they evaporate easily when they melt, since the parts are not well-bound and release each other; in such cases, the moisture does not protect the dry part from burning, and the dry part does not hold the moisture back from flowing away and evaporating. 

The evidence for what we have said is that when **lead** and **tin** have sat solidified for some time, they develop a roughness on the outside and become dark—perhaps even black over a long period. This happens, without a doubt, for two reasons. The first is that when the metal is compressed toward the interior by cold, the moisture leaves the earthy and dry part on the outside, which then creates a dark color. The second reason is that the small amount of moisture remaining on the surface evaporates due to the heat of the surrounding air, and then, once again, the dark, earthy matter remains to color the surface. 

For this reason, **lead** cannot be joined <term>consolidatur: the process of soldering or fusing two pieces of metal together</term> to lead, even when the edges of both are melted with a glowing hot iron, unless the hard surface is first scraped away to remove the dry, earthy layer. This layer prevents **bonding** <term>conglutinatio: a "gluing" or sticking together of materials</term> because the joining of one thing to another happens through the power of the moisture that flows into the other, and not through the power of the dryness, which stands apart on its own. 

Furthermore, bonding does not occur unless, after scraping, the area is smeared with **tallow** <note>original: "sæpo" (sebum); animal fat used as a flux to prevent oxidation during soldering</note> or some other oily substance. This is done because the **quicksilver** <term>argentum uiuum: mercury, which medieval alchemists believed was a primary component of all metals</term> within lead contains an oily moisture, as has been said many times before; therefore, it will not stick to the surface unless it is joined by something sharing a similar nature <note>The author is referring to the principle of "like attracts like."</note>. **Bronze**, however, joins iron and silver.

### On the malleability of metals.
### Chapter 2.

Only those metals appear to be truly malleable <term>ductibilia: literally "leadable," meaning they can be drawn out or hammered into thin sheets and wires</term> which can be drawn out further and better than all others. The cause of malleability in general is what was stated above: namely, moisture enclosed in dryness but not entirely bound. When this moisture is released by the expulsion of the cold that binds it, it then floats so much in the "earthy" part of the metal that even **iron** and stones float within it and do not sink, owing to the force of the boiling and the thickness of the metallic moisture. For when moisture is bound by cold, it is nevertheless still present; and when the metal is struck, that moisture causes the metal to yield by shifting to the surrounding areas. Thus, by yielding, it is continually extended. However, in this physical state <note>original: *passione*, referring to how the metal "suffers" or reacts to the force of a hammer</note> they have very different capacities.

**Gold** is malleable above all else, followed by **silver**; then highly purified **copper**, and after that **iron**. **Tin** and **lead**, however, are less so. **Gold** is drawn out into expan— <note>The text cuts off here and likely continues with "expansion" or "dilatation" on the following page.</note>

### On the color of metals.
### Chapter 3.

It is not difficult to determine the colors of metals, for three colors are found in them in varying degrees. One of these is common to all: a shining brilliance, like light incorporated into a colored body. Another color is white, which several metals possess in varying degrees; that which is whitest is **silver**, followed by **tin**, thirdly **lead**, and **iron** least of all. The third color is yellow <note>original: *citrinus*; lemon-yellow</note> or reddish, which **gold** possesses most of all, and beneath it **copper**; for the color of copper tends toward a burnt black. 

Let us assume here what has been proven in the treatise *On Sense and the Sensible* <note>Aristotle’s *De Sensu et Sensibili*, a standard university text in the Middle Ages</note>: that color is the boundary of the "perspicuous" <term>perspicuum: in Aristotelian science, this refers to a substance's capacity to receive light, similar to transparency or translucency, which becomes "color" when it is bounded by a surface</term> within a finished object. Therefore, in whatever body this "perspicuous" substance is condensed, clear, and pure, that body possesses a brilliance that seems incorporated into its color. ...earthy <note>original: *reſtre*; completing the word *terreſtre* from the previous page</note> nature, as appears in soot. **Lead**, therefore, always tends toward a dark color because of an unburnt, muddy earthiness, and **tin** less so than lead because it contains less muddiness. **Silver**, however, always shines with whiteness because of an earthy substance that is subtle and well-digested <term>digeſtum; in alchemy, this refers to a substance being refined or "ripened" through steady heat</term>. **Iron**, however, because of the burnt earthiness within it, is sooty and black; and for this same reason it always contracts rust <term>rubigo</term>. The cause of this is nothing other than its burnt earthiness; for just as rot occurs in soft, moist things, so rust occurs in iron. For once the moisture is "drunk up" <note>meaning evaporated or consumed by the internal heat</note>, there remains a dry, parched, burnt substance, and it returns to ash. A sign of this is that iron contracts rust most especially when something corrosive <term>adurens; literally "burning" or caustic</term> is cast upon it, such as salt, sulfur, or orpiment <note>original: *auripigmentum*; arsenic trisulfide, a yellow mineral used as a pigment and in alchemical transformations</note> or something of this sort.

But **silver** does not tend toward rust, but rather toward an azure color because of the great transparency <note>original: *perſpicuum*</note> within it, which generates from it a sapphire-like color of a fine azure. For this reason, **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the "father" of alchemy</note>, the leader and father of alchemy, says that thin sheets of silver should be smeared with sal ammoniac <term>ſale armoniaco; ammonium chloride</term> and vinegar and suspended over an *alemec* <term>alemec; a type of chemical vessel or fuming chamber</term>, so that the plates turn to an azure color. And then, if the plates are reduced to ash with sulfur so that a powder is made, and it is stirred from above with vinegar and *zeruph* <note>original: *zeruph*; likely a medieval Latinization of an Arabic term for a dyeing herb, possibly woad or dyer's weed</note>, which is a certain herb, it will ferment together and the azure pigment will be completed. 

But it is true that many things "burn" <gloss>corrode</gloss> silver which do not burn gold, because its earthy and moist components are less purified and less perfectly mixed; and therefore, because when over silver something boiling or very hot is spr[inkled]...

...[is] joined <note>original: *gatur*; completing a word like *adiungatur* (is joined) or *coniungatur* from the previous page</note>, sulfur turns it black, because it burns the earthy substance that is within it.
