The **citrine** <term>citrinus; a lemon-yellow color highly prized in alchemy as a sign of successful transformation</term> color in metals is caused by the sulfur coloring it; for the heat, strongly boiling down <note>original: *decoquens*</note> the moisture mixed with the earthy substance, turns it to a yellow or reddish color. This is evident in the **science of urines** <note>the medieval medical practice of uroscopy, where doctors diagnosed health by observing the color and "digestion" of urine</note> and in alchemical works, as well as in red or reddish **lye** <term>lixivium; a caustic alkaline solution leached from ashes</term> and **saffron-colored bile** <note>one of the four humors of the body, associated with heat and a yellow-orange color</note>. Similarly, this occurs in honey and gall, in which digesting heat has exerted a strong influence. 

If, therefore, the earthy part is very pure, and the watery part likewise, and the heat within them cannot separate them by burning <note>combustion</note>, but instead has ripened and altered their color into a brilliant yellow, this is the cause of the color of **gold**; for this reason, gold is not burned when sulfur is thrown upon it. 

If, however, the earthy part is impure and not well mixed, then the ripening and mixing heat burns it, and it becomes a yellow that after a short time declines into a sooty blackness, as is the case in **bronze** <note>original: *ære*; referring to copper or its alloys</note>. This is why all ancient bronze statues and vessels turn black; and if sulfur is thrown upon hot bronze, it burns very violently. This is because there is in it a burnt and combustible earthy substance, as we have said, which is not sufficiently mixed with moisture. 

So much, then, has been said concerning the colors of metals.

## On the tastes & colors of metals. Chapter 4.

It is necessary to determine the tastes of these metals together with their smells, because smell is a certain consequence of taste. In general, it is true of every metal that because of the **sulfurous substance** <note>In medieval alchemy, sulfur represented the principle of combustion and "oiliness" within a metal</note> it contains, its taste has a certain sharpness. Although this is hardly seen in **lead** and **tin**, it is nevertheless proven in them by the fact that water which runs for a long time or stands in lead or tin pipes becomes corrosive to the intestines or viscera <note>original: *excoriatiua*; this shows an early historical awareness of the health risks associated with lead plumbing</note>. 

Regarding **copper** <note>original: *æs*; can refer to copper, bronze, or brass, but in this chemical context usually denotes the base metal copper</note> and **gold**, there is no doubt, since they are hot—especially copper, which is of a "burnt" substance—as is **iron** to some extent. From this also, their smells possess a certain sharpness. Again, it is generally true that the tastes and smells of all metals are somewhat foul because of that same sulfurous substance we mentioned; however, the more foul they are, the less the harmfulness of the sulfur has been broken down within them. 

In **gold**, for instance, there is the least foulness, because its sulfur has no harmfulness at all, being **subtle** <note>original: *subtile*; meaning refined or composed of very fine particles</note> and possessing nothing but a compositional oiliness, and it is well mixed, as we shall show below. However, because of the uniformity of its composition and its density, it evaporates less, and therefore also smells less, or almost not at all. **Silver**, however, has an earthy part that is not indeed "burnt," but **combustible** <note>original: *adustibile*; capable of being scorched or oxidized by heat</note>; and therefore it is more vaporous and more fragrant than gold, but much less than copper and ha- <note>The text breaks off here; likely *habet* (has) or *hali-* (other metals)</note>

[...has.] **Silver**, in comparison to **copper** <note>original: *æs*; while this can mean bronze or brass, here it refers to the base metal copper</note>, has a sweet taste and a sweet smell, though it leans toward a slight sulfurousness. **Gold** has an even sweeter quality, but it changes taste so little that it is almost imperceptible to the senses. **Iron**, however, has an earthy quality mixed with a little sulfur. **Lead** and **tin** have very dull tastes and smells because of the great amount of "wateriness" <note>In the Aristotelian sense, "wateriness" refers to the liquid/flexible element within the metal's composition</note> that is in them.

This is because the constituents sometimes have entirely different tastes and smells than the final mixture itself; thus, in a way, the vapor and temperament of a metal can hardly be detected through its smell or taste alone. 

Among all metals, copper is the most "vaporous" <note>meaning it is the most prone to releasing particles or fumes</note>, followed by iron. Consequently, these metals strongly taint the flavor of waters that flow over their ores. This is why water emerging from earth rich in copper—such as in the place called **Goslar** <note>original: *Goslaria*; a town in Lower Saxony, Germany, famous for the Rammelsberg metal mines which operated for over a millennium</note>—is rendered so bitter that nothing can live in it at all; it is exceedingly bitter and loathsome. A proof of this is that if wine or any liquid other than water is poured into a copper vessel, it is immediately tainted with a foul bitterness so that it can hardly be drunk. Water, however, is not immediately tainted so much that its flavor changes, because of the natural coldness of water which suppresses evaporation. Yet, if water stands for a long time, and especially deep underground where heat is trapped and causes the ores to vaporize continuously, the water becomes tainted in both taste and smell. ### Chapter 5: On the combustibility and incombustibility of metals.

Among the qualities that happen to metals and which serve as great indicators of their substances are **combustibility** <term>cremabilitas; the capacity to be burned</term>—or "burnability"—and **incombustibility**. It is necessary to recognize the causes and differences of these within the natures of metals. We know that water, as such, is not among the things that can be burned; rather, it is those things that possess a highly **oily** <note>original: *unctuosam*; meaning fatty or resinous, referring to the "sulfur" principle</note> moisture mixed with an earthy substance. We know, moreover, that **sulfur** is highly oily and earthy. However, it has another moisture that is more watery...

...floating in the parts of a thing. The third type of humidity, however, is radically fixed and immersed within the parts, which defines its **constitution** <term>complexio; in medieval science, the specific balance of qualities—hot, cold, wet, dry—that makes a substance what it is</term>. Therefore, this constitutional humidity alone cannot be easily separated from the thing without destroying the substance entirely. This same principle must exist in the nature of sulfur. For this reason, the more expert **alchemists** <note>original: *alchimici*</note> advise that the first two types of humidity be removed from sulfur through "sharp" washes—such as vinegar, sour milk, goat whey, chickpea water, and the urine of young boys—as well as through boiling and multiple **sublimations** <term>sublimatio; the process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then collecting it as it cools back into a solid, used to purify substances</term> performed in an **alembic** <term>alembico; a specialized flask with a cooling neck used for distillation</term>. 

This is because one of those humidities undoubtedly cannot withstand heat; being combustible, it burns the very substance of the metal when ignited in the fire. Thus, it is not only useless for the task at hand but actually harmful. The second humidity is fleeting and evaporates in the fire, so it also contributes nothing to alchemical intentions. The third, however, remains radically inherent and intrinsic, and thus serves the purpose. 

One must consider **quicksilver** <term>argentum uiuum; mercury</term> in a similar way, as it is the second element of metals. When quicksilver is pure, well-washed of its earthy substance, and made refined and "subtle," it is held together strongly by its mixture with a watery humidity. When this watery humidity is neither excessive nor lacking, but is equal to the **constitution** of the earthy forces within it, then each part defends the other from the fire (as we have often said). For in that state, the earthy part holds the moist part and does not allow it to evaporate, while the moist part "extinguishes" the earthy part and prevents it from catching fire. However, if the earthy part is muddy, or if it is too abundant or too scarce compared to the humidity...

**Iron** <term>ferrum</term>, meanwhile, is scorched greatly until it turns red, because the earthy element predominates in it and catches fire.

### That the generation of metals into one another is circular.
### Chapter 6.

To these things must be added that it is common to all metals that their matter is very similar. We know from those things determined in the science of **generation and corruption** <note>original: "perigeneos"; likely a reference to Aristotle’s *De Generatione et Corruptione*, a foundational text for understanding how things come to be and decay</note> that among things having a common bond in their matter, virtues, and natural powers, **transmutation** <term>transmutatio; the changing of one substance into another</term> into one another is easy. 

Because of this, it is the assertion of many philosophers—whose father is **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>A legendary figure said to be the author of the *Hermetica*, often called the "prophet of philosophers" in medieval alchemy</note>, who is called the prophet of philosophers—that the generation of metals is circular, and that they arise from one another just as the generation of the **elements** <term>elementorum; the four classical elements: earth, water, air, and fire</term> is circular. This also seems most true to me. 

For since they do not differ in their basic matter—whether distant or near—it is clear from what was said before that their differences are determined by whether the parts of both types of matter are purified and **digested** <term>digestio; in medieval science, a process of maturation or slow heating that brings a substance to its ideal state</term>, or whether they remain unpurified and undigested. It happens, however, that every impure and undigested thing can be purified and digested, if the natural powers of digestion prevail...

BOOK III.

# ON THE FOURTH BOOK
## IN WHICH IT IS DETERMINED
->concerning metals specifically.<-

### Preface.

THE NATURAL ORDER NOW REQUIRES that we discuss metals in particular. This could not happen unless the principles of their nature and their **accidents** <term>accidentia; the non-essential properties of a substance, like color or smell, that can change without changing the substance itself</term> were first established; for scientific inquiry proceeds from general principles to specific elements, just as it is laid out in the beginning of the *Physics* <note>Referring to Aristotle’s *Physics*, which argues that we must learn general laws of nature before specific applications</note>. Therefore, in speaking of metals specifically, we will first touch upon those things which are, as it were, the universal components of metals—the "father" and "mother," as the authors of **alchemy** <term>alchimia; the medieval art and science of metallic transformation</term> say metaphorically. For **sulfur** <note>original: "sulphur"; viewed here as the active, masculine principle of minerals</note> is like the father, and **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury, viewed as the passive, feminine principle</note> is the mother. This is more appropriately expressed if sulfur is said to act in the mixture of metals like the substance of the father’s seed, and quicksilver like the **menstrual fluid** <note>original: "menstruum"; in medieval biological theory, the fetus was believed to be formed by the "seeding" or curdling of menstrual blood</note> which is coagulated into the substance of embryos.

Regarding the substance and **generation** <note>the process of coming into being</note> of sulfur, it should be noted that since it liquefies when exposed to dry heat and solidifies through cold, it must contain **watery elements** <note>original: "aquam"; refers to the element Water, which provides fluidity and the ability to melt</note>, based on the principles established in the book on *Meteorology* <note>Aristotle’s *Meteorologica*, the standard textbook on earth sciences in the Middle Ages</note>. Finally, because it can be ground down and refined, it must be of an **earthy substance**. It possesses all these substances so abundantly that they are expressly and evidently manifested in its actions and the ways it is affected. As we have said in earlier sections, it must have three types of moisture—two extrinsic and one intrinsic—and there is no need to repeat that here. 

But this must be observed: its smoke indicates the **earthy substance** within it, which is highly ignitable and combustible; and its stench indicates that this substance is very "undigested" and "undetermined" <term>digestion; in alchemy, the process by which heat matures or "cooks" a substance into its final, perfect form</term>. This **lack of a fixed complexion** <term>incomplexio; a state where the elemental qualities are not yet balanced into a stable, final form</term> is what allows it to be a "universal matter" for all elements. # BOOK IV.

...it is convertible into all things just as a woman <note>In medieval alchemy, the "female" principle refers to the passive, receptive matter that is shaped into various forms</note> and other things from which natural things are generated; and for this reason, wise nature abounds in sulfur wherever there is a place for the generation of metals. Since, moreover, it is hot, it will necessarily be "opening" and "limiting" to any moisture touching it. Because it is also dry, it will be sharp—for whatever is hot and dry is sharp—and therefore it possesses the powers of sealing and forming rather than receiving. For this reason, sulfur is identified as the seed of the father and the male by **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy; his name was frequently invoked to authorize natural philosophy theories</note>.

But it must be observed that a certain "hot-dry" quality can be joined to a "cold-moist" quality in the same temperament <term>complexio: the specific balance of the four primary qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that determines the nature of a living thing or mineral</term>. This temperament is **hermaphroditic**, as is seen in plants, which are both impregnated and do the impregnating in the same body. Sulfur, however, is not like this in its own substance. Because of this, it does not generate within its own substance, just as a father does not; but just as a male generates from his substance in another—that is, in the menstrual blood—so sulfur acts upon **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento uiuo"; mercury, which was viewed as the passive "mother" of all metals</note>, and it does not generate within itself at all. 

Its color is lemon-yellow <note>original: "citrinum"</note>, and sometimes whitish, having a straw-like whiteness—that is, like the whiteness of wheat straws. The cause of this color is heat, which "cooks down" <term>decoquens: a process of refining or maturing a substance through heat, similar to digestion</term> the moisture and converts it to a yellow color. Because of this, sulfur appears to be that which results in the "bowels of the earth." For when the earthy is mixed with the watery by a cooking heat—just as in the bodies of animals where food and the **chyme** <note>original: "chimus"; the semi-fluid mass of partly digested food</note> are mixed, and the foam boiling on the surface is converted to **yellow bile** <note>original: "coleram citrinam"; one of the four bodily humors, characterized as hot and dry</note>—so it seems that sulfur is like the foam of that which is mixed in the bowels of the earth. # BOOK III.

...for if it is sublimated <term>sublimatio: the process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then collecting it as it cools back into a solid form</term> by itself in a glass vessel prepared with a long neck, it always remains the same no matter how many times it is sublimated; it neither dries out further nor hardens, unless it has a vent <note>original: "respiraculum"; literally a "breathing hole" or vent to allow pressure to escape</note> through which it might flee. Quicksilver is, moreover, like the material substance of metals, just as the menses <note>original: "menstruum"; in medieval biology, the maternal fluid that provided the physical matter for an embryo</note> is to the embryo; from it, by the power of sulfur digesting it and "burning" <note>The text uses "adurentis" (burning) to describe the chemical reaction and maturation within the earth</note> it, metals are generated. When it begins to transform into a specific type of metal, it first becomes granular, and afterward it gradually begins to solidify and transform.

There are differences in quicksilver: some is extracted from its ore and found "live" <note>native mercury found in liquid form in nature</note>, and some is drawn from the stone in which it was generated by means of fire, just as silver or gold is extracted from stone. Because of this "sharpness" <note>original: "acumen"; referring to its chemically active or corrosive nature</note>, it is said to belong to the category of poisons. It is, moreover, cold and moist in the second degree <term>gradu secundo: a classification in Galenic medicine used to measure the intensity of a substance's primary qualities</term>; because of this, it "loosens the nerves," causing paralysis, and kills lice, nits, and similar things generated from the rot of the pores. 

Quicksilver, when sublimated with sulfur and sal ammoniac <term>sal armoniacum: ammonium chloride, a salt used as a flux in alchemy</term>, is converted into a shining red powder <note>This describes the creation of vermilion or cinnabar (mercury sulfide)</note>. When burned again in fire, it returns to a moist and flowing substance. Perhaps even that which is "suffocated" <note>original: "præfocatur"; meaning condensed or trapped by a lack of air</note> in the neck of the vessel in which the sublimation occurs—which is called an aludel <term>alutel: a pear-shaped pot or condenser used in the sublimation process</term>—and is converted into the likeness of a stone which is in color like alabaster, returns to quicksilver when it is later roasted in fire. There are also differences in quicksilver that are found more in metals than in simple quicksilver, such as yellowish, pure, and others which were enumerated above.

### ON METALLIC THINGS

->**DE REBUS METALLICIS**<-

And it is a marvelous thing about this matter that whenever it is sublimated <term>sublimatio: the process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then collecting it as it cools back into a solid form</term> by itself alone, no residue of powder ever remains in the bottom of the vessel; and when it returns to the appearance of quicksilver, almost no loss is found in its weight. This undoubtedly occurs because of the excessive mixing of its earthy part with its watery substance; for its viscous moisture so holds the earthy element that when it vaporizes, it carries everything with it into the neck of the alutel <term>alutel: a pear-shaped ceramic pot or series of pots used as a condenser in the sublimation process</term>. There, its spirit, being suppressed, returns to its original form; otherwise, it would be hardened at the bottom or changed in color, weight, taste, or smell. 

Yet it is "fleeing" <note>original: "fugiens"; a common alchemical term for a volatile substance that evaporates or escapes when heated</note> in the fire and "incorporating" whenever it is mixed with metals, which is why it is called a "spirit" by Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure and purported author of the Hermetic Corpus, often cited as the founder of alchemy</note>, just as sulfur is. Moreover, Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, the influential Persian physician and philosopher whose works on minerals were foundational to medieval European science</note> says that its whiteness comes from its wateriness and a subtle earthiness cooked with air, which is trapped in a spiritual state within the mixture. 

All these things have been said so that it might be understood that quicksilver is nothing but the material substance within metals. Without doubt, it is "mortified" <term>mortificatio: the "killing" or alteration of a metal's primary characteristics, such as turning liquid mercury into a solid or powder</term> by "sharp waters" <note>original: "aquas acutas"; referring to corrosive mineral acids or caustic solutions used to dissolve or react with metals</note> and by both nature and art. After it has been mortified, it can be mixed with "bodies" <note>In alchemical texts, "bodies" (corpora) refers to the solid metals, such as gold, silver, or lead</note> and colors them; however, by the power and vapor of sulfur, it is congealed and brought to the hardness of the form of various metals. Because it is absorbed beyond measure and retained by what is dry and earthy, it does not flee from the bodies with which it is mixed when in the fire. These things, therefore, are what have been said concerning quicksilver.

BOOK IV.

## On the nature of lead.

### Chapter 2.

In the same manner, we define lead, which adds less to the material of quicksilver <term>argentum uiuum: literally "living silver," the medieval term for mercury</term> than all other metals. Because of this, Aristotle <note>The Greek philosopher whose works on meteorology and minerals formed the basis of medieval science</note> and Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, the Persian polymath whose theories on the "sulfur-mercury" composition of metals were central to alchemy</note> also say that when lead flows in a molten state, it undoubtedly appears to be quicksilver. Regarding the composition of lead’s substance, then, it is certainly believed that its quicksilver is plentiful in proportion to its sulfur; perhaps sulfur enters into the composition of lead’s substance only slightly, but it influences it greatly through its "quality" <note>In medieval science, "quality" refers to the primary characteristics of heat, cold, moisture, or dryness that dictate a substance's behavior</note>. Therefore, the sulfur cooks the mercury with its heat and converts it into the form of lead, just as a small amount of rennet <term>coagulum: a substance used to curdle milk into cheese</term> curdles a large amount of milk. 

However, the quicksilver found in lead is not of good quality; it is watery and muddy. For this reason, its wateriness evaporates easily when exposed to fire, and there remains an earthy powder like ash, which is left behind from the "muddy" substance of the lead. And because the power of sulfur is present in lead, as we have mentioned, its vapor dries out the quicksilver just as the vapor of sulfur does. It cannot be that two different substances produce the exact same effect in the same way unless there is some single shared element within them. We have already explained in the preceding sections why lead has such a dark, dull color. 

In terms of its medicinal effect, lead is cold and constricting. It possesses a specific power against sexual desire and against nocturnal emissions <note>original: "pollutiones nocturnas"; a common medieval medical concern believed to be caused by excess heat in the body</note>, especially if a plate <note>original: "circulus"; likely referring to a lead plate or waistband worn against the skin</note> is made from it with a width of...

Now Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational alchemical and philosophical texts were attributed</note>, who demonstrated much concerning the transmutations of metals in his alchemical works, recorded that if sheets of lead are suspended over a vessel containing a large amount of strong vinegar so that the vapor of the vinegar continually touches those sheets, that vapor will break down and corrupt the substance of the lead and convert it into a powder, which has a white color and is called ceruse <term>cerusa: white lead, a pigment and medicinal base produced by the corrosion of lead</term>. 

If, however, vinegar is poured directly onto the sheet itself, it turns very white, and in turn destroys the strength of the vinegar. The certain cause of this is that although vinegar is dull in its substance due to its coldness, it is nevertheless sharp in its action. This is because it contains the remnants of a certain fire that has flown out from it, just as ash is the remnant of fire in wood. That sharpness, therefore, penetrates into the substance of the lead when the lead has been worn down, and it washes away the impurities from the frozen quicksilver <term>argentum uiuum: literally "living silver," the medieval term for mercury</term> which is contained within it. It causes this mercury to rise to the surface of the sheet like grains of millet, and then they turn white because of their greater purification.

...the fire might be more distinct and stronger. If, however, that substance is calcined <term>calcinetur: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to powder</term> with vinegar and dried, the white color of ceruse <term>cerusa: white lead pigment</term> returns. The cause of this transmutation is that it truly contains Sulfur and quicksilver <term>argentum uiuum: literally "living silver," the traditional name for mercury</term>, as we have already said, in the composition of its substance. 

When Sulfur is burned and intensified <note>original: "algetur", perhaps a transcription error for "augetur" (increased) or related to the heat of the process</note>, it turns red. The sign of this is that those who make minium <note>original: "nimium", likely an OCR error for "minium" (red lead), a common pigment made by roasting lead</note> produce it from a sublimate of Sulfur and quicksilver. The color is dark, however, because of the "muddiness" of the lead. When the fire is made stronger, that initial muddiness is consumed and the color brightens. Because Sulfur is burned away more than quicksilver is during a longer exposure to fire, the redness—which arises from the burnt earthy Sulfur—is diminished and is tempered by the whiteness <term>albedo: the quality of being white, often a specific stage in alchemical work</term> of the remaining quicksilver. Then, a citrine <term>citrinus: a lemon-yellow color</term> color results, which is like a white that penetrates into red and tempers its redness. 

Nevertheless, as Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> believes, if a fire stronger than all these is applied and these materials are roasted forcefully in the fire, the entire substance of the Sulfur is consumed and the power of the vinegar is destroyed through evaporation. Then, from the aforementioned powders, the substance of lead will return just as it was before; however, it will not be of the same weight, nor the same purity, nor the same quantity as it was originally.

It must not be overlooked that, as we have said, lead has a great deal of "wateriness" and a weak mixture of components. Therefore, in the process of purifying other metals, it protects them from the fire; for example, silver and gold are protected by lead when they are being prepared <note>A reference to cupellation, where lead is used to separate precious metals from base metals by absorbing impurities</note>. For this reason, certain unskilled men have said of lead that it has the property to "gather like things and separate unlike things" <note>original: "congregare homogenea & ſeparare etherogenea", an Aristotelian principle of how heat and certain substances act on matter</note>.

And the cause of their error is this: because when lead is melted with silver or gold, the silver runs together to one place, and any small stones <note>original: "lapilli", referring to impurities or non-metallic dross</note> that may be present run to another, and the lead likewise runs to its own place. Nor does lead purify silver through its own power, but by accident <term>per accidens: an indirect or secondary cause, rather than the primary agent</term>. For the heat of the fire purifies by its own power by gathering the pure with the pure and separating out the impure, as has been said. But since silver is "moist" and fire is "dry," the heat of the fire would recoil from the silver unless it were united to it by something else; and this something is lead. Once heated in its own moisture, the lead "digests" <term>digerit: an alchemical term for refining or maturing a substance through heat, similar to digestion</term> and purifies the silver as if by boiling it <note>original: "elixando", literally to boil or seethe</note>. A great weight of lead, however, consists of its own earthy <note>original: "lutea", literally 'muddy' or 'clay-like'</note> and moist substance, the parts of which are very close together—even if they are soft—because they have suffered from a lack of "digestion" or refinement due to their softness, as was determined above.

# BOOK IV.
->T iij<-

It contains little sulfur, or rather, it is refined into a metallic form by the power of sulfur and vapor, rather than by the mixture of much sulfurous substance. It possesses a very **stuttering** <note>original: "balbutientem". This is a famous historical description of the "cry of tin," the crackling sound produced when a bar of tin is bent, which medieval scholars likened to a stuttering voice.</note> composition, and the cause of this can be the **killing** <term>mortificatio: in alchemy, the process of "fixing" or changing a liquid metal (like mercury) into a solid state, often perceived as "killing" its fluid life</term> of the **mercury** <note>original: "argenti vivi", literally 'living silver'</note> by some vapor, or a dissolution, or some other washing by **sharp water** <note>original: "aquæ acutæ", referring to corrosive acids or mineral waters used to treat metals</note>, which separates a part of it. Now, I speak of vapors or water not as something through which the mercury has merely passed after it has already taken the form of mercury, but rather those things which enter into the very substance of the mercury itself. For such an aqueous substance is already broken within itself and possesses little viscosity; it causes the earthy parts mixed with it to become rigid, and prevents them from being well-mixed or continuous. For a substance that is rigid and hardened on its surface does not mix well with another, and cannot be easily joined to what is placed near it. This, therefore, must be considered the cause of its "stuttering" mixture.

Since it "stutters" in itself, it causes all metals with which it is mixed to stutter as well, and it takes away their **ductility** <term>ductibilitas: the ability of a metal to be hammered thin or drawn into wire without breaking</term>, as **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational alchemical and philosophical texts were attributed</note> says; and when it is drawn out, it is quickly and easily split. This metal agrees with **lead** in this respect: that neither contracts **rust** <note>original: "rubiginem", referring generally to oxidation or corrosion</note>, but instead they contract a certain foulness and filth from corrupting influences and from their own nature—though lead does so more than tin. They also agree in this: that neither is very resonant <note>original: "sonorum", referring to the "ring" or sound a metal makes when struck</note> on its own. After this, we shall speak of **silver** <term>argentum</term>, because in its color it appears to agree somewhat with the aforementioned metals. Indeed, from the "color" of sulfur it derives its **fermentation** and **digestion** into the form of a metal; and though it contains little of the actual substance of sulfur—which is why the sulfur does not color the silver itself—it receives much of its power and quality from sulfur. 

This is because the heat of the sulfur has consumed the two types of moisture we mentioned, and the third humor is perfectly mixed with a refined, earthy element. For the heat and vapor of sulfur—especially sulfur that has been well-cleansed and **sublimated** <term>sublimati: a process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then purified as it cools back into a solid</term>—whitens most effectively and refines through digestion. **Tutty** <term>tuthia: zinc oxide sublimated from smelting furnaces</term> will be discussed in the following book where we deal with "intermediates" <note>substances classified as between metals and stones</note>, but what suffices for our purpose here is that by the "burning" of **Tutty**, the earthiness is consumed and the superfluous moisture of the **copper** <term>aes</term> is purged. **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic founder of alchemy</note> also says—and experience agrees with him—that if copper is sprinkled with salt and placed over vinegar or the urine of a virgin male boy, the power of the urine or vinegar will penetrate the substance of the copper and convert it into a **greenness** <note>original: "virorem," referring to verdigris</note>. If, however, **orpiment** <term>auripigmentum: arsenic trisulfide</term> or **arsenic** is brought near this color—especially if it has been "burnt" <note>calcined or oxidized</note>—it decisively destroys the greenness and induces a dark, earthy color declining toward opacity. The cause of this is easily shown from what has been said: for salt is **opening** <term>sal aperitivum</term>, and therefore it opens the substance of the copper, especially if it has been beaten into thin sheets. Then, the sharp vapor of the vinegar or urine "ignites" it. This, however, comes from an excess of ignited sulfur, because of which the light, attached earthy moisture (which is ignited within it) takes on a green color—just like the hottest and most harmful **bile** <term>cholera</term> which physicians say is like the **rust of copper** <term>erugo aeris: verdigris</term>.

### On the nature and mixing of gold.
### Chapter 6.

We must now add a discussion on the nature of **gold**. According to **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note>, gold is the only metal in which no "sickness" <note>original: "aegritudo," meaning impurities or chemical instability</note> appears, for neither part of its matter is imperfect or out of balance. Although gold, like other metals, is composed of **sulfur** and **quicksilver** <term>argentum uiuum: mercury</term>, its sulfur is exceptionally bright and pure. It has been refined to purity through the most rigorous washings so that it contains no combustible oiliness at all, nor any phlegmatic, watery moisture that might evaporate. 

It is perhaps formed in hollow places with solid surfaces, where it is frequently **sublimated** <note>turned into vapor and resolidified to purify</note> and matured by a temperate heat through the process of digestion called **maturation** <term>pepansis: a Greek medical and alchemical term for the ripening of substances through gentle heat</term>. Its earthy substance, which is incorporated into the sulfur, is clean and extremely subtle, suspended like a vapor throughout the entire substance of that sulfur's **radical moisture** <term>humidum radicale: the fundamental, life-sustaining fluid of a substance</term>. *The purity of its material ensures that it is very rarely found mixed with other bodies, but almost always as if pure; for when it is mixed with others, it cannot retain such great purity, and thus it degenerates into **bronze** <term>æs: a general term for copper or its alloys like bronze or brass</term>; on the contrary, [silver] is very rarely found except incorporated in stones <note>original: "lapidibus incorporatum"; refers to silver ore being bound in rocky matrices compared to gold's "alluvial" or pure state</note>. The substances that purify gold are sharp and very dry, such as salts, and especially **sea salts**, the **soot** of oily but dry bodies, and **crushed brick**. When gold must be purified, a clay vessel is made in the shape of a **gourd** <note>original: "cucurbitæ"; a common shape for alchemical flasks</note> or a small dish, and another similar vessel is placed over it and glued at the points of contact with a tenacious mud, which the alchemists call the **clay of wisdom** <term>lutum sapientiæ: a specialized, airtight sealant made of clay, hair, and other binders used to prevent vapors from escaping</term>. In the upper part, however, many holes are made through which vapor and smoke may escape; afterwards, the gold is thinned into short, thin plates and arranged in the vessel so that every layer of plates has above and below it a powder of soot, salt, and crushed brick mixed together, and it is cooked in a strong fire until it is most pure, and the ignoble substances within it are consumed.

This they call the **Red of the Sun** <note>original: "rubeum solis"; the Sun is the traditional alchemical symbol for gold</note>. For **silver**, however, they strive to have an elixir with the coloring of whiteness, and one that is penetrative, does not evaporate in the fire, and possesses **subtlety**.

### Chapter 7: On the composition of iron

Finally, we must speak of iron, for this metal is more "ignoble" <note>original: "ignobilius"; meaning more base or less pure in the alchemical hierarchy of metals</note> than the other liquefiable metals. It does not melt easily like wax, but rather it is "softenable" through heat. Its composition consists of an earthy quicksilver <term>argentum vivum; mercury, which was believed to be a primary component of all metals</term> that is heavy, muddy, and very impure, combined with an impure, earthy sulfur. The power of this sulfur converts the quicksilver into the form of iron. 

Consequently, iron is very rough and contracts rust easily due to the "burning" <term>adustio; a chemical process in alchemy where impurities are scorched out</term> of the sulfur. It leaves a soot-like mark on what it touches. It is possible that the earthy substance of its sulfur is vitriolic <term>atramentosa; having the properties of "atramentum," a term for black vitriol or ink-making substances</term>, which is why iron filings are used to give blackness to ink. Furthermore, it is not cleansed of oily moisture, and therefore it burns easily. 

A sign of this is that when certain fats, such as tallow or pitch, are applied to it, they "open" the metal. If tin is then poured over it, the tin enters into the very substance of the iron; once this happens, the iron becomes so brittle that it can no longer be forged. The burning of its earthy substance is proven by the large amount of slag <term>scoria; the stony waste matter separated from metals during smelting</term> that is separated from it, and especially by the fact that it is frequently found as grains in the earth. 

According to this, it is clear why iron does not liquefy like other metals but only softens; the cause of this is its "earthiness." Therefore, Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure to whom many foundational alchemical texts were attributed</note> elegantly states that the cause of slow melting in iron is the excessive earthiness of its parts, which prevents it from flowing, but nevertheless...

It is refined and purified by a great fire, especially when sprinkled with sand and sulfur. It is therefore harder and more compact because of the power of the fire and because of the refinement of its parts, which are made harder when they are burned.

It is, moreover, whiter because of its greater separation from "earthiness" <note>original: "terrestritate"; referring to the stony impurities or slag found in ore</note>, and when it is hardened too much, it then splits and shatters when struck because of its excessive dryness. There is, however, a difference in the power of various waters to "dry" <note>referring to the tempering or quenching process</note> to a greater or lesser degree; for this reason, blacksmiths specifically seek out certain waters in which to **quench** <note>original: "extinguant"</note> the iron from which they fashion swords. 

For when the metal is plunged into the water, it is hardened because the heat—fleeing the coldness of the water into the interior parts of the iron—burns up the **material moisture** <note>original: "materiale humidum"; according to the science of the time, metals were composed of "moist" and "dry" principles which determined their malleability</note> within it. Through this consumption of moisture, the metal is made harder and harder. 

Let this, therefore, be enough of what has been said concerning iron and the other metals, both in particular and in general.

# BOOK FIVE
### ON INTERMEDIATE MINERALS
### and on everything that pertains to intermediates.

->Preface.<-

It remains in this fifth book of minerals to investigate the natures of those things that seem to be intermediate <note>substances that fall between the categories of stone and metal, such as minerals that can be melted but are not malleable</note> between the natures of stones and metals. For although **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian polymath whose "Book of the Healing" contained a highly influential classification of minerals</note> in his fourth book divides mineral bodies into stones, fusible substances, sulfurs, and salts, it seems to us that **sulfur** is more of a mineral in its own right than **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum uiuum"; mercury</note> is, for it [sulfur] enters into the composition of the matter and the one into the other.

Therefore, speaking of these intermediates, let us speak first in general about the nature of intermediates, and afterward, we will briefly touch upon some of them specifically in a summary; in this way, we shall fulfill our intention for this book. Everything, then, that in some way shares the **properties** <note>original: "passionem"; here referring to the physical "affections" or ways a substance reacts to environmental forces</note> of stones and in some way shares the properties of metals, we call an "intermediate." For it is a property of stone not to be **liquefied** <note>original: "liquefieri"; to melt or become fluid</note>, while the property of metal (which it derives from its material) is to be liquefied by dry heat. For this reason, stones belong to the category of "moist" things and water. <note>In the scientific tradition of this period, stones were believed to be formed from a watery, mineralizing vapor that had been "congealed" or solidified.</note>

Intermediates, therefore, are those which are in some respect made of "earth" and in some respect made of "water." Some of these, which are found deep within the earth, consist of heat and dryness; others, however, are closer to water, and from those di- <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword "di" suggests the next page begins with a word such as "diversis" (various) or "distinguuntur" (are distinguished).</note>

# ON METALLIC MATTERS

It [the steel] is whiter because it has been further separated from earthy impurities; however, when it is hardened too much, it becomes brittle, splitting or shattering into pieces when struck due to its excessive drying <note>original: "desiccationem"; in medieval alchemy, flexibility was linked to "moisture," so hardening a metal was seen as a process of removing that moisture</note>. 

Different types of water vary in their ability to dry [the metal] to a greater or lesser degree; for this reason, blacksmiths <term>fabri</term> <note>skilled metalworkers or craftsmen</note> seek out specific sources of water in which to quench the iron used for making swords. When the metal is plunged into water, it hardens because the heat, fleeing the coldness of the water, retreats to the center of the iron. There, it burns up the "material moisture" <note>Aristotelian science taught that metals were composed of a balance of moisture and earth; the "fleeing heat" was thought to consume the internal moisture, leaving the metal harder but more prone to breaking</note> within, and through this consumption of moisture, the metal becomes harder and harder. 

This concludes our discussion of iron, as well as our general and specific observations on all other metals.

# ON THE FIFTH BOOK CONCERNING INTERMEDIATE MINERALS
### and concerning everything that pertains to intermediate substances.

->Preface.<-

IT REMAINS IN THIS FIFTH BOOK to investigate the natures of minerals that *seem to be intermediates between the natures of stones and metals*. For although Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the influential Persian philosopher whose "Book of Minerals" was a standard reference in the Middle Ages</note> in his fourth book divides mineral bodies into stones, liquefiable substances, sulfurs, *and salts*, it nevertheless seems to us that sulfur is more a mineral in its own right than quicksilver <term>argentum uiuum</term> <note>literally "living silver"; mercury</note>, for it enters into the composition of matter and one is transformed into the other. 

Therefore, speaking of intermediates, let us first speak in general about the natures of intermediate substances, *and afterwards we shall briefly touch upon some of them in particular; in this way, we shall fulfill our intention for this book*. 

Therefore, everything that shares in some way the qualities <note>original: "passionem," referring to the physical properties or "suffering" of an external influence</note> of stones *and in some way shares the qualities of metal, we call an "intermediate." For it is the property of stone not to be melted <term>liquefieri</term>, and the property of metal (which it derives from its material) is to be melted by dry heat; thus, stones belong to the category of moist things and water*. <note>In Aristotelian science, stones and metals were thought to originate from different types of "exhalations": a dry, smoky one (earth) and a moist, vaporous one (water). Stones were surprisingly categorized as "moist" because they were thought to be frozen or solidified liquids.</note>

Furthermore, intermediate substances are also those that melt by dry heat but afterwards, through cold and even through fire, begin to solidify after being refined <note>original: "elixata," literally "boiled" or "cooked," referring to the process of purification by heat</note>. For they would not melt unless they were in some way watery, nor would they solidify through refining unless they were in some way earthy, as is gathered from the teachings of the *Meteorology* <note>Aristotle’s "Meteorologica," particularly Book IV, which deals with the properties of materials and how they are affected by heat and cold</note>. 

Moreover, intermediates are all those things composed of the substances of both stones and metals, even if they do not melt under dry heat. In this way, all types of slag <term>scoriae</term> <note>the stony waste matter separated from metals during the smelting of ore</note> are intermediates, which are released from the mines along with the stony parts. Marcasite <term>marchasita</term> <note>in the Middle Ages, this term usually referred to iron pyrites or "fool's gold"</note> is also an intermediate of this kind; it does not melt in fire like a stone, yet its color and weight indicate that its nature is metallic. 

Additionally, all substances that are crumbly in their substance and whose "waters" are highly consolidating and restrictive <note>original: "restrictiuæ," meaning astringent or binding</note> possess the matter of intermediates, as is the case with all alum <term>alumen</term>. Every kind of vitriol <term>atramentorum</term> <note>literally "inks," referring to mineral sulfates used to make black pigment and ink</note> also appears to be intermediate, because something stony is found within their substances. 

The cause of these intermediates is a "vaporous mixing" of the material of stone and of metals (or liquefiable materials). For they are mixed with much sulfur and a moisture <note>original: "humor"</note> possessing something of the nature of quicksilver <term>argenti uiui</term> <note>literally "living silver"; mercury</note>. From humors, vapors, and other materials mixed in such a way, it is fitting for certain things intermediate between the two to be produced by nature. For wise and diligent nature, which provides a fitness for all matter, does not pass from one extreme to the other—as Aristotle says—unless it completes every intermediate stage. ### BOOK IV

Therefore, many intermediate substances exist between stones that cannot be melted and metals that can, so that in all things there is a display of harmony and that "desire for the good" which everything possesses. This occurs through every possible state of matter so that it may reach its completion <note>The author uses Aristotelian teleology here, suggesting matter "strives" toward a more perfect or complete state—in this context, the perfection of gold or a stable metallic form</note>. 

The nature of these intermediates is particularly noteworthy for the **transmutation of metals** <term>transmutatio metallorum</term>, because much of the knowledge of those who strive to convert one thing into another lies within them. For intermediates are, in a sense, the raw materials <term>materia</term>. We have already shown above that anyone who improperly intends to convert one metal into another must first reduce that metal to its "first nature" <term>natura prima</term>, which is the state closest to the metallic category. 

Then, its natural potential is assisted by the powers of substances that easily prepare its nature, and it takes on the true "form" <term>species metalli</term> of the intended metal. Furthermore, the principles of physics established in the *Physics* <note>original: "physico auditu," referring to Aristotle's *Physica*, a foundational text for medieval natural science</note> demonstrate that movement from one extreme to another is impossible except through an intermediate stage. 

It is characteristic of all metals that they seem to be incomplete in their specific form, and are therefore capable of being converted into any other metal. For an intermediate substance, properly speaking, has a formless nature, whereas the "extremes" <term>extrema</term> (the starting and ending materials) maintain a distinct, formed nature, as is taught in the science of sensory things. In an intermediate <term>media</term>, the extremes are present in a way, though their forms are blended or "confused." Because of this, the extremes can be extracted from intermediates through human skill and natural processes when the power of one extreme is brought to bear upon the other.

->Thus, let this be what is said concerning intermediates in general; for it is not necessary to say more, as the knowledge of intermediate substances is understood through their extremes.<-

DE REBVS METALLICIS.

### On the Nature of Salt, its Types, and Varieties.
### Chapter 1.

One of the intermediates, and the first among them, is salt. We already know about salt in a general sense from the science of *Meteorology* <note>original: "Metheo.," referring to Aristotle’s *Meteorologia*, a foundational text for medieval science regarding the formation of minerals from "earthy smoke" and "watery vapor"</note>: it is formed from a thick earthy substance and is "burnt" <note>In this context, "burnt" refers to the process of evaporation or the concentration of minerals through heat</note> after it has been mixed with water. For this reason, all salt begins to dissolve in cold water and in cold, moist air. Salt is categorized into many divisions. There is **sea salt**, which is solidified from salt water; and there is **rock salt** <term>sal gemma</term>, which is transparent like crystal and is found most abundantly in Hungary. Its composition is a mixture of earth, and because of this, it is easily scraped into a powder. However, it is not made of earth alone; rather, it possesses a watery substance frozen by the cold of the earth and by its binding together. From this watery nature, it gains its transparency; likewise, it is because of this nature that it melts in heat and moisture, and water distills from it while its earthy part remains.

There is also a salt called **black naphthic salt** <term>sal napticum</term>, named for the naphtha <note>A naturally occurring flammable liquid or bitumen</note> that is within it. But when it is smoked with heat, the naphtha melts and is separated from it, and then it becomes white. There is also **black root salt** <term>sal radicum</term>, which is naturally black due to the heavy burning of the earth within it. Furthermore, there is **sal ammoniac** <term>sal armoniacum</term>, which is clearer and approaches transparency. Perhaps other varieties of salt may be found in different lands, since sea salt has one character in the "Great Sea" <note>The Mediterranean Sea</note> which touches **Italy**, and another in the **Ocean** to the north which touches **Flanders** and **Germany**.

<summary>This page identifies salt as the primary 'intermediate' substance between stones and metals, categorizing various types like rock salt, sea salt, and sal ammoniac based on their geographic origins and physical properties.</summary>
<keywords>salt, sal gemma, rock salt, sea salt, sal ammoniac, Hungary, naphtha, mineralogy, Aristotle, Meteorology</keywords>

### BOOK V.

For that which is in the great sea <note>likely referring to the Mediterranean</note>, in the ebb of the tide in places where it flows back or is diverted into pits, in those places where the sun’s heat remains at the bottom, it is turned into salt. This salt consists of large grains, like snow rolled into hailstones. However, that which is boiled from the northern Ocean <note>original: "mari Oceano aquilonari," likely the North Sea or Baltic</note> is made from the earthy sediment of the seafloor and the marine soil. There are also salt springs in various parts of Germany <note>original: "Theutonia"</note> from whose waters a good salt is boiled; this is of a small quantity and is powdery, almost like flour. Salt is also cooked from human urine, and especially that of boys, through the alchemical operations of sublimation and distillation.

In whatever way salt is made, it is generally of a single nature. It is composed of an earthy substance that was a moist mixture of burnt material. Because it was mixed with moisture, the burnt part is white; and the more it is burnt through boiling <term>elixation</term> <note>the process of boiling or decocting a substance in a liquid</note> or roasting <term>assation</term> <note>the process of heating or parching a substance without additional liquid</note>, the whiter and more bitter it becomes. Indeed, a salty flavor is mixed with bitterness, as will be determined in the science of the senses <note>original: "scientia de sensibilibus," referring to Aristotle’s *De Sensu et Sensibili*, which explores how flavors are composed</note>. Because of its earthiness, all salt is found to be astringent <term>styptic</term>; and because of its dryness, it is itself drying and prevents rot by binding substances together. Due to the combination of heat and dryness, it is cleansing <term>abstersive</term>, and because it has a sharp, penetrating flavor, it seasons food. Crystalline salt <term>cristallinus</term> is specifically effective at consuming thick vapors, but any salt that is hotter will dissolve frozen humors within mixed bodies; and indeed, every salt possesses this quality to a greater or lesser degree. Similarly, because of its dryness and the irregularity of its pores—the irregularity of which—

### On the nature & substance of atraments <term>atramentum</term> <note>originally meaning "blacking," this term was used by medieval mineralogists to describe a group of metallic sulfates, including vitriol, used for making ink and dyes</note> Chap. 2.

The nature of atrament, according to its kind, is a mineral substance of uniform parts <term>homeomerous</term> <note>original: "omiomera," a term from Aristotelian physics meaning a substance that is the same throughout, like gold or water, rather than made of distinct organs like a plant or animal</note>. It is dissolvable through a decoction made in water mixed with stony substance, though the stone itself is never dissolved by boiling <term>elixation</term>. Without a doubt, the liquid form is the primary kind of atrament, from which the solid form was later coagulated by its own nature. Conversely, every atrament, according to its kind, has a rancid, astringent <term>styptic</term>, and strongly burning taste; for this reason, it induces a hard crust <note>original: "cratiam duram," likely referring to the cauterizing or astringent effect on skin</note> when applied to bodies.

It exists, moreover, in many species. There is a white kind which the Arabs call *al Kadidis* <note>likely white vitriol or zinc sulfate</note>; a red kind which they call *assuriae* <note>likely "sory," a weathered or roasted iron sulfate</note>; a yellow kind which they call *al Kosol* <note>likely "chalcitis" or "colcothar," a yellow-brown iron oxide/sulfate</note>; a green kind which they name *al Kacautum* <note>likely "shoemaker's black" or green vitriol (iron sulfate)</note>; and a dark kind declining toward blackness which has taken on some stoniness.

The green kind, which is called *vitriol* <term>vitreolum</term> <note>literally "glassy-like," referring to its crystalline appearance</note> by some and is used for a certain kind of ink <term>incaustum</term>, is more strongly coagulated than the yellow kind and has thicker layers. The most effective among the dark kinds of atrament is that which shows a certain golden splendor—as if golden powder scattered within it were shining through obscurely. It is clear that all atraments are composed of earth and water, and primarily...

### On the nature & genus of alums <term>alumen</term> <note>Alums are a group of double sulfate salts, historically vital for fixing dyes to cloth and in tanning leather</note>. Chap. 3.

Alum is of an earthy composition; specifically, it consists of an earth that is coarse and solidified with moisture. It falls short of the perfection of quicksilver <term>argentum vivum</term> <note>mercury; in medieval alchemy, mercury and sulfur were considered the primary "parents" of all metals and minerals</note> and yet it approaches it in some way. It seems to be solidified by a certain force which is not exactly that of sulfur, but has some affinity with the sulfur present. It is, therefore, more frequently white in color; when it has been roasted <note>original: "optesi," likely referring to the process of calcination or heating</note>, a certain water distills from it, almost like from rock salt <term>salgemma</term> <note>pure crystalline sodium chloride</note>.

There are three species of alum that occur most frequently and are of the greatest utility. The first is long and very fissile <term>scissile</term> <note>easily split into layers</note>; in its cracks it appears feathery <note>likely "plume alum," often a form of asbestos or fibrous sulfate minerals</note> and has a color similar to silver. The second is that which is dry and round like a soft stone; in its silver-like luster and whiteness it differs very little from the previous kind, but it is not as effective as the first one mentioned. Some call this "round" alum. The third, however, is dry as if...

### On the manner and nature of Arsenic.
### Chap. 4.

It remains for us to conclude our discussion of Arsenic for the time being. We say, therefore, that because it is composed of a fine <term>subtle</term> matter and is similar to sulfur, it should not be defined differently than sulfur. However, it differs from sulfur in this regard: arsenic is easily a tincture for whiteness <note>referring to the alchemical stage of *albedo*, or the whitening of a metal to resemble silver</note> but only with great difficulty for redness <note>the *rubedo* stage, associated with the creation of gold</note>; sulfur, on the other hand, easily produces redness but only with great difficulty whiteness.

There are two types of both sulfur and arsenic: yellow <note>likely orpiment, a yellow arsenic sulfide</note> and red <note>likely realgar, a red arsenic sulfide</note>. These are useful to the art of Alchemy, whereas the many other varieties are not. Arsenic is fixed <note>made non-volatile so it does not evaporate when heated</note> just like sulfur.

The sublimation <note>the process of heating a substance to a vapor so it can be purified upon cooling</note> of both is better when performed from the calxes <term>calcibus</term> <note>the powdery metallic oxides or residues left after intense heating</note> of metals. However, sulfur and arsenic are not the actual materials that bring the alchemical work to its final perfection, as some have mistakenly thought. They are not complete enough for that perfection, though they can provide support for perfection in certain cases. When selecting arsenic, one should choose that which is bright, scaly, and fissile.

## On the nature and manner of marcasite and Magnesia. Chap. 5.

We have sufficiently determined the nature and essence of vitriols <note>original: "atramentorum," literally "inky substances," usually referring to metal sulfates like green vitriol</note>, alums, and arsenic; now we shall proceed to the nature of marcasite and magnesia itself. We say, therefore, that marcasite <note>a historical term for iron pyrites or other metallic-looking minerals often mistaken for ores of silver or gold</note> possesses a dual substance in its creation: namely, "mortified" quicksilver <term>argentum uiuum</term> <note>meaning mercury that has been processed or stripped of its fluid, "living" state</note>—which is nearing a state of fixation <note>becoming resistant to heat</note>—and burning sulfur. We have found through clear experience that it possesses a sulfurous quality. For when it is sublimated <note>heated until it turns to vapor and then collected as a solid</note>, a clear, burning sulfurous substance emanates from it. Even without sublimation, its sulfurous nature is similarly weighed and considered; for if it is placed in a fire, it does not catch light until it is ignited and burned by the flame of its own sulfur.

Indeed, it is perceptibly shown to contain the substance of quicksilver. For it grants the whiteness of pure silver to Venus <note>the alchemical name for copper</note>, just as quicksilver itself does. We also see that it provides a "celestial" color during its sublimation and possesses a clear metallic luster. These things make the practitioner <term>artificem</term> of Alchemy certain that marcasite contains these substances in its very root.

As for Magnesia <note>in this period, this often referred to manganese ore or magnetite rather than the modern element magnesium</note>, you will be able to prove clearly through the same experiments that it contains a more clouded sulfur and a more earthy and drossy <term>fœculentum</term> quicksilver. Its sulfur is likewise more "fixed" and less flammable, and it expresses more of the nature of Mars <note>the alchemical name for iron</note>.

### On the nature of nitre. Chap. 6.

Nitre is so named either from the island of Nitria, where it was first discovered, or it is called *Baurach* <note>original: "Baurach", an Arabic term historically used for borax, saltpeter, or various alkaline salts</note> by the Arabs. It belongs to the category of salts, being darker than rock salt <term>Salgẽma</term> <note>halite or common stone salt</note>, yet it is translucent and consists of thin layers. It can be roasted in fire, and once its superfluous watery substance is lost, it becomes drier and more "burnt," at which point the salt itself becomes sharper <note>meaning more chemically reactive or caustic</note>. Its varieties are distinguished according to the places where they originate.

Among us, it is found in three varieties: namely, Armenian, African, and Teutonic <note>German</note>. The Teutonic variety is found in abundance in the place called Goslar <note>a famous mining town in the Harz Mountains of Germany</note>. When rain falls upon the mountain, which is full of copper ore, and the rainwater filters through the mountain for a hundred paces into a pit made by miners, the water is seen to be converted into nitre. Although the inhabitants believe it to be rock salt, I have proven by sight and touch that it is nitre. It stands in the hollows of the mountain in the same way and shape as ice forms on roofs when water drips from a roof during freezing cold; and this variety is not flaky, but rounded <note>describing stalactite-like formations of minerals</note>.

The comparison of African nitre to other species of nitre is like the comparison of nitre to common salt <note>suggesting African nitre is the most potent or "purest" expression of the substance</note>. The "foam" of all nitre, which is sometimes called the "flower of nitre" <term>flos nitri</term> <note>efflorescence, or the powdery crust that forms on the surface of the mineral</note>, is of a more subtle substance and power than the nitre itself; that foam which resembles the color of marble and is very brittle is considered the best. All nitre is hot and dry, and therefore its operations are such that it is incisive <note>original: "incisiuum", a medical term meaning able to cut through or break up thick humors</note>, cleansing, excoriating <note>skin-stripping</note>, and corrosive—especially the African variety, which is sharper than the others.

<summary>This page describes the origins, classification, and physical properties of nitre, identifying three regional varieties and providing an eyewitness account of its formation in the mines of Goslar.</summary>
<keywords>nitre, saltpeter, Baurach, Goslar, copper ore, flos nitri, medieval mineralogy, salt varieties</keywords>

## On the nature of tutty. Chapter 7.

Tutty <term>tuthia</term> <note>original: "tuthia"; a substance produced from the soot and fumes in copper-smelting furnaces, primarily composed of zinc oxide</note>, which is frequently used in the transmutation of metals, is an artificial rather than a natural mixture. Tutty is formed from the smoke that rises to the upper parts of the furnace and hardens by adhering to solid bodies during the process where copper is purified from the stones and tin <note>original: "stanno", which in this context may refer to impurities or lead-like contaminants rather than pure modern tin</note> contained within it. The best kind of this substance is that which is sublimated <note>vaporized and then solidified</note> from the ore; that which remains at the bottom during such sublimation is called *climia* <term>climia</term> <note>cadmia or furnace calamine</note>, which some call *succudus*. There are many varieties of tutty: it can be white, or lemon-yellow leaning toward red. When tutty is washed, a certain black sediment remains at the bottom like dregs; this is sometimes called "Indian tutty" by some. The difference between *succudus* and tutty is as we have stated: namely, that tutty is sublimated, while *succudus* is what remains unsublimated at the bottom of the furnace channel. The volatile white variety is the best, followed by the lemon-yellow, and then the red; for the fresher material is more effective than the old. Furthermore, all tutty is cold and dry <note>referring to the Galenic qualities of the substance in medieval science</note>, and that which has been washed is more effective for these operations.

## On the nature and properties of electrum. Chapter 8.

Many of the ancients placed electrum <term>electrum</term> <note>a natural or artificial alloy of gold and silver</note> not among the intermediate substances, but among the metals themselves. The Arabs call it *tinchar* <note>original: "tinchar"; while often meaning borax, here it refers to an alloy or soldering agent</note>, while others have called it the "bridle of gold" <note>original: "capistrum auri"</note>. It possesses a color that is a mixture of gold and silver.

<summary>This page describes the production of tutty (zinc oxide) as a furnace byproduct used in metallurgy and introduces electrum as a gold-silver alloy known to the ancients and Arabs.</summary>
<keywords>tutty, zinc oxide, copper smelting, climia, electrum, tinchar, metallurgy, sublimation, alchemy</keywords>

->### ON METALLIC MATTERS.<-

and therefore there are also two kinds of this metal: one is artificial, which is made from silver and nitre <note>original: "nitro"; in this context, likely natron or soda rather than modern saltpeter</note> mixed together; the other, however, is mineral and natural. The ancients said this natural variety was better than any other metal—I know not why, unless because they attributed this effect to it: that a vessel made from such electrum <term>electrum</term> <note>a naturally occurring or artificial alloy of gold and silver</note> emits a hissing sound when poison is placed in the drink within the vessel, just as nitre hisses when vinegar is poured over it. Since it has a color that is a mixture of silver and gold, it undoubtedly possesses the property and nature of both. Therefore, let this be what is said concerning homogeneous mixtures that are neither complexioned <note>referring to the "complexio" or balance of humors found in living beings</note> nor animate, according to this manner of classification. For from what has been said, all things that have not been named here can easily be understood.

### and on metallic matters.

The Book of Minerals by Albertus Magnus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280) was a Dominican friar and one of the most influential medieval philosophers, known for integrating Aristotelian science with Christian thought.</note> contains five individual books.

->They are sold in Venice at the shop of Giovanni Battista <note>Giovanni Battista Pederzano (active c. 1520–1550) was a major Venetian publisher and bookseller known for his distinctive "Tower" shop sign.</note><-
->under the sign of the Tower. <note>original: "sub insignio Turris"; before street numbers existed, businesses were identified by pictorial signs hanging above their doors.</note><-

There is a shift in both author and printing location from the previous entry.</meta>

# RAYMUND 
## LULL, THE MOST LEARNED
### AND MOST CELEBRATED
*philosopher’s book, which is titled the Codicil <term>Codicil</term> <note>original: "Codicillus"; literally a "little book," this term often refers to a supplement or a concise summary of a larger body of work.</note>, or the Hand-book <term>Hand-book</term> <note>original: "vade mecum"; a Latin phrase meaning "go with me," used to describe a portable manual or guide intended to be carried by the reader for constant reference.</note>, in which the sources of the Alchemical art and of more hidden philosophy are handed down, never before printed until now.*

<image-desc>An oval printer's mark depicting a hen standing in front of a tree. A ribbon or scroll at the bottom of the oval contains the name "ARNOLD BIRCKMAN".</image-desc>

->COLONNE <note>original: "Coloniae"; the Latin name for Cologne, Germany, which was a major European center for printing and the book trade during the 16th century.</note><-
->At the house of the Heirs of Arnold Birckman <note>The Birckmans were a prominent family of booksellers and publishers with branches in Cologne, Antwerp, and London; the "Heirs" continued the business after Arnold's death.</note>,<-
->In the Year 1563.<-
->With the Privilege of His Imperial Majesty for ten years <note>A "privilege" was an early form of copyright protection granted by the Holy Roman Emperor, which legally prohibited other printers from copying or selling the book for a set period (in this case, ten years).</note>.<-

<summary>This is the title page for the first printed edition of "Codicillus," an alchemical treatise attributed to Raymund Lull. It establishes the book as a guide to "hidden philosophy" and identifies the prominent Birckman family of Cologne as the publishers.</summary>
